calendars-tasks-5.territory: The person is a parent running air-traffic control at 7:15am, juggling three kids, two work schedules, and the eternal question of who drives whom. The interface answers with daylight order: a clean white grid where every family member is a color and one glance resolves the whole afternoon. It should feel like the kitchen wall calendar finally learned to answer back.

palette.note: Chrome stays white and quiet so the five family colors (teal, orange, purple, green, yellow) carry all the meaning; the blue accent is reserved for today and confirmations.

calendars-tasks-5.typography: Inter with tabular figures for times and a slightly rounded weight for names and chips; the type stays administrative and calm while the color does the emotional work.
calendars-tasks-5.motif: Member lanes: every view is built from five thin parallel color lanes, one per person, so 'who is where' reads like a train timetable even before you read a single word.

calendars-tasks-6.territory: A second-year law student at 11pm, syllabus PDFs everywhere, feels the semester as one undifferentiated dread. The interface answers like a well-ruled ledger: every deadline already attached to a class meeting, crunch weeks visible from September, dread converted into a plan she can argue with.

palette.note: Ink blue carries all structure, and a single highlighter-yellow (#FFD43B) wash is reserved for crunch weeks on the load map, exactly like a marker dragged across paper.

calendars-tasks-6.typography: Tiempos Headline gives course names lecture-hall gravity while Inter with tabular numerals runs the schedule underneath, like a serif syllabus over a sans timetable.
calendars-tasks-6.motif: The crunch ridge: the semester rendered as a 15-week skyline where each week's stacked deadlines form a bar, and heavy weeks rise like a ridge you can see coming from a month away.

calendars-tasks-7.territory: A nail tech between clients, checking her phone with one clean hand, tired of chasing reference photos through DMs and eating the cost of no-shows. The interface answers with the orderly confidence of a well-run studio: gallery-white space, a strict day grid, and everything about an appointment living on one beautiful card. It should feel like her work — precise, aesthetic, professional — not like a point-of-sale terminal.

palette.note: Gallery white and near-black editorial ink; the deep lacquer crimson is used sparingly, like a single painted nail — deposit-paid badges, the current time line, and the confirm action.

calendars-tasks-7.typography: Reckless Neue for client-facing headlines and service names, Neue Montreal for the working UI; the serif gives the booking page a salon-card elegance while the grotesk keeps the stylist's day grid strictly legible.
calendars-tasks-7.motif: The clipped reference: every appointment card carries the client's inspiration photo clipped to its top corner at a slight angle, like a swatch pinned to a work order.

calendars-tasks-8.territory: A rep in a parked car with the engine running, eleven stops left, deciding what happens at the next door in the next ninety seconds. The interface answers like a printed manifest: numbers big, order settled, one thumb, full sun on the screen. Confidence here is knowing what you're walking in to say.

palette.note: Near-print black on white for sunlight legibility; safety orange marks exactly one thing, the current stop, and never decorates.

calendars-tasks-8.motif: The bead thread: the day is a vertical thread of numbered stop beads you can pinch and re-pin, with the locked first and last beads wearing visible pins.

car-maintenance-1.territory: The person is six hours into a night shift, eyes on the road, phone mounted on the dash, and their one recurring dread is finding out at 2 AM that nothing was recording. The interface answers like a dashboard instrument built for exactly that: dark so it never glares, one huge rolling counter, and a recording light you can read at arm's length at highway speed. Everything else waits until the engine is off.

palette.note: Safety orange means one thing, recording state, blazing steady when miles are being written and switching to a pulsing warning the second they are not.

car-maintenance-1.typography: DIN Next, the typeface of highway signage, with heavy tabular numerals for the odometer, so miles read like an instrument cluster, not an app.
car-maintenance-1.motif: The odometer drum: shift miles roll on mechanical-style digit wheels, and every screen that touches money or deductions reuses the same drum digits, tying the whole product back to the counter that earns them.

ia.coreObject: The shift, one open-to-close recording session holding its GPS trail, mile total, and platform comparison
ia.primaryLoop: The driver opens a shift at first ping and drives all night trusting the lock screen counter, then closes the day by checking the tracker's total against what Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash reported.

screens.title: First launch: the deal on tracking
screens.purpose: The empty state that earns location permission by stating the boundary before iOS asks.
screens.hero: A dark card with a dormant odometer at 000.0 and the line 'Recording runs only inside a shift you open.'
screens.data: 'No shift, no tracking. Points are written to this phone, not to a cloud you have to trust.' Button: 'Set up my first shift'. Small print: 'You can verify: close a shift and the location icon goes away.'

screens.title: Onboarding 1 of 2: your platforms
screens.purpose: Pick the apps the end-of-day comparison will be checked against.
screens.hero: Three large toggle plates styled like dash switches.
screens.data: Uber: on. Lyft: on. DoorDash: on. Others field: 'Instacart, Grubhub'. Line: 'At day's end you will enter each platform's reported miles once, we do the cross-check.'

screens.title: Onboarding 2 of 2: work hours and auto-start
screens.purpose: Set the window where the app watches for driving so a forgotten Start never costs a shift again.
screens.hero: A time-band dial from 5 PM to 2 AM with the auto-start toggle beneath.
screens.data: Work hours: 5:00 PM to 2:00 AM, Thu to Sun. Auto-start: on, 'if the car moves during work hours, the shift opens itself'. iOS location prompt appears here with 'Allow While Using plus Always explained in one line'.

screens.title: Mid-shift: the counter
screens.purpose: The main screen while driving, readable from the mount in the dark without focusing.
screens.hero: The odometer drum at 87.4 mi in huge digits with the steady orange RECORDING lamp above it.
screens.data: RECORDING, solid orange dot. 87.4 mi, shift time 4:12:33, opened 5:04 PM. Last GPS point 3 s ago. One giant End Shift button, nothing else on screen.

screens.title: Lock screen counter
screens.purpose: The Live Activity that answers 'is it still recording' at every red light without unlocking.
screens.hero: A lock screen strip with the mini drum and the orange recording dot.
screens.data: 87.4 mi, recording, 4:12 elapsed. Dynamic Island compact: orange dot plus 87.4. If recording stops, the strip itself flips to the warning state, no notification needed to notice.

screens.title: Recording dropped
screens.purpose: The alert state the whole product is built around: silence broken within seconds, not discovered at 2 AM.
screens.hero: The lamp switched to a pulsing hollow ring, 'Recording paused 28 seconds ago', over a one-thumb resume button.
screens.data: Cause line: 'iOS suspended background location.' Resume button full-width. Reassurance: '87.4 mi already on this phone and safe. Gap will be marked in the log: 11:37 to 11:38 PM, est. 0.4 mi.'

screens.title: The restart that didn't lose the night
screens.purpose: The recovery state after a dead battery or reboot, proving the on-device promise.
screens.hero: A stitched trail map fragment with the seam marked, headline 'Phone restarted at 11:18 PM. The shift survived.'
screens.data: '142 GPS points were already written to the device. Recording resumed 11:21 PM.' Shift total intact: 121.8 mi. Marked gap: 3 min, est. 1.1 mi, listed honestly in the log.

screens.title: Auto-start caught it
screens.purpose: The moment the forgotten Start button stops mattering.
screens.hero: A notification-style card: 'Looks like you started driving at 5:04 PM. Shift opened for you.'
screens.data: 'First movement detected on I-35 frontage road during work hours.' Buttons: 'Correct, keep recording' and 'Not working, discard'. Note: 'Discarded auto-starts delete their points immediately.'

screens.title: End of day: the cross-check
screens.purpose: The earning moment, tracker total against what the platforms admitted, gap in plain miles and dollars.
screens.hero: A side-by-side board of drum digits: tracker 212.6 mi versus platforms 179.5 mi, the 33.1 mi gap highlighted in orange.
screens.data: You enter: Uber 118.3 mi, Lyft 61.2 mi. Tracker logged 212.6 mi over 8:41. Gap: 33.1 mi of dead miles between rides, at the 2026 IRS rate of $0.70 that is $23.17 of deduction the platforms would not have shown you. Button: 'Close shift and file it'.

screens.title: Mileage log export
screens.purpose: The IRS-ready output that the whole year of shifts adds up to.
screens.hero: A date-range picker over a ledger preview with the year's deduction in drum digits.
screens.data: Jan 1 to Mar 5: 4,218.7 mi across 47 shifts, deduction so far $2,953.09. Columns: date, start, end, miles, platforms, gaps disclosed. Formats: CSV, PDF. Line: 'Log and export stay available on any paid plan, always.'

screens.title: Paywall, shift number four
screens.purpose: Ask after three free shifts proved the counter, priced against what one lost shift costs.
screens.hero: A dark sheet with a single drum showing 212.6 and the line 'Your last shift was worth $148.82 in deductions.'
screens.data: $5.99 a month or $50 a year. Free: 3 full shifts, all features. Factual line: 'MileIQ and Everlance run $100 to $140 a year.' No trial that silently converts, the free shifts just end. Restore purchases at the bottom.

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Work hours, platforms, and the privacy boundary, adjustable in under a minute at a gas stop.
screens.hero: A grouped dark list opening with the work-hours band.
screens.data: Work hours: 5 PM to 2 AM, Thu to Sun. Auto-start: on. Platforms: Uber, Lyft, DoorDash. Units: miles. IRS rate: $0.70 per mile, editable per year. Data: 'GPS points on this device, cloud backup off by default'. Delete a shift: allowed, logged as deleted.

car-maintenance-2.territory: The person logging an oil change is doing quiet diligence today for a negotiation that happens in four years, and they want the app to feel like the well-kept service book a fastidious owner keeps in the glovebox. The interface answers with drafting-table competence: ruled lines, exact odometer figures, and the standing promise that every entry is already part of the document they will hand over with the keys.

palette.note: Blueprint blue is the working ink for odometer figures, due-dates, and the export action, laid on tool-steel white; cost totals stay in plain black because money is data here, not drama.

car-maintenance-2.typography: IBM Plex Mono carries every odometer reading, date, and dollar figure with tabular exactness; Suisse Int'l does the labels and headings, giving the whole log the tone of a well-drawn workshop manual.
car-maintenance-2.motif: The stamped line: every service entry renders as a ruled ledger line that receives a small blueprint-blue date stamp when saved, so a full history looks like a factory service book filled in by someone who never missed a page.

ia.coreObject: The service entry (date, odometer, work done, cost, receipt photo), accumulating into a vehicle's sale-ready file
ia.primaryLoop: Log each service with its receipt in under a minute, and return whenever a mileage reminder fires, because every entry visibly thickens the file that will earn hundreds back at resale.

car-maintenance-3.territory: A self-employed realtor spends the year half-trusting that the app is catching her drives, and every January she braces for an evening of stitching monthly exports for the accountant. The interface answers with ledger-book competence: green-tinted paper calm, a dollar odometer that rolls upward with every classified trip, and a January that is one tap instead of one evening. Garage practicality applied to paperwork.

palette.note: Accountant's ledger paper with fine rule lines, where the currency green is spent only on deduction dollars and confirmed business trips, so green literally equals money kept.

car-maintenance-3.typography: Libre Franklin, the Franklin Gothic lineage of federal forms, for all labels, with dollar amounts and mileage set in large tabular figures so $6,306.04 reads like a stamped total, not a suggestion.
car-maintenance-3.motif: The dollar odometer: the year-to-date deduction is always shown as odometer-style rolling digit wheels that physically tick upward when a trip is classified as business, converting miles into visible money.

ia.coreObject: The trip (route, miles, date, category) that compounds into an annual deduction and its January report
ia.primaryLoop: Drive as usual, spend one minute a day swiping trips into business or personal, and watch the deduction odometer climb toward a January report that is already finished.

car-maintenance-4.territory: The check engine light just came on and the driver's stomach dropped: is this a $200 sensor or a $2,000 catalytic converter, and can I still drive to work. The interface answers like a trusted machinist reading a printout: steel-calm, mechanically precise, translating the code into a decision and handing over a benchmark to walk into the shop with.

palette.note: Interface chrome stays steel-neutral, safety orange marks actions, and green, amber, red exist only inside the severity gauge so the verdict owns all the color.

car-maintenance-4.typography: IBM Plex Sans speaks in the flat voice of a shop manual, IBM Plex Mono sets every trouble code, odometer figure and dollar range so the numbers read like a printout.
car-maintenance-4.motif: The bezel chip: every trouble code sits in a machined, screw-cornered mono chip like a stamped plate on an engine block, and that chip is the unit that travels through diagnosis, history and shop mode.

ia.coreObject: A scan: one ECU read tied to a code, a verdict, a cost benchmark and an odometer stamp
ia.primaryLoop: When the light comes on, plug in the $20 adapter, scan, get the drive-or-stop verdict and cost range, then reopen the history at the shop counter to check the quote.

screens.title: Plug in the adapter
screens.purpose: Onboarding step one: pair any ELM327 Bluetooth adapter, hardware-agnostic on principle.
screens.hero: A line diagram of the OBD2 port under the dash with the adapter half-seated
screens.data: Steps: '1. Find the port under the steering column. 2. Seat the adapter. 3. Turn ignition to ON, engine can stay off.' Detected list: 'ELM327 v1.5 (OBDII)'. Note: 'Any $15 to $25 ELM327 adapter works. We do not sell hardware.'

screens.title: Which car is this
screens.purpose: Onboarding step two: describe the car in plain fields, deliberately no VIN gate so older cars get in.
screens.hero: A short spec form with the odometer field styled as a mono counter
screens.data: Fields: 'Year: 2014, Make: Honda, Model: Accord, Engine: 2.4L'. Odometer: '91,412 mi'. Footnote: 'No VIN needed. OBD2 codes are a standard, your 1998 pickup is welcome too.'

screens.title: No codes yet
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state that doubles as the healthy-car reading.
screens.hero: An empty bezel chip with a dashed outline waiting for its first code
screens.data: Header: 'No scans yet.' Adapter status: 'ELM327 connected, ignition ON detected.' Button: 'Scan now'. Sub: 'A scan takes about 15 seconds and reads stored and pending codes.'

screens.title: Talking to the ECU
screens.purpose: The scan-in-progress state, kept technical and literal instead of a spinner.
screens.hero: A terminal-like readout printing protocol lines in mono
screens.data: 'Protocol: ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/500)... connected. Reading stored DTCs... 1 found. Reading pending DTCs... 0. Freeze frame captured at 91,412 mi.' Progress: 'about 6 seconds left'.

screens.title: P0420, in English
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the code translated into what happened and what to ask the mechanic.
screens.hero: The P0420 bezel chip on top, plain-language diagnosis beneath
screens.data: Chip: 'P0420'. Title: 'Catalyst efficiency below threshold, Bank 1.' Plain read: 'Your catalytic converter is cleaning exhaust less effectively than the ECU expects. Often it is actually a tired oxygen sensor, not the converter.' Ask the mechanic: 'Was the downstream O2 sensor tested before quoting a converter?'

screens.title: Can I keep driving
screens.purpose: The severity verdict, the single decision the driver came for.
screens.hero: A three-position gauge rendered like an instrument bezel, needle resting on amber
screens.data: Verdict: 'Amber: get it looked at within 1 to 2 weeks.' Detail: 'Safe to drive short-term. Expect slightly worse fuel economy. Ignore it for months and a failing converter can clog and strand you.' Legend: green 'safe to drive', amber 'this week or two', red 'pull over now'.

screens.title: What this costs to fix
screens.purpose: The benchmark mechanic: a typical repair range in hand before seeing the shop's quote.
screens.hero: A cost range bar with two labeled scenarios plotted on it
screens.data: 'If it is the O2 sensor: $180 to $320 parts and labor. If it is the converter: $950 to $2,400 for a 2014 Accord (aftermarket vs OEM).' Note: 'Ranges from national repair-cost data, updated March 2026. Your region and shop rates vary.'

screens.title: Shop mode
screens.purpose: One screen designed to be shown across the counter, turning the file into leverage.
screens.hero: A high-contrast summary card, type enlarged for arm's-length reading
screens.data: '2014 Honda Accord, 91,412 mi. P0420, first seen Mar 14 at 87,230 mi, recurred twice after clearing. Freeze frame attached. Benchmark: O2 sensor $180 to $320, converter $950 to $2,400.' Button: 'Compare against their quote'.

screens.title: Scan history
screens.purpose: The longitudinal file: when each code first appeared, at what mileage, and when it was cleared.
screens.hero: A vertical timeline of bezel chips stamped with dates and odometer readings
screens.data: 'Jun 2, 91,412 mi: P0420 stored.' 'Apr 20, 89,655 mi: P0420 cleared by user.' 'Mar 14, 87,230 mi: P0420 first seen.' 'Jan 8, 85,010 mi: no codes, clean scan.' Filter: 'This car'.

screens.title: Clear codes?
screens.purpose: A confirmation that explains the real consequence of erasing, protecting the user from hiding evidence they need.
screens.hero: A full-width warning card in shop-manual deadpan, no red panic
screens.data: Copy: 'Clearing erases the code and freeze frame from the ECU and resets emissions monitors. If your state inspection is soon, monitors will read Not Ready for up to 100 miles. Your scan history in this app stays.' Buttons: 'Clear codes' and 'Keep them'.

Optional: 'Repair-cost data refresh, $19.99 per year, entirely optional.' Links: 'Restore purchase', 'Terms'. Note: 'No subscription required. Codes do not expire, neither does your purchase.'

car-maintenance-5.territory: The user is at a gas pump with one hand on the nozzle, mildly suspicious that the car is drinking more than it should. The interface answers with machinist calm: a paper logbook with engineering-grade math behind it, where every number is traceable and nothing you fix breaks anything else. It should feel like a well-kept service binder, not a dashboard of gamified charts.

palette.note: Cream graph paper background with white log cards, safety orange reserved strictly for anomalies and the record button, so when orange appears you know the math noticed something.

car-maintenance-5.typography: IBM Plex Mono for every number, odometer style with tabular figures, paired with Söhne for labels, so the log reads like a calibrated instrument, not a lifestyle app.
car-maintenance-5.motif: The interval bracket: every stretch between two full tanks is drawn as a machined bracket on a horizontal rail, solid when complete, dashed when a fill-up is missing or partial, and repairs to the log visibly touch only the two brackets on either side.

ia.coreObject: The fill-up interval (two full-tank entries and the miles, gallons, and tags between them)
ia.primaryLoop: At every pump the owner enters three fields in fifteen seconds, and the MPG trend line quietly compares the new interval against the seasonal baseline, calling them back only when the car starts telling on itself.

screens.hero: A toggle row (mi/km, gal/L) above a small worked example of one interval calculation.
screens.data: Miles plus US gallons selected. Example: 412.6 mi ÷ 14.2 gal = 29.1 MPG. Caption: Mixed units in one history is fine, we store raw numbers and convert on display.

car-maintenance-6.territory: This person walks their driveway like a small harbor master: truck, motorcycle, boat, generator, mower, each with a different idea of what wear even means, and the anxiety is quiet but constant, what did I forget to service. The interface answers like a well-kept barn ledger: warm khaki paper, stenciled tags on every machine, and one list that says exactly what the property needs this week.

palette.note: Barn red is spent only on overdue and due-now work, everything serviced and healthy rests in ink on khaki so a calm screen means a caught-up property.

car-maintenance-6.typography: Bitter's slab weight sets equipment names and counters like stenciled crate lettering, Inter runs the task lists underneath without ceremony.
car-maintenance-6.motif: The brass tag: every machine wears a riveted equipment tag showing its own counter unit, mi, hrs or a calendar month, the way real gear gets tagged in a working shop.

car-maintenance-7.territory: A driver at a fuel island or a roadside inspection, tired, gloves off for two minutes, needing the log to look exactly like the paper form they have filled for twenty years, with zero math to do in their head. The interface answers with workshop competence: the familiar federal grid, ink-on-form clarity, and totals that are simply already correct.

palette.note: Manila-folder ground and navy form ink keep everything document-calm; safety orange appears only where hours are at risk, an approaching 14-hour window or a missed 30-minute break.

car-maintenance-7.typography: Public Sans in its narrow government-form weights for labels and the grid, with IBM Plex Mono for every hour total, so the page reads like an official document filled by a machine that never miscounts.
car-maintenance-7.motif: The duty line: the driver's own finger-drawn stepped line across the 24-hour grid, rendered like fresh ballpoint ink, the one living element on an otherwise printed form.

couples-relationship-1.territory: It is after dinner or just before sleep, phones down to a whisper, and two people want a reason to talk about something other than logistics. The interface answers like good stationery: unhurried, private, slightly literary, a letter exchanged across the pillow. Nothing gamified, nothing pink, no audience but the two of them.

couples-relationship-1.motif: The sealed fold: your partner's answer arrives as a folded sheet that physically unfolds only after you have written yours, so honesty is built into the paper itself.

couples-relationship-5.territory: Two people are circling a conversation they have been avoiding for weeks, stomachs tight, each rehearsing grievances and bracing for the other's. The interface answers with the stillness of a good mediator's office: even-handed, slow on purpose, giving each person visible equal ground so neither feels ambushed. Nothing celebrates, nothing gamifies, the design's only job is to keep the temperature down.

palette.note: Quiet pine belongs to the guide alone; each partner gets a muted personal tone (amber #D08B3C and slate #5B7A99) that only ever marks whose turn it is, never who is right.

couples-relationship-5.typography: Tiempos Text gives the guide's questions and reframes the measured warmth of a counselor's voice, while Inter keeps timers, turns and buttons administratively neutral so the interface never sounds like a third opinion.
couples-relationship-5.motif: The turn token: a small tactile disc resting on the hairline that divides every shared screen into two equal halves, physically sliding across to the partner whose turn it is to speak.

ia.coreObject: The conversation, one hard topic packaged as private preparation, a guided shared session and a written outcome
ia.primaryLoop: A couple picks the conversation they keep postponing, each answers alone, then they sit down together while the app deals turns and reframes, and they return when the summary says 'to revisit' or the next topic surfaces.

couples-relationship-7.territory: It is late, the door is shut, and two people who already paid for two disappointing apps are half-braced to be bored or pushed past a line again. The interface answers like low candlelight and a well-written page: unhurried, frank about being for adults, and absolutely certain of where each person's edges are before a single card is dealt.

palette.note: Candle amber warms only what is touchable and breathes slowly on the active card, nothing in this interface ever flashes.

crypto-investing-2.territory: This person has read the horror stories, a wallet drained overnight through an approval signed a year ago, and they are quietly unsure whether they are the next story. The interface answers like a harbor radar room: dark, unhurried, zero hype, sweeping the water and reporting exactly what is out there. Confidence comes from specificity, contract names, dates and gas costs, never from reassurance.

palette.note: Muted harbor teal means verified and safe, a dry amber marks risk, and nothing on screen glows neon because a radar room does not celebrate.

crypto-investing-2.typography: Inter Display holds the headings quiet and technical, JetBrains Mono sets every address, contract and amount so the address is always the most legible thing on screen.
crypto-investing-2.motif: The sonar ring: every audit renders your address at the center of a slow radial sweep, with approvals plotted on the ring by age and risk, like contacts on a harbor radar.

ia.coreObject: An audited address: a public address with its live map of approvals, balance traps and history anomalies
ia.primaryLoop: Run an audit after any new dapp interaction, revoke what the sweep flags, and let the weekly patrol watch the address in between so silence means safety.

screens.title: Paste an address, that's all
screens.purpose: Onboarding step one: establish the zero-trust entry point, a public address and nothing else.
screens.hero: A single mono input field with the no-keys statement set as large as the field itself
screens.data: Field placeholder: '0x… or ENS name'. Statement: 'We never ask for a seed phrase or private key. Not at signup, not at revoke, not ever.' Pasted: 'vault-main.eth resolves to 0x7c3A…9fE2'. Button: 'Sweep this address'.

screens.title: What we read, what we never keep
screens.purpose: Onboarding step two: an explicit data contract before the first scan, because this audience trusts disclosures, not promises.
screens.hero: A two-column manifest, read versus stored, with the stored column nearly empty
screens.data: We read: 'Active approvals, token balances, transfer history, all public on-chain.' We store: 'Nothing server-side, unless you turn on Patrol, then only the address itself.' Networks: 'Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon.' Button: 'Understood, sweep'.

screens.title: Sweeping
screens.purpose: The scan state: the sonar motif doing literal work while findings accumulate.
screens.hero: The address at the center of the radar, a sweep arm revealing contacts as it passes
screens.data: 'Sweeping 0x7c3A…9fE2 on 4 networks. Found: 14 active approvals, 47 tokens, 1,204 transfers checked.' Ticker: 'Checking contracts against 3 scam-address databases and known-protocol registry…'

screens.title: The risk map
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the full picture in one glance, the flagged few separated from the known many.
screens.hero: The completed sonar ring, 3 amber contacts near the rim, 11 teal contacts resting inner
screens.data: Summary: '14 active approvals. 3 need your attention.' Flagged list: 'Unlimited USDC to 0x91bb…44d1, unknown contract, granted 384 days ago', 'Unlimited WETH to 0x3d0a…c2e7, matches 2 scam-database reports', 'Stale: OpenSea legacy contract, 2022'. Known: 'Uniswap V3 Router, Aave V3, verified protocols.'

screens.title: Sign it where your keys live
screens.purpose: The revoke handoff: the transaction leaves for the user's own wallet, making the custody boundary a visible moment.
screens.hero: A handoff card showing the prepared transaction crossing to a wallet icon via WalletConnect
screens.data: 'Revoke prepared: set USDC allowance for 0x91bb…44d1 to zero. Review it in your wallet, we never see your keys.' Status: 'Waiting for signature… Confirmed, block 20,914,382. Gas paid: $1.79.' Ring update: 'Contact removed, 2 flags remain.'

screens.title: The coin that won't sell
screens.purpose: Honeypot detection: traps sitting in the balance identified before the user tries to exit through them.
screens.hero: A token row turned inside out, its transfer mechanics exposed like an x-ray
screens.data: 'ZKDROP, 15,000 tokens, airdropped 3 weeks ago. Verdict: honeypot, sell function reverts for all holders, 100% transfer tax in contract. Value shown on trackers: $612. Realizable value: $0.' Advice: 'Do not interact, interacting can trigger approval prompts. Hide from balance view.'

screens.purpose: Poisoning detection: lookalike addresses seeded into transfer history to bait a fatal copy-paste.
screens.hero: Two mono addresses stacked with the two differing characters highlighted amber
screens.data: Yours: '0x7c3A…9fE2'. Impostor in your history: '0x7c3A…9eF2, sent you $0.00 USDT on May 12, a poisoning attempt.' Warning: 'Never copy addresses from history. 2 more zero-value contacts flagged.' Action: 'Mark all as poisoned, they will be flagged everywhere in the app.'

crypto-investing-3.territory: The person opens this app the way they open a bank statement they half-dread: years of trades scattered across exchanges, and a nagging suspicion they don't actually know if they're up. The interface answers with the calm of a good accountant closing the books — no tickers flashing, no candles, just reconciled numbers that hold still. Confidence here means the number stops moving when you look at it.

palette.note: A graphite ledger where the analyst blue marks only reconciled, drill-downable figures; gains render in a muted #57A773 and losses in #C25B4E on numerals only, never as background washes or glows.

crypto-investing-3.typography: Söhne for labels and Söhne Mono for every figure — all money is set in tabular mono so columns align like a printed ledger, and headings stay small and quiet because the numbers are the voice.
crypto-investing-3.motif: The reconciliation stitch: wherever two of your own accounts touch, the two transaction lines visibly braid into one with a fine cross-hatch seam, so a merged transfer literally looks sewn together rather than sold.

ia.coreObject: The position — one asset with its true average cost basis assembled from every exchange and wallet
ia.primaryLoop: Glance at net P&L after the morning coffee, tap into whichever position moved, and trust that transfers, fees and gas are already folded in — the return visit is the honest bottom line no exchange shows.

crypto-investing-4.territory: A portfolio holder going to bed with a position open: not greedy, just unwilling to be the last to know. The moment of use is setup and verification, calm hours spent buying certainty for the loud ones. The interface answers like a night-shift control room: graphite quiet, no tickers screaming, every promise stamped with a delivery receipt.

palette.note: Flat graphite with zero gradients; duty-amber marks armed rules and confirmations only, and a restrained red appears in exactly one place, a delivery that failed, which is the one thing this product exists to prevent.

crypto-investing-4.typography: JetBrains Mono renders every price, threshold, and timestamp with fixed-width accountability, while Neue Haas Grotesk keeps labels terse and unexcited, the voice of an operator log rather than a trading floor.
crypto-investing-4.motif: The double stamp: every fired alert carries a two-line punch-clock stamp, event time over delivery time, the visual contract that the watchdog was awake and on time.

ia.coreObject: The rule: a server-side condition with an escalation path and a delivery log
ia.primaryLoop: Arm rules on prices and the portfolio, sleep or work while the server watches, confirm the rare alert that fires, and check the delivery log to see the watchdog earning its keep.

crypto-investing-5.territory: It is 11 p.m., a trader has open positions on three exchanges, and the one on the phone is the one without a stop. The interface answers not with hype but with the flat, procedural confidence of a cockpit checklist: every position visible, every exit order placed, every dollar of downside counted. The feeling is of finally being covered.

palette.note: Matte instrument black with zero gradients; amber marks everything risk-related (rails, total exposure, warnings) while muted green and red are reserved strictly for realized direction, never for decoration.

crypto-investing-5.typography: IBM Plex Mono for all prices, sizes and dollar risk so figures align into scannable columns, with Suisse Int'l for labels; nothing italic, nothing glowing.
crypto-investing-5.motif: The risk rail: every position anywhere in the app carries its two horizontal amber-edged rails (stop below, target above) with grab handles, the same physical object on the chart, in lists, and in confirmations.

ia.coreObject: The protected position: an exchange position plus its linked stop-loss and take-profit rails
ia.primaryLoop: Open the unified positions screen, scan total dollar risk, drag any rail that the market has outgrown, and leave; the trader returns every session because this is the only place all exits live together.

crypto-investing-6.territory: The person can see their own money on a screen and cannot touch it; they arrive in a state of panic, humiliation, and 2am forum-scrolling. The interface answers as a calm case officer: procedural, unhurried, allergic to hype, turning a shapeless catastrophe into numbered steps with dates. Dark, but the dark of a late office where work is getting done, not a trading terminal.

palette.note: Muted slate darkness with zero gradients; the amber accent is rationed to deadlines and the current rung of the ladder, so urgency always means something.

crypto-investing-6.typography: IBM Plex Sans for guidance prose and IBM Plex Mono for case numbers, dates, and dollar amounts; the mono figures make the app feel like a filing system that cannot be argued with.
crypto-investing-6.motif: The escalation ladder: a fixed five-rung vertical diagram (support ticket → follow-up → public escalation → regulator → outcome) that appears on every case screen with the current rung lit amber, so the person always knows exactly where they stand in the process.

ia.coreObject: The case: one frozen-account file holding documents, drafted letters, deadlines, and the escalation ladder position
ia.primaryLoop: The person checks in when a deadline fires or a reply arrives, logs what happened, and the app hands them the next concrete action already drafted, which is the only thing keeping the panic at bay.

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Control notifications and the fate of extremely sensitive data.

crypto-investing-7.territory: The person is about to move five years of savings across a gap with no undo button, and every crypto interface they know is either a casino or a cliff edge. The interface answers like a pre-flight checklist read by a calm engineer: dark, quiet, procedural, where every step is verified before the next one unlocks and nothing celebrates until the recovery rehearsal has actually passed.

palette.note: Verification green appears only when a checkpoint has objectively passed; pending steps stay in gray outline and hazards in a flat amber, so color is a verdict, never a mood, and no gradients exist anywhere.

crypto-investing-7.typography: Söhne carries the procedure text with unexcitable authority; JetBrains Mono renders every address, network name, and amount so a single wrong character stays visually catchable.
crypto-investing-7.motif: The checkpoint rail: a single vertical rail runs through the entire migration, each station a physical-feeling seal that flips from outline to filled green only on verified proof, and the rail is the product.

ia.coreObject: The migration plan: an exchange-to-wallet procedure of sealed checkpoints, from setup through recovery rehearsal to quarterly re-checks
ia.primaryLoop: Work down the rail one verified checkpoint at a time during the migration, then return quarterly and on every phone change when the app asks you to re-prove you can still recover.

screens.title: Onboarding — the route
screens.purpose: Pick the exact exchange and wallet so the plan is tailored, not generic.
screens.hero: Two selectors joined by the first segment of the rail.
screens.data: From: 'Coinbase'. To: 'Ledger Nano X'. Assets to move: '0.42 BTC · 3,100 USDC'. Note under selectors: 'Plan adjusts for Coinbase withdrawal limits ($100k/day) and Ledger's supported networks.' Button: 'Build my plan'.

screens.title: Onboarding — what we never see
screens.purpose: State the trust boundary before anything else: no seed phrases, no custody, all checks on-device.
screens.hero: A flat card with three struck-through items behind a lock glyph.
screens.data: 'We never see your seed phrase or private keys.' 'We never custody or touch your assets.' 'All verification runs on this device.' Single button: 'Understood — show the plan'. No skip ambiguity, no marketing copy.

screens.title: First launch — empty rail
screens.purpose: Empty state for a user who built no plan yet: the whole rail visible, every seal in outline, so the scope of the procedure is honest upfront.
screens.hero: The full vertical rail with six outlined, unlabeled-value seals.
screens.data: Stations: '1 Wallet setup · 2 Address & network check · 3 Test transfer · 4 Recovery rehearsal · 5 Main transfer · 6 Ongoing health'. Caption: 'About 45 minutes, most of it waiting for confirmations.' Button: 'Start checkpoint 1'.

screens.title: The plan
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the rail with real progress, the current checkpoint expanded.
screens.hero: The rail with seals 1–2 filled green, seal 3 expanded and active.
screens.data: 'Checkpoint 3 of 6 — Test transfer'. Passed above: '✓ Ledger initialized, firmware 2.2.4' and '✓ Address verified on-device'. Current: 'Send 25 USDC first. Never move the full amount on an unproven route.' Elapsed: '22 min'.

screens.title: Address & network verification
screens.purpose: The checkpoint that catches the classic catastrophic error before any money moves.
screens.hero: The receive address in large mono, first and last four characters emphasized, network badges compared side by side.
screens.data: Address: '0x7f3C…9aE2 · checksum valid'. Comparison: 'Coinbase withdrawal network: Ethereum (ERC-20)' vs 'Ledger account network: Ethereum (ERC-20)' → seal fills green: 'Networks match'. Reminder line: 'Confirm the same address on your Ledger screen, not just here.'

screens.title: Network mismatch caught
screens.purpose: The conflict state: the app blocks progress when the withdrawal network does not match the wallet, the moment the product earns its price.
screens.hero: The rail physically interrupted by a flat amber barrier card between checkpoints.
screens.data: 'Stopped: Coinbase is set to BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20). Your Ledger account expects Ethereum (ERC-20).' Consequence line: 'Funds sent this way are difficult or impossible to recover.' Buttons: 'Show me where to change it on Coinbase' and 'Re-check'. No override button exists.

screens.title: Test transfer
screens.purpose: The mandatory small send, tracked to confirmation before the rail continues.
screens.hero: A single in-flight transaction card riding the rail, confirmation ticks accumulating.
screens.data: '25 USDC · Coinbase → Ledger · Ethereum'. Status: '7 of 12 confirmations · ~4 min remaining'. Fee shown: '$1.84 network fee'. On arrival: seal fills, line reads '✓ Route proven. 25 USDC arrived at 0x7f3C…9aE2.'

screens.title: Recovery rehearsal
screens.purpose: The most important checkpoint: prove on-device that the wallet restores from the backup phrase before savings move.
screens.hero: An airplane-mode banner over a 24-slot word verification grid, three random slots active.
screens.data: Banner: 'Airplane mode is on. This rehearsal never touches the network.' Prompt: 'Enter words 4, 11, and 19 of your recovery phrase into your Ledger's check tool.' Result: '✓ Rehearsal passed at 3:41 PM. You have proven you can recover.' Footnote: 'Most people first test recovery on the day everything already went wrong. You just did it early.'

screens.title: Main transfer
screens.purpose: The full move, permitted only because every prior seal is green, executed in staged sends.
screens.hero: The rail's fifth seal expanded into a staged send list, each stage with its own confirmation count.
screens.data: 'Stage 1 · 0.10 BTC · confirmed (6/6)'. 'Stage 2 · 0.32 BTC · 2 of 6 confirmations'. 'Stage 3 · 3,075 USDC · queued'. Note: 'Staged sends limit exposure if anything fails mid-route.' Total moved so far: '$11,830 of $49,120'.

screens.title: Ongoing health
screens.purpose: Post-migration screen: quarterly access checks and phone-change triggers so recovery ability never silently rots.
screens.hero: A quiet calendar card with the next rehearsal date and a device row.
screens.data: 'Next access check: October 11, 2026 (quarterly)'. History: '✓ Jul 11, 2026 — rehearsal passed'. Device row: 'New phone detected? We will prompt a rehearsal within 48 hours.' Toggle: 'Quarterly reminders · on'.

screens.title: Pay for the procedure
screens.purpose: The paywall before checkpoint 1 unlocks: one-time pricing framed alongside the hardware wallet already on the desk, no urgency mechanics.
screens.hero: A flat surface card listing exactly what is bought, the rail dimmed but fully visible behind it.
screens.data: 'Guided migration, one wallet — $29.99 one time.' 'Family: up to five wallets — $99.99 one time.' Line: 'You spent $149 on the hardware. This is the procedure that gets your savings onto it safely.' Buttons: 'Buy the migration' and 'Restore purchase'. Footer: 'No subscription. No token. No upsell mid-transfer.'

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Reminders, hardware profile, and data boundaries, kept terse.
screens.hero: A short list opening with the trust boundary restated.
screens.data: Rows: 'On-device only — no analytics on addresses or amounts', 'Quarterly check reminder · on', 'Hardware: Ledger Nano X · firmware 2.2.4', 'Hardware guides: NFC cards, security keys, multisig', 'Restore purchase', 'Version 1.2.1'.

crypto-investing-8.territory: The person is thirty seconds from aping into a token, adrenaline up, tab-switching between a screener and a chart, and they know one wrong contract erases a month of wins. The interface answers not with more dashboards but with the cold flat certainty of a customs inspection: papers checked, verdict issued, reasons stated. It slows the moment down just enough to save them.

palette.note: Ink on bone like an inspection form; the interface stays monochrome until a verdict lands — rust-red #A63D2A stamps a trap, a deep #1F6B3D stamps a pass, and nothing else in the app is ever those colors.

crypto-investing-8.typography: Founders Grotesk for verdicts and reasons set large and flat, JetBrains Mono for addresses, tax percentages and contract lines — the two voices of the inspector and the evidence.
crypto-investing-8.motif: Three tripwires: every check renders as three taut horizontal wires (sell test, contract rights, people) that either hold steady or visibly snap one by one as the scan runs — the verdict is readable from across the room by which wires broke.

ia.coreObject: The check — one token address, one simulated exit, one plain-language verdict with three reasons
ia.primaryLoop: Paste the address of whatever just started trending, watch the three wires test for thirty seconds, get the verdict before the FOMO wins — then come back later to see how past verdicts aged.

screens.title: Empty — first launch
screens.purpose: One paste field and three slack wires; the whole product explained by its idle state.
screens.hero: A large paste field above three loose, untensioned wires
screens.data: Placeholder 'Paste a token address — 0x… or a Solana mint'; caption 'Three checks a day free. We answer one question: can you get out.'; sample chip 'Try a known honeypot' loading a real archived example

screens.title: Onboarding — what this is and isn't
screens.purpose: Single step: sets the contract with the user before the first check, no account needed.
screens.hero: Two flat columns — 'We answer' vs 'We never'
screens.data: 'We answer: can you sell it, who controls supply, have these deployers rugged before. We never: tell you what to buy, predict price, rate CEX listings.'; chain picker: Ethereum ✓, Base ✓, Solana ✓, BSC ✓; button 'Run my first check'

screens.title: Check running — mid-use
screens.purpose: The main screen mid-scan: thirty seconds of visible work, each wire testing in sequence.
screens.hero: Three wires under tension with the middle one mid-test, a thin timer at 0:18
screens.data: 'PEPEWIFHAT · 0x3f4a…a9d2 · Base'; wire 1 'Simulated sell — routing 0.1 ETH worth through the pair…'; wire 2 'Reading contract — 412 lines…'; wire 3 'Tracing 2 deployer addresses…'

screens.title: Verdict — trap
screens.purpose: The earning-its-keep moment: a flat, quotable verdict with exactly three reasons.
screens.hero: Rust-red stamped panel 'Trap likely' over two snapped wires
screens.data: '1. Sell simulation reverted — buys execute, sells do not. 2. Owner can mint 41% more supply at will. 3. Deployer wallet funded three tokens abandoned within 9 days.'; footer 'Checked Jul 11, 14:02 UTC · share card'

screens.title: Verdict — no obvious trap
screens.purpose: The honest pass: three reasons why nothing snapped, with the caveat that keeps trust.
screens.hero: Deep-green stamped panel 'No obvious trap found' over three intact wires
screens.data: '1. Simulated sell executed, 2.1% round-trip cost. 2. Minting renounced, no pause function. 3. Top 10 wallets hold 24%, no team wallet outflows in 30 days.'; caveat line 'A clean contract is not a good investment. This checks the exit, not the upside.'

screens.title: Contract findings in plain words
screens.purpose: Drill-down for wire 2: each contract mechanism translated into one sentence a non-developer can repeat.
screens.hero: A two-column ledger — mono contract line on the left, plain English on the right
screens.data: 'setTaxes(uint256) — owner can raise sell tax any time; currently 3%, was 18% for the first 24 hours'; 'pauseTrading() — trading can be halted by one address'; 'renounceOwnership() — never called'

screens.title: Holders — who really owns it
screens.purpose: Drill-down on concentration and how the big wallets have been behaving.
screens.hero: A horizontal supply bar sliced by holder, team slice hatched
screens.data: 'Top 10 wallets: 62.3% of supply · team-tagged wallet 0x9c1…e04 holds 18%, sold on 6 of the last 10 days · 3,204 total holders, median position $41'

screens.title: The people behind it
screens.purpose: Drill-down for wire 3: deployer funding graph traced to prior projects.
screens.hero: A short funding chain diagram, three nodes, oldest node flagged
screens.data: 'Deployer 0x77b…c21 was funded by 0x2ae…901, which deployed DOGEMOON (liquidity pulled Nov 2025, $340k) and two tokens abandoned within two weeks. Pattern seen in 14 prior checks.'

screens.title: History with outcomes
screens.purpose: The trust ledger: what actually happened to tokens after our verdicts, wins and misses both.
screens.hero: A dated list where each row pairs the old stamp with a 7-day and 30-day outcome
screens.data: 'BRETT2 — Trap likely, Jun 28 → liquidity pulled 6 days later'; 'TURBO — No obvious trap, Jun 12 → still trading at day 30'; 'WAGMI — No obvious trap, Jun 3 → sell tax raised to 25% on day 11. We missed the timelock. Detection added.'

screens.title: Node unreachable
screens.purpose: Degraded state: when the simulation can't run, the verdict is withheld rather than guessed.
screens.hero: One wire greyed out with a 'Verdict withheld' band instead of a stamp
screens.data: 'Base RPC congested — the sell simulation did not complete. We don't issue verdicts on partial checks. Retrying in 40 s (attempt 2 of 3). Your daily check was not spent.'

screens.title: Paywall — fourth check of the day
screens.purpose: Shown only when the free three are spent, priced against the cost of one missed honeypot.
screens.hero: The paste field politely locked behind a plan card, today's three used checks listed above it
screens.data: 'Three free checks used today — resets 00:00 UTC. Unlimited: $12/month. Communities and bots: API at $50/month, 10k checks. One honeypot costs more than a year of this. Restore purchase' — no countdown timers, no 'offer expires'

screens.hero: Grouped flat list, API section on top for paid users

cycling-3.territory: A commuter is 14 km into a ride when the phone rings, the app gets backgrounded, and an old fear surfaces: is it still recording? The interface answers like a flight recorder answers a pilot: with stoic, mechanical proof that every minute is already on disk. The feeling it gives is not excitement but the deep calm of equipment that does not fail.

palette.note: Asphalt-gray daylight surfaces built for sun glare; safety orange is reserved for the recording indicator and destructive-edit handles, exactly like reflective tape on a gray frame.

cycling-3.typography: Archivo for labels and headings with Roboto Mono for every distance, time and elevation figure, so the numbers read like a bike computer's segment display rather than a social feed.
cycling-3.motif: The tape: every ride is drawn as a continuous horizontal ribbon of one-minute segments, and that same tape is what you scrub, trim and heal in the editor.

ia.coreObject: The ride: a tape of auto-saved minute segments with GPS points, editable and exportable
ia.primaryLoop: Tap start, ride to work, glance once at the live tape to see it is writing, tap stop at the rack; the growing yearly odometer is what pulls them back every evening.

screens.title: Onboarding: permissions with a reason
screens.purpose: Get background location by explaining it as the crash-proofing mechanism, not a legal chore.
screens.hero: A diagram of the tape writing minute segments to disk while a phone-call icon interrupts on top.
screens.data: 'We save your ride every 60 seconds, even during calls or if the app crashes.' Row 1: Location 'Always' - required to record while the screen is off. Row 2: Motion - improves auto-pause. Button: 'Allow and continue'. No account step exists.

screens.title: Onboarding: units and you are done
screens.purpose: One screen of setup, then straight to the start button.
screens.hero: A single segmented control km/mi above a preview of the start screen.
screens.data: Units: km selected. Wheel of common ride types: Commute, Road, Gravel (Commute preselected, changeable later). Footnote: 'That is all the setup. No registration.' Button: 'Ready to ride'.

screens.title: First launch: empty odometer
screens.purpose: Make the first start irresistible and show what the history will become.
screens.hero: A giant zeroed odometer (0000.0 km) in mono digits above one full-width Start button.
screens.data: Odometer 0000.0 km, 'Rides: 0'. Ghost tape below with the caption 'Your first ride's tape will appear here, saved minute by minute.' Button: 'Start ride'.

screens.title: Recording, 38 minutes in
screens.purpose: The mid-ride glance: prove recording is alive without inviting fiddling.
screens.hero: The live tape crawling right, each written minute clicking into place as a filled segment, orange REC dot pulsing.
screens.data: 17.4 km · 38:12 · 27.3 km/h avg · 142 m climbed. Tape shows 38 filled segments, last one filling. Status line: 'Last saved to disk: 41 s ago.' Auto-pause chip appeared at minute 22: 'Paused 1:40 at traffic light'.

screens.title: Recovery after a crash
screens.purpose: The keystone moment: the app died mid-ride and the ride did not.
screens.hero: A restored tape with a small stitch mark where the app restarted, framed by a calm confirmation card.
screens.data: 'Your ride was restored.' Tape: 52 of 53 minutes intact, stitch mark at 09:42. 'The app closed at 09:42. Recording resumed automatically. 24.1 km recovered, about 40 m of track estimated across the gap.' Buttons: 'Continue this ride' / 'Finish and save'.

screens.title: Ride editor: trim the forgotten stop
screens.purpose: Fix the classic error of hitting stop at home 25 minutes after arriving.
screens.hero: The full ride tape with two orange trim handles, the tail segment visibly flat at 0 km/h.
screens.data: Ride 'Thu 9 Jul, commute home': 12.6 km recorded, tail shows 24 min at 0.0 km/h at one location. Handle dragged to 17:48. Preview: '12.6 km → 12.6 km, time 58:10 → 34:20, avg 13.0 → 22.0 km/h.' Buttons: 'Apply trim' / 'Undo'.

screens.title: Ride editor: cut a pause
screens.purpose: Remove a mid-ride stop (bakery, puncture) without deleting distance.
screens.hero: A selected span of flat segments in the middle of the tape, highlighted for excision.
screens.data: Selected 11:05-11:31 (26 min, 0.1 km, 'Cafe Sprocket' on the mini-map). 'Cut this pause? Distance stays 43.2 km, moving time becomes 1:47:12.' The cut leaves a thin scar mark on the tape so edits stay visible.

screens.title: Add a ride manually
screens.purpose: Backfill a forgotten ride so the yearly total stays true.
screens.hero: A plain form styled like a logbook line: date, distance, duration, type.
screens.data: Date: Sun 5 Jul. Distance: 62 km. Duration: 2:41. Type: Road. Note: 'club ride, forgot the phone'. Saved entry shows a hollow (no-GPS) tape with the label 'manual entry' and counts into all totals.

screens.title: Totals
screens.purpose: The odometer that makes daily riders come back: month, year, lifetime.
screens.hero: Three stacked mono odometers with a bar chart of weekly kilometers underneath.
screens.data: July: 214.8 km · 11 rides. 2026: 2,417.5 km · 128 rides · 18,940 m climbed. All time: 5,102.3 km. Weekly bars for 12 weeks, tallest 96 km (week of 8 Jun). Subline: 'Longest ride this year: 84.2 km, 26 Apr.'

screens.title: Export
screens.purpose: Prove the history belongs to the rider, one ride or all of it.
screens.hero: A file manifest listing what will be written, like a packing list.
screens.data: 'Export 128 rides of 2026': GPX (tracks, 41.2 MB) or CSV (date, km, time, avg, climb). Single ride export from any ride page. Caption: 'Files save to your phone. Works offline. No account needed to leave.'

screens.title: One-time unlock
screens.purpose: Sell the editor and totals for the price of an inner tube, after trust is earned.
screens.hero: A single toolbox-style card splitting Free from Owned, no subscription option at all.
screens.data: 'Recording is free forever.' Owned for $4.99 once: ride editor (trim, cut pauses, fix time), manual rides, yearly and lifetime totals, GPX/CSV export. Buttons: 'Buy once, $4.99' / 'Restore purchase'. Footnote: 'Saved rides are never locked, paid or not.'

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Recording reliability controls and honest data ownership, nothing social.
screens.hero: A grouped list led by a 'Recording health' status row with a green check.
screens.data: Recording health: 'Background access OK, battery optimization off.' Auto-pause: below 3 km/h for 30 s. Units km. Save interval 60 s (fixed, explained). Storage used: 48 MB, 133 rides. Export all data. Delete all data. Restore purchase. Version 2.1.

dating-apps-3.territory: She has exactly two child-free evenings this week and zero patience for chat that goes nowhere, opening the app in the twenty minutes after bedtime. The interface answers with warmth and bluntness at once: real faces in inviting light, and a promise stated up front that nobody shown is out of reach. It feels less like a slot machine and more like a good friend saying: he's free Thursday too, and he's fifteen minutes away.

palette.note: Coral appears only where two lives actually overlap: the shared-evening badge, the confirm button, a match. Everything else stays candlelight-warm and neutral.

dating-apps-3.typography: Tiempos Headline for names and the big evening proposals, Graphik for everything else: warm editorial confidence over clean, unfussy utility.
dating-apps-3.motif: The overlap: two soft rounded calendar shapes that intersect on every profile and match, with the shared evenings glowing coral inside the intersection.

ia.coreObject: the shared evening (a concrete date-night window two calendars both hold open)
ia.primaryLoop: After bedtime, check who overlaps with this week's free evenings, then propose a night or confirm one with a single tap.

dating-apps-4.territory: The buyer is a pastor or diaspora chair who has watched their young people drift to apps full of strangers, and feels responsible in a way no growth dashboard understands. The interface answers with the warmth of a parish hall and the competence of good admin software: ivory paper, wine-deep accents, and a ledger of actual couples formed, because that is the number this person is accountable for.

palette.note: The wine burgundy marks membership, approval, and formed couples, while each organization's own brand color takes over the member-facing preview, so the admin tool stays constant and the product they ship stays theirs.

dating-apps-4.typography: Recoleta for community names and milestone numbers, Figtree for the dashboard workhorse: the soft round serif keeps warmth in a tool that is fundamentally about people finding each other, the grotesk keeps the roster work brisk.
dating-apps-4.motif: The linked rings ledger: every couple formed adds a pair of interlocked rings to a growing engraved band on the dashboard, the one chart a pastor actually wants to show the board.

ia.coreObject: The community platform: roster, member approvals, events, and the couples formed under its name
ia.primaryLoop: The organizer checks pending member approvals against the roster a few times a week, publishes an event a month, and returns for the linked-rings ledger that proves the platform is doing its one job.

dating-apps-6.territory: The person arrives mid-doubt: a widowed teacher wondering why her charming match can't ever video-call, or an adult son who found a wire-transfer mention in his father's chat and doesn't know how to raise it. Warmth here can't be the warmth of romance — it has to be the steadiness of a good nurse: unhurried, unembarrassed, never scolding. The interface answers with lamplight calm and plain language that makes checking feel like care, not paranoia.

palette.note: Warm linen and soft ink at reading-lamp contrast; the mulberry accent carries actions and matched-script threads, while risk is voiced in a muted amber underline rather than alarm red — concern without siren.

dating-apps-6.typography: Tiempos Text at a generous 18px body minimum carries every explanation like a well-set book page for 45+ eyes, with Graphik for buttons and labels — literary warmth over quiet utility.
dating-apps-6.motif: The annotation thread: every flagged phrase in a pasted conversation is tied by a fine hand-drawn thread to a named script card in the margin, so the evidence and the pattern are physically connected on one page.

ia.coreObject: The check — one pasted conversation or profile, annotated against the playbook of known scripts
ia.primaryLoop: Whenever a new match says something that lands oddly, paste the exchange and read the annotated page; people return at each new relationship stage because the scripts escalate in stages too.

dating-apps-7.territory: The moment of use is tender and slightly guarded: two people in year two or three, scrolling their own history in bed, quietly aware that everything precious lives on someone else's server. The interface answers with warm album light and vault-grade reassurance at once, the softness of a photo book bound to the visible, checkable fact that every memory is already sitting in both of their own clouds.

palette.note: Warm ivory like album paper; the raspberry-garnet accent beats only on the day counter, milestone dates, and the twin backup marks, never on upsells.

dating-apps-7.typography: Canela for the day counter and milestone numerals, Graphik for everything else, so the big dates feel engraved while daily use stays light and unfussy.
dating-apps-7.motif: The twin marks: every photo and note carries two small cloud ticks, one per partner's own storage, and a memory is only shown as 'kept' when both marks are lit.

ia.coreObject: The entry: a photo or note on the couple's shared timeline, mirrored to both partners' personal clouds the moment it lands
ia.primaryLoop: One of you drops in a photo or a line from the day, both phones show it with twin marks lit, and the ticking day counter plus upcoming milestones pull you back to look at how far you've come.

dating-apps-8.territory: The user arrives bruised: thirty openers into silence, Gold paid for and useless, quietly wondering if the problem is him. The interface answers like a good editor's desk, warm gray paper and red grease-pencil marks, blunt but on his side, turning humiliating guesswork into a fixable draft.

palette.note: The grease-pencil red belongs exclusively to reviewer markup on the user's own screenshots, all app chrome stays quiet gray so every drop of red reads as a correction worth money.

dating-apps-8.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk for the interface, Caveat for reviewer handwriting on the markups: the cool grotesk keeps the product from feeling like a pity service, the handwritten layer makes each fix feel like a real person leaned over your shoulder.
dating-apps-8.motif: The red grease-pencil markup: reviewers circle, strike through, and annotate directly on the uploaded profile screenshots, and those marked-up frames are the product.

ia.coreObject: The review: the user's uploaded profile with three signed, marked-up fixes and a follow-up check
ia.primaryLoop: The user uploads a profile, gets three fixes within 24 hours, applies them on the dating app, then comes back two weeks later to log replies and compare before and after.

driving-test-prep-3.territory: The person studying is not a student, they are a driver between paychecks: every passed endorsement is a different set of job boards and a different rate per mile. The interface answers with the clarity of the road itself: green guide signs, one destination per panel, and a drill rhythm calm enough to keep at a truck stop at 9 pm.

driving-test-prep-3.typography: Overpass everywhere, the open descendant of Highway Gothic, so every screen reads like the road signage the exam itself is about, with drill questions set large and unhurried.
driving-test-prep-3.motif: The guide sign: every endorsement track is a green highway sign panel with white lettering and its own exit number, and the destination printed on the sign is always the job and its pay.

fishing-6.territory: It is hour six of a tournament, sun off the water, wet hands, and a sixth keeper just hit the deck: which of the five in the well goes back? The interface answers like a good co-angler with a clipboard: instant, loud, certain, readable at arm's length in full glare. The feeling is competitive clarity under a ticking clock.

palette.note: Glare-proof near-white deck surfaces with black weight digits; chartreuse, the classic lure color, fills cull tags and the release verdict, always carrying black text for contrast.

fishing-6.typography: Barlow Condensed Bold for weights and rankings so 4.86 lb reads like a stadium scoreboard from six feet away, with Inter for everything quieter.
fishing-6.motif: The cull tag: every fish in the app lives on a colored oval tag with a punched hole, matching the physical tags clipped to fish in the livewell, in any color the angler runs.

ia.coreObject: The bag: today's best five fish, each on a colored cull tag with a weight
ia.primaryLoop: Boat a fish, enter its weight from the scale in two taps, read the cull verdict, clip the matching tag; between fish, watch the boat and club leaderboards move.

flashcards-2.territory: Six weeks to the JLPT and she no longer trusts the app that hides why it does things. The interface answers like a clean card catalog: every card wears its return date openly, the reason is printed under the stamp, and the machinery is hers to reach into without breaking it.

palette.note: Graphite ink on paper with one library-stamp teal that marks every return date, so the algorithm's decisions are literally inked onto each card.

flashcards-2.typography: Charter carries the card faces like a good textbook, Public Sans runs the chrome, and return dates sit in a slightly imperfect stamp treatment that stays typographic, never cute.
flashcards-2.motif: The return ticket: every card has a due-date tab stamped on its edge like a library lending card, with the reason line printed beneath the stamp.

flashcards-3.territory: You just heard a word you didn't know, mid-conversation or mid-chapter, and there is a five-second window before it evaporates. The person arrives slightly hurried and slightly delighted at having caught something real from their own life. The interface answers with the calm of a good paper dictionary: instant on entry, unhurried once you're in, the word already typeset for you.

palette.note: Cream paper stays constant across every screen; the only strong color is a marigold highlighter stroke that marks the word you caught and the button that saves it.

flashcards-3.typography: Source Serif 4 sets every headword like a printed dictionary entry, with IPA and sense numbers doing the quiet detail work, while Inter handles UI chrome so your words are always the loudest thing on screen.
flashcards-3.motif: The dictionary headword block: every caught word rendered as a bold serif headword with IPA and part of speech, underlined by a hand-drawn marigold highlighter stroke, as if you'd marked it in a real book.

ia.coreObject: the caught word (a card that assembles itself)
ia.primaryLoop: Encounter a word in real life, type or paste it in five seconds, then return each morning to clear a short review queue made only of words from your own life.

flashcards-4.territory: It is 11 PM in the medical library, the pharmacology exam is at 9 AM, and she has forty slides and zero trust in AI slop landing unsupervised in her deck. The interface answers as a triage desk under a lamp: cream index cards on a dark work surface, each one passing through her hands before it earns a place. Fast, physical, and respectful of the fact that tonight she is the editor, not the passenger.

palette.note: Warm lamp-lit charcoal desk with generated cards rendered as bright cream paper (#F7F2E4 with ink text) so the content, not the chrome, holds the light; the chartreuse highlighter stroke fires only on accept.

flashcards-4.typography: Tiempos Text set on the cream cards so questions read like a well-printed study card, Söhne Mono for counters, page references, and language tags, keeping the machinery visibly separate from the content.
flashcards-4.motif: The triage desk: every generated card is a physical cream card that must be swiped off the desk or into the deck slot, where the deck's paper edge visibly thickens with each accept, so a deck's height is literally the sum of her decisions.

ia.coreObject: The draft card: a generated question-answer pair holding a source-page reference and a language tag, existing only until judged
ia.primaryLoop: Feed in tonight's lecture, triage the draft cards in batches of five, and study the deck knowing every card in it passed through her own hands.

screens.title: Feed it the lecture
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: take the source and, critically, the target count before anything generates.
screens.hero: A drop zone holding a recognizable lecture PDF thumbnail with the card-count stepper directly beneath it.
screens.data: Source: 'Cardio_Pharm_Week9.pdf, 42 slides'. Alternatives shown: photo of notes, pasted text. Target: 40 cards, stepper 10-50. Line under the stepper: 'You will get 40, not 12, not 90. The count is a contract.' Detected language chip: 'English'. Button: 'Generate the draft'.

screens.title: Nothing saves itself
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: teach the three gestures on one throwaway card, and state the gate rule once.
screens.hero: A single practice card on the desk with the three gesture paths traced: left off the desk, tap to edit, right into the slot.
screens.data: Practice card: 'Q: What does this app never do? A: Save a card you have not approved.' Gesture labels: swipe left, delete. Tap, edit in place. Swipe right, into the deck. Footer: 'The generator drafts. You decide. That is the whole product.' Button: 'Start reviewing'.

screens.title: Drafting, concepts first
screens.purpose: The generation moment: show that the machine hunts key concepts rather than slicing pages in order.
screens.hero: The lecture's slide strip dimmed in the background while concept labels lift off it into a draft pile.
screens.data: Progress: 'Reading 42 slides. Found 31 concepts so far: beta-blocker contraindications, ACE inhibitor cough mechanism, warfarin INR targets, digoxin toxicity signs.' Counter: 'Draft: 34 of 40 cards.' Skipped, stated openly: 'title slides, references, and the syllabus page contributed nothing.'

screens.title: The triage desk
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the hero mechanic at full speed, batch of five, card 12 of 40 in hand.
screens.hero: One cream card center-desk, the rest of its batch fanned behind, the deck slot at right with a visible paper-edge stack.
screens.data: Card 12 of 40. 'Q: Why are beta-blockers contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure? A: They reduce contractility, worsening low cardiac output.' Source tag: 'slide 17'. Counters: accepted 9, edited 2, deleted 1. The deck edge at right shows 11 cards of thickness. Batch dots: 2 of 5.

screens.title: Fix the wording where it stands
screens.purpose: The edit-in-place mechanic: tighten a clumsy question without leaving the desk or losing the rhythm.
screens.hero: The card flipped to editable, ink text live under the cursor, keyboard up, desk still visible behind.
screens.data: Before: 'Q: What can be said about the relationship between digoxin and potassium levels?' After her edit: 'Q: How does hypokalemia affect digoxin toxicity risk?' Answer untouched. Save returns it to the desk face-up with a small 'edited' corner fold. Time cost: one screen, zero navigation.

screens.title: Off the desk
screens.purpose: The rejection moment: deleting a junk card is fast, satisfying, and consequence-free.
screens.hero: A weak card mid-swipe, tilting off the desk edge into the dark.
screens.data: Departing card: 'Q: What is covered on slide 3? A: An overview of the lecture outline.' Small toast: 'Gone. 3 deleted so far. Undo.' Spec note: deletion trains nothing secretly and triggers no plea; a bad card leaving is the system working, and the copy never argues.

screens.title: The language guard
screens.purpose: The language mechanic at its earning moment: German notes stay German, and the app says so before drafting.
screens.hero: A pasted block of German pathophysiology notes with the language chip caught and locked above it.
screens.data: Pasted text begins: 'Herzinsuffizienz: Unfähigkeit des Herzens, das benötigte Herzzeitvolumen zu fördern.' Chip: 'Deutsch erkannt. Questions will be written in German.' Sample draft card shown: 'Q: Was kennzeichnet eine Herzinsuffizienz?' Override available: 'Generate in another language' behind a deliberate extra tap.

screens.title: The deck receipt
screens.purpose: Batch complete: the save moment states exactly what she approved, in her numbers.
screens.hero: The finished deck as a thick cream stack, edge-on, with the tally printed on its top card.
screens.data: 'Cardio Pharm, 36 cards. Your calls: 28 accepted as drafted, 8 edited, 4 deleted. Every card traces to a slide.' Buttons: 'Study now', 'Add to existing deck'. Line: 'Saved locally and to your account. Nothing entered this deck without your hand on it.'

screens.title: Study, 11:40 PM
screens.purpose: The flip at its moment: the deck in use the same night, physical and quick.

flashcards-6.territory: Six weeks to the NCLEX, forty minutes between clinicals, and a hundred drug names that all sound alike. The interface answers with the confidence of a well-organized study table: bright, tactile cards that flip with real weight, absurd images treated completely seriously. It should feel like the one place where reps actually accumulate.

palette.note: Cool paper-white keeps focus on the story art, indigo carries structure and progress, and a single coral #FF6B5E is reserved for the phonetic tokens inside scenes.

flashcards-6.typography: General Sans for interface and card terms, with Caveat used only inside story scenes for handwritten mnemonic labels, so the app stays clinical while the stories stay absurd.
flashcards-6.motif: Phonetic tokens: every term breaks into syllable chips, war·far·in becoming warrior, fairy, inn, that visibly assemble into the scene, on library cards and on the student's own cards alike.

ia.coreObject: The card with a story: term, scene, and its place in one repetition queue
ia.primaryLoop: Clear today's due queue between classes, and turn every new lecture term into a story card the same day.

flashcards-7.territory: Standing on a packed train or behind the wheel with an exam six weeks out, holding an hour that usually evaporates. The interface answers like good transit signage: legible in one glance, then out of the way entirely, because the ears are doing the work and the screen is mostly in a pocket.

palette.note: Built to be read in one glance and put away: signal orange marks only the live card, everything else recedes like stations passing in a dark window.

flashcards-7.typography: Neue Frutiger, the signage typeface, set large with generous tracking; questions read like platform announcements and numbers are legible from arm's length in a moving carriage.
flashcards-7.motif: The route line: every deck is a transit line and every card a stop, the session advancing dot by dot toward the terminus.
