flashcards-8.territory: He is pacing a hallway with a printed monologue folded in quarters, audition in nine days, mouthing lines at the wall. The interface answers with the hush of a rehearsal room and the dignity of a well-set page: the text is the star, and the app's whole job is to make it disappear from the screen in stages until it exists only in him. Reverent about words, unsentimental about the work.

palette.note: Warm letterpress paper and near-black ink, with a deep curtain oxblood used only for the words currently being tested; as text is learned it fades through grey to paper, so mastery literally looks like the page emptying.

flashcards-8.typography: Miller Text at generous book sizes carries every passage like a printed playbill page, with Founders Grotesk small caps for stage directions, section numbers, and the schedule, keeping the apparatus quiet around the words.
flashcards-8.motif: The first-letter skeleton: any learned passage can be shown dissolved to its initial letters standing in the original layout like a typographic ruin, an image so particular to word-perfect work that a screenshot of it identifies the app instantly.

ia.coreObject: The piece: one long text with a deadline, split into sections that each move through three stages of disappearance
ia.primaryLoop: Run today's section through its current stage on the walk or in a spare ten minutes, and watch the schedule keep the whole piece solid as the date closes in.

screens.title: Bring your text
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: paste the piece and give it a date, the two facts the whole system runs on.
screens.hero: A generous paste field already holding a real text, with the deadline field set beneath it like a title page imprint.
screens.data: Pasted: 'Invictus, W. E. Henley, 4 stanzas, 103 words.' Suggested examples above the field: a monologue, Psalm 23, a best man speech, a closing argument. Deadline: 'Audition, May 12, 9 days away.' Line: 'Word-perfect means your words, in your order. We never turn text into quiz questions.' Button: 'Divide it'.

screens.title: Cut into workable pieces
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: approve the sectioning, because the chunk is the unit of every rehearsal.
screens.hero: The full poem set on one page with the four proposed section breaks drawn as thin rules, each draggable.
screens.data: Section 1: 'Out of the night that covers me...', 26 words. Sections 2-4 similar. Note: 'Drag any break. Actors often cut at beats, not stanzas.' Estimate beneath: 'At your deadline, about 12 minutes a day keeps all four solid.' Button: 'Begin with section 1'.

screens.title: Stage one, the full page
screens.purpose: Reading stage at its moment: the complete text, beautifully set, read aloud with nothing hidden yet.
screens.hero: Section 1 set full-bleed in Miller Text like a fine edition, one line of apparatus at the bottom.
screens.data: 'Out of the night that covers me, / Black as the pit from pole to pole, / I thank whatever gods may be / For my unconquerable soul.' Footer: 'Read it aloud twice, then let it start disappearing.' Button: 'I have it in my mouth'. Small caps tag: 'Stage 1 of 3, section 1 of 4'.

screens.title: Stage two, first letters
screens.purpose: The signature mechanic: the text dissolved to initials, typed back at the speed of thought.
screens.hero: The stanza as a first-letter skeleton holding its exact original line breaks, cursor on the next initial.
screens.data: 'O o t n t c m, / B a t p f p t p, / I t w g m b / F m u s.' He types 'b' where 'B' of 'Black' belongs, the letter blooms into the full word in oxblood, then settles to ink. A miss shows the correct initial without wiping the run. Progress: 71 of 103 words placed across the piece.

screens.title: Stage three, the blank page
screens.purpose: Recitation against nothing: the paper is empty and the only help is a deliberate, costed peek.
screens.hero: An empty cream page with just the section title in small caps and a single 'peek' affordance at the margin.
screens.data: Screen: 'Section 3' and blank paper. He recites to himself or aloud; a tap-and-hold at the margin ghosts the first letters for as long as held, logged as one peek. End of run: 'Clean, with 1 peek at line 2.' Line: 'A peek is a note to the schedule, not a failure.'

screens.title: The pieces join
screens.purpose: Assembly mechanic: learned sections lock back into the whole, because the audition is the whole.
screens.hero: Four section cards sliding together into one continuous page, seams dissolving where both sides are solid.
screens.data: Sections 1, 2, 4: solid, set in quiet ink. Section 3: still grey, holding its seam visible. Header: 'Full run available when section 3 reaches stage 3. Estimated: Thursday.' Button: 'Rehearse the join, sections 2 into 3', a targeted run across the weak seam only.

screens.title: Record it the way you will say it
screens.purpose: The voice mechanic: his own reading, with his pauses, becomes the rehearsal track.
screens.hero: A recording page with the text scrolling as he reads and pause markers dropped where he breathes.
screens.data: Recording: 'Invictus, full read, 1 min 42 s, recorded April 30.' Pause markers at stanza breaks, one long hold before 'I am the master of my fate' kept at 2.1 seconds. Retake per section without redoing the whole. Line: 'Your intonation is part of the memory. No robot voice option, on purpose.'

screens.title: Rehearsal on the move
screens.purpose: The listening mechanic at its true location: lock screen and headphones on the walk to work.
screens.hero: A lock-screen player mockup: piece title, section, and a gap-mode toggle in the compact player.
screens.data: Player: 'Invictus, section 2 of 4'. Gap mode on: playback drops to silence at line ends for him to speak into, then his recording confirms. Controls: back one line, replay section. Spec note: works offline, audio processed on device.

screens.title: The schedule holds it
screens.purpose: Deadline-driven repetition: the calendar shows exactly how the piece stays solid until May 12 and after.
screens.hero: A two-week calendar strip with rehearsal marks shrinking in frequency as sections harden.
screens.data: Today: section 3, stage 2, about 6 minutes. Tomorrow: full run, blank page. May 8: full run with recording. May 11: one light pass, 'never cram the night before, one clean run and stop.' After May 12: 'keep-it week' marks at 3, 7, 21 days. Header: '9 days to audition, piece 78% solid.'

screens.title: Three weeks later
screens.purpose: The fading state the mechanics demand: a learned piece drifting, caught early and refreshed in minutes.

The other pieces sit in full ink: 'Best man speech, solid. Psalm 23, solid, next touch June 3.' Line: 'What you learned stays learned only if it is touched. We schedule the touching.'

screens.purpose: Quiet controls: type size for stage reading, peek behavior, audio, and data ownership.

focus-productivity-2.territory: She is eleven weeks from the MCAT with a spreadsheet open next to her timer app, doing the division in her head again: hours left over days left. The interface answers by taking the arithmetic away and leaving one calm number on a clean desk: today's quota, recalculated honestly after every session, with no cheerleading and no shame. The whole product is the feeling of a cleared desk and a known number.

palette.note: Cool paper white with a steady ink-navy for the quota number; the only second color is a dry amber used when the plan is behind, because a deficit is information, not an emergency.

focus-productivity-2.typography: Lyon Text for the exam name and section heads, giving the calm of a well-set textbook, with Inter tabular numerals for quotas and timers so 2h 10m always occupies the same width as it counts down.
focus-productivity-2.motif: The descent line: one thin ink line drawn from total hours down to zero on exam day, with today's dot sitting exactly where her real logged hours put it, above or below the line, no other chart in the app.

ia.coreObject: The quota: today's required hours for one exam, derived live from hours remaining over days remaining
ia.primaryLoop: Open to one number, run a topic-tagged session against it, watch the quota close or honestly grow, and check the widget at night to know exactly where tomorrow starts.

focus-productivity-4.territory: It is Friday afternoon and the freelancer is dreading the weekly ritual: screenshots of a timer, mental math on a rate, an email that looks unprofessional next to a $1,000 retainer. The interface answers with the calm of a document that has been writing itself all week: generous paper whitespace, one running timer, and a total that is always already correct. Nothing to assemble, only something to send.

palette.note: Ink on paper almost everywhere; the ledger red appears only where money is decided, the running total, the invoice rule lines, and the PAID stamp, so red always means a number that matters.

focus-productivity-4.typography: Suisse Int'l for interface text and Suisse Int'l Mono for every duration and dollar figure, so 14.2 h and $923.00 sit in strict tabular columns like a typeset invoice long before the PDF exists.
focus-productivity-4.motif: The living invoice: the week is always rendered as the actual document, and stopping the timer visibly appends one more ruled line item to the sheet, so the user watches their invoice write itself in real time.

ia.coreObject: The time entry (project, task, duration, rate) that is simultaneously a line item on this week's invoice
ia.primaryLoop: Start the timer from the widget when work starts, stop it when work stops, and watch the week's invoice total grow until Friday, when one button turns it into a sendable PDF.

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: The quiet back room: identity, numbering, currency, and the on-device promise in writing.

focus-productivity-5.territory: It's 9:40 PM and the thumb is already moving toward Instagram on autopilot; the person has lost this fight with software toggles a hundred times and is done negotiating with themselves. The interface answers with the stillness of a switched-off machine: a matte, near-silent dark surface that treats the lock as a settled physical fact, not a temptation to argue with. The only warmth on screen is the ember of the tap ripple — the mark of the one physical act that changes anything.

palette.note: Matte charcoal with zero gradients and zero glow; the ember orange exists only at the moment of physical contact — the tap ripple, the tag icons — so color itself means 'something real happened'.

focus-productivity-5.typography: Space Grotesk for interface text with JetBrains Mono for the lock timer and session log; the mono clock gives the locked state the impassive character of equipment rather than an app asking for attention.
focus-productivity-5.motif: The tap ripple: three thin concentric ember rings expanding from the exact point where the phone touched the tag — the app's only animation, earned only by physical contact.

ia.coreObject: The session: a block on chosen apps that can be opened only by a named physical key
ia.primaryLoop: Tap the desk tag to seal the evening, feel the phone go quiet, and tap again tomorrow — the user returns because the barrier held while every software toggle before it folded.

screens.title: Onboarding: choose what gets locked
screens.purpose: Grant Screen Time access and pick the apps in one sober step.
screens.hero: A plain app list with three toggles already on
screens.data: Permission card: 'Screen Time access — this is how the lock is enforced by iOS itself.' Selected: Instagram, TikTok, X. Suggested: YouTube, Reddit. Footnote: 'Calls, Maps and Messages are never blockable. This is a lock, not a cage.'

screens.title: Onboarding: write your first key
screens.purpose: Turn a one-dollar NFC sticker into the only way out.
screens.hero: A phone outline meeting a tag outline, ripple firing at the contact point
screens.data: 'Hold your phone to any NFC tag.' Progress: 'Tag written ✓ · Name it: Garage'. Alternative: 'No tag? Print this QR code instead' with a print button. Advice line: 'Now put it somewhere your feet, not your thumb, have to reach.'

screens.title: Lock screen, mid-session
screens.purpose: The main screen while the block is active — calm, factual, unarguable.
screens.hero: The mono timer, huge and unhurried: 1:22:47
screens.data: 'Locked since 9:14 PM · key: Garage tag'. Blocked row: Instagram, TikTok, X — small gray icons. Line: 'The key is where you left it.' No unlock button exists on this screen; the only affordance is 'Start a 15-min allowance (requires tag)'.

screens.title: The unlock
screens.purpose: Reward the physical walk with the app's single moment of ceremony.
screens.hero: The tap ripple expanding across the whole screen from the contact point
screens.data: 'Garage tag recognized · 10:37 PM'. 'Unlocked. Session lasted 1h 23m.' Session log line added: 'Tue Jul 14 · 9:14–10:37 PM · Garage'. Button: 'Lock again' — one tap re-seals with the same key.

screens.title: Timed allowance
screens.purpose: Let one tap open a measured window instead of the whole evening.
screens.hero: A 15:00 mono countdown already running
screens.data: 'Allowance: Instagram for 15 minutes · started with Desk tag'. Countdown: 12:41 remaining. Line: 'When it hits zero, the lock returns by itself. No tap needed, no decision to make.' History: '3 allowances this week, average 14 min used'.

screens.title: Keys
screens.purpose: Manage multiple tags for different rooms, contexts and people.
screens.hero: Three key cards, each with a name, a role and a last-used stamp
screens.data: 'Garage — full unlock · last used Tue 10:37 PM'. 'Desk — starts focus sessions + 15-min allowances only'. 'Anna's wallet (QR) — emergency key, held by Anna'. Button: '+ Write a new tag'. Footnote: 'Any blank NFC tag works. They cost about a dollar.'

screens.title: Schedule
screens.purpose: Make the evening lock automatic so willpower isn't consulted at 9 PM.
screens.hero: A week band with the nightly lock window shaded ember at the edges
screens.data: 'Weeknights: locks itself 9:00 PM → 7:00 AM'. 'Weekends: off'. Rule line: 'A scheduled lock can only be lifted with a key, same as manual.' Next: 'Tonight at 9:00 PM, in 2h 14m'.

screens.title: Emergency exit
screens.purpose: Provide a real way out with honest friction and no shame.
screens.hero: A 10:00 delay countdown, plainly explained before it starts
screens.data: 'Emergency unlock: starts a 10-minute delay, then the lock opens.' 'Anna gets a message the moment you start it: "Mark used the emergency exit, 10:52 PM."' Buttons: 'Start the 10 minutes' · 'Never mind'. Log shows: 'Used once in 62 days.'

screens.title: Tag won't read
screens.purpose: Handle a failed NFC read without turning it into a loophole or a trap.
screens.hero: The ripple rendered broken at one ring, with the fallback path beneath
screens.data: 'Tag not reading? Try the top edge of the phone, remove thick cases.' Fallback: 'Every tag has a paired backup QR — yours is printed in Keys → Garage → backup code.' Hard case: 'Tag destroyed or lost: emergency exit still works, delay and message apply.'

screens.title: Paywall
screens.purpose: Price the barrier against the hardware it replaces, without pressure.
screens.hero: Two plain price cards next to a one-dollar tag illustration
screens.data: '$19.99/year' or '$39.99 once, lifetime'. Comparison, stated flat: 'A hardware key fob with the same job sells for $50–100. Your key is a $1 sticker; you're paying for the lock.' Included: unlimited tags, schedules, allowances, emergency exit. Links: 'Restore purchase' · 'Keep the free plan: one tag, one schedule'.

screens.title: First launch: no key yet
screens.purpose: The state between installing and owning a physical key.
screens.hero: An unlit ripple mark, gray instead of ember
screens.data: 'No key written yet. The lock can't start without one — that's the point.' Buttons: 'Write an NFC tag now' · 'Print a QR key instead'. Line: 'Grocery stores sell NFC tags. So does the junk drawer, if there's an old tag in it.'

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Set strictness once, then stop touching it.
screens.hero: A short matte list with 'Strictness' at the top
screens.data: 'Strictness: Standard (emergency exit on, 10 min) / Strict (exit off — a lost key means waiting out the schedule)'. 'Blocked apps: 3'. 'Screen Time access: active ✓'. 'Trusted person: Anna'. 'Session log: export CSV'. 'Notifications: only lock start and end, nothing else — ever'.

focus-productivity-7.territory: It is 7:12 AM and the person is already behind, half-dressed, with no internal clock telling them how long anything takes. The interface answers with one enormous, calm instruction at a time, like a patient friend standing in the doorway saying what comes next. Nothing competes for attention because the whole screen is the current step.

palette.note: Morning-air blue is reserved for the one live thing on screen, the draining time fill, so color itself tells you where time is going.

focus-productivity-7.typography: GT Walsheim in light and regular weights with oversized thin timer numerals, so the biggest thing on screen always reads as air, not alarm.
focus-productivity-7.motif: The draining fill: during a step the entire screen slowly empties of accent color from top to bottom like a water level, so remaining time is felt peripherally without reading a single digit.

ia.coreObject: The routine, an ordered list of steps each carrying its own time budget
ia.primaryLoop: Every morning the user hits Start once, the app walks them step by step to the door hands-free, and the planned-versus-actual recap afterwards makes tomorrow's budgets a little more honest.

screens.title: First morning, empty
screens.purpose: Turn a blank app into a first routine in under a minute without a lecture.

focus-productivity-8.territory: The thumb is already on the Instagram icon before the mind has said anything; the person arrives here mid-reflex, slightly embarrassed, not looking to be punished. The interface answers with the stillness of a held breath: one question, acres of warm white, and the quiet confidence that a person who names their reason will keep their word. It never blocks the door, it just makes the doorway conscious.

palette.note: Warm fog-white with a single sage accent that lives only in the breath ring and the kept-promise moments, so color appears exactly when intention does.

focus-productivity-8.typography: GT Alpina Light for the pause questions and Untitled Sans for everything else: a soft literary serif that makes the interruption feel like a thought rather than an alert, over a deliberately plain workhorse.
focus-productivity-8.motif: The breath ring: one thin sage circle that swells with a single inhale during the pause, then quietly shrinks into the corner as the live session countdown, so entry and exit are the same drawn breath.

ia.coreObject: The intentional session (a named reason plus a chosen number of minutes)
ia.primaryLoop: Several times a day the pause intercepts a reflex, the person names why and picks minutes, and the evening summary shows how often they kept their own word.

screens.title: Choose what gets a pause
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: pick the apps that deserve a doorway, with the privacy promise up front.
screens.hero: A short app list with gentle toggles, the promise line set in the serif
screens.data: Instagram — on · TikTok — on · X — on · YouTube — off · Reddit — off. Line beneath: 'Everything runs through Apple's Screen Time on this phone. No account, no server, we never see what you open.'

screens.title: One permission
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: the Screen Time grant, explained in one honest sentence.
screens.hero: A single card with the system permission framed by calm whitespace
screens.data: 'To place a pause before Instagram, iOS asks you to allow Screen Time access. That is the entire setup.' Button: 'Allow in Settings'. Sub-line: 'Takes about 20 seconds. Nothing else to configure.'

screens.title: Nothing yet, on purpose
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state: the product's value happens elsewhere, and this screen says so gracefully.
screens.hero: The breath ring at rest in the center of an almost empty page
screens.data: 'All set. The first pause will meet you the next time you open Instagram. There is nothing to check here until then.' Small line: 'Today so far: 0 pauses, which is fine.'

screens.title: The pause
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the reflex interrupted with one breath, one question, one choice of minutes.
screens.hero: The breath ring swelling over five seconds with the question set beneath it
screens.data: Ring caption: 'One breath.' Question: 'Why Instagram, right now?' Intent chips: 'Reply to a DM' · 'Post something' · 'Just checking'. Time row: '2 min · 5 min · 10 min'. Bottom, quiet and equal-weight: 'Never mind'. Selected: 'Reply to a DM · 5 min'.

screens.title: Your five minutes are up
screens.purpose: The honest exit, the half of the mechanic users have been asking for: a soft close that quotes the user to themselves.
screens.hero: The shrunken breath ring completing its circle over a dimming Instagram
screens.data: 'You came to reply to a DM. You gave yourself 5 minutes, they are up.' Buttons: 'Done, close it' (primary) · '2 more minutes'. Footnote: 'Going back in is allowed, through the same doorway.' No red, no siren, the ring simply completes.

screens.title: Turned around
screens.purpose: The deflection moment celebrated at the exact scale it deserves: small, real, counted.
screens.hero: The ring exhaling closed with a modest counter beneath
screens.data: 'Never mind, then. That is the 4th time today the pause turned you back at the door.' Sub-line: 'Roughly 11 unplanned minutes stayed yours, by your own past averages.' Single button: 'Back to your day'.

screens.title: Today, on one screen
screens.purpose: The daily summary: sessions, intentional minutes and deflections, with no scolding charts.
screens.hero: Three large serif figures on white, a thin timeline of the day's sessions below
screens.data: '7 sessions · 23 intentional minutes · 4 turnarounds.' Timeline entries: '08:12 Instagram, DM reply, 5 min, closed on time' · '13:40 TikTok, just checking, 2 min, ran 4 min over' · '19:05 Instagram, turned around'. Caption on the overrun: 'ran over', in gray, stated once, not colored.

screens.title: Words in your own voice
screens.purpose: The custom prompt editor: the pause question becomes something only this user would write.
screens.hero: A prompt card mid-edit in the serif, with per-app assignment beneath
screens.data: Prompts: 'Did you reply to Anna's brief?' → shows before Instagram, weekdays 9:00 to 18:00. 'You already saw everything at lunch.' → TikTok, after 20:00. 'Two, five, or zero minutes?' → X, always. Note: 'Your words interrupt better than ours.'

screens.title: After eleven, softer still
screens.purpose: The late-night state the mechanic demands: past a chosen hour the pause dims and lengthens by a breath.
screens.hero: The pause screen in an evening-dimmed warm gray, ring swelling a touch slower
screens.data: 'It is 23:40.' Question: 'Will this help you sleep?' Time chips reduced: '2 min · 5 min'. Toggle referenced from settings: 'Wind-down pause after 23:00 — on'. Same 'Never mind' in its usual place; nothing is blocked, the doorway is just quieter.

screens.title: A fair price for a doorway
screens.purpose: Paywall in the product's calm register: two plain prices, the free part stated first, no countdowns.
screens.hero: One centered card with generous margins and the ring as a faint watermark
screens.data: 'The pause before one app is free, forever. Everything: all your apps, timed sessions with the soft close, custom prompts, the daily summary. $14.99 a year, or $29.99 once for lifetime.' Buttons: 'Try free for 7 days' · 'Restore purchase'. Footnote: 'Cancel anytime; your pauses keep working through the paid period.'

screens.purpose: Pause length per app, wind-down hour, and the data statement, all on one quiet page.
screens.hero: A grouped list with the per-app pause sliders drawn as small rings
screens.data: 'Instagram: 8-second pause · TikTok: 15 seconds · X: 3 seconds.' 'Wind-down after: 23:00 — on.' 'Breath pace: slow.' 'Data: everything on this phone, nothing leaves it. Export summary (CSV) · Erase history.'

food-delivery-1.territory: A driver is parked outside a Wingstop with the engine running, a ping buzzes, and they have about eight seconds to decide whether this order feeds their family or burns their gas. The category's daylight-appetite tone flips to the other side of the counter: this is a work cockpit, glare, night shifts, one hand on the wheel. The interface answers like a good dispatcher: instant, legible at arm's length, all verdict and zero decoration.

palette.note: Color is the verdict and nothing else: signal green means the order pays, worn red #E14D4D means trap, and every other element stays asphalt-grey so a two-second glance at a mounted phone can't misread.

food-delivery-1.typography: Barlow Condensed, the DNA of highway signage, sets the giant per-mile figures readable from a dash mount, while Inter keeps restaurant names and shift logs plainly clerical.
food-delivery-1.motif: The verdict plate: every incoming order condenses into a license-plate-styled card, embossed edge and all, stamped with its $/mile figure, that the driver mentally screws on or throws away.

ia.coreObject: The order verdict, one incoming ping scored on pay, miles and kitchen wait before the accept timer runs out
ia.primaryLoop: A ping arrives, the plate renders the verdict in under two seconds, the driver accepts or passes with real numbers, and every closed shift feeds the log that sharpens tomorrow's verdicts.

screens.title: Pick your platforms

food-delivery-5.territory: The manager checks the phone between lunch and dinner rush, braced for another platform penalty they'll learn about too late. The interface answers with expo-line clarity: every complaint is a ticket on a rail, sorted and priced, in bright daylight tones that feel like a clean kitchen at 10am, not a corporate BI tool. Speed of comprehension is the whole product — one glance, one culprit, back to the pass.

palette.note: Warm daylight paper with kitchen-white cards; the charred-orange accent is reserved for error counts and penalty dollars so heat literally means money burning.

food-delivery-5.typography: Söhne for labels and headlines, Söhne Mono for order numbers, dollar amounts and timestamps — the mono gives every ticket the terse authority of a kitchen printer chit.
food-delivery-5.motif: The expo rail: complaints ride across the top of every view as kitchen tickets clipped to a horizontal rail, and resolving one physically slides it off the line.

ia.coreObject: The error ticket (one complaint or refund, categorized, priced, and pinned to a shift and menu item)
ia.primaryLoop: Twice a day the manager scans the rail, sees which item and shift are bleeding, fixes the prep or the pack station, and watches tomorrow's rail come back shorter.

habit-tracking-1.territory: The person has deleted thirty trackers, each one after a sick day turned months of effort into a zero, and they open this one flinching in advance. The interface answers with the crisp, rhythmic satisfaction of laying one brick at a time on a wall that cannot be knocked down: a tap lands with weight, a miss leaves a gap that gets mortared over, and nothing on any screen is capable of resetting. Guilt is a design defect here, not a motivator.

palette.note: Green is laid, never lost: it accumulates brick by brick along each habit's course and no state in the app can take laid green away.

habit-tracking-1.typography: Circular with a slightly heavy medium for habit names and springy rounded checkmarks, so every tick lands with the pleasure of a well-made switch.
habit-tracking-1.motif: The brick course: each habit's progress is a horizontal course of small bricks, one laid per done day, misses leaving gaps that get visibly mortared over when forgiven, so history reads as a wall being built, not a chain that can snap.

ia.coreObject: The habit, a name and a daily time window whose history is a growing course of bricks
ia.primaryLoop: Once a day inside each habit's window the user lands a single tap, watches the brick set, and comes back tomorrow because the wall only ever grows.

screens.title: First open: one habit, twenty seconds
screens.purpose: The empty state that gets a first habit in before doubt catches up.
screens.hero: A single card with a name field, a time-window slider, and a running 20-second unobtrusive counter proving the promise.
screens.data: Name: 'Take meds'. Window: 7:00 to 10:00 AM. Done. Counter reads 0:14 when finished. Line: 'That is the whole setup. No icons to choose, no goals essay.'

screens.title: Onboarding 2 of 2: the forgiveness math
screens.purpose: State the rules that make this tracker safe before the first miss ever happens.
screens.hero: A brick course with one gap being mortared over in a short looping demo.
screens.data: 'Three misses a month do not count. Illness or travel: pause with one tap, history stays. Did it yesterday: log it today, no penalty.' Single button: 'Sounds fair'. No permissions requested yet.

screens.title: Today, mid-use
screens.purpose: The main screen at 8 AM: big tap targets, courses growing, forgiveness balance visible without being loud.
screens.hero: Three habit cards with fat circular checks, 'Take meds' already ticked with its newest brick still settling.
screens.data: Take meds, done 8:02, course 78% of June laid. Stretch 10 min, window until 11 AM. Journal one line, window opens 8 PM. Corner note: '2 forgiven misses left in June'. No streak number anywhere.

screens.title: The tick
screens.purpose: The core interaction at full satisfaction: one tap, one brick, dopamine without a leaderboard.

habit-tracking-10.territory: A systematic person seven years into tracking opens the app not for a dopamine badge but to add today's row to a body of work, with a low hum of fear that one phone upgrade could erase it all. The interface answers like a bank ledger and a family archive at once: unhurried, verifiable, built to outlive the device it runs on. Every mark feels deposited, not gamified.

palette.note: Cool archival gray-green paper with a ledger-green accent that only ever fills completed cells, so density of green literally equals accumulated life.

habit-tracking-10.typography: IBM Plex Mono for every date, count, and checksum, IBM Plex Sans for prose; the monospace numerals make the archive feel audited rather than decorated.
habit-tracking-10.motif: The core sample: each habit's full multi-year history rendered as one continuous woven strip of day-cells, drilled through time like a glacier core, that you can pinch from a decade down to a single week.

ia.coreObject: The record: one habit's unbroken day-by-day ledger stretching back years, exportable and verifiable at any moment
ia.primaryLoop: Check off today's habits in ten seconds, then glance at the strip growing one cell longer, with the pull of never breaking an archive you have kept since 2020.

screens.title: Bring your history

screens.data: 'Exercise · 2020–2026 · 1,413 of 2,310 days'. Visible texture: the sparse 2020 rows, dense 2023, a pale two-week gap labeled on tap 'Nov 2024 — you paused for 16 days (broken wrist note)'. Yearly totals in the margin: '2020: 96 · 2023: 289 · 2026 so far: 121'.

habit-tracking-2.territory: He is mid-stride between the kitchen and the car, wrist raised, with four seconds of attention to give a habit before the day takes over. The interface answers like a precision hand tool: the click of a good tally counter, instant, mechanical, done before doubt arrives. The app itself is almost never opened, and that is its proudest feature.

palette.note: Matte tool-grey neutrals with a single international-orange strike used only at the instant of a completed log, like the painted tip of a switch that has just been flipped.

habit-tracking-2.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk for labels at glance-size, IBM Plex Mono for every count and timestamp so the numbers feel machined; nothing is ever set smaller than the wrist can read.
habit-tracking-2.motif: The tally notch: every log carves one short orange stroke, strokes gang into groups of five, and a month becomes a wall of hand-cut marks that users screenshot and show their friends.

ia.coreObject: The log event: one habit, one timestamp, one notch, captured from whichever surface was closest
ia.primaryLoop: Tap the lock screen, the watch, or say the phrase without breaking stride, feel the notch land, and glance at the growing tally wall in the evening.

screens.title: Pick your three

You may never need to open this app again.'

screens.data: Widget row: creatine, run, reading, each a tap target with today's state. Tap on creatine: the notch strikes, haptic fires, widget reads 'creatine, 7:42'. No unlock, no app launch, no confirmation dialog. Caption in spec: total interaction time 0.8 seconds.

screens.title: Wrist only, phone at home
screens.purpose: The standalone watch mechanic at its earning moment: logging on a run with the phone two miles away.
screens.hero: A watch face mockup with the complication, then the full-screen tap target after one press.
screens.data: Watch screen: 'Morning run' with a single large notch button, logged at 6:58 AM. Status line: 'Saved on watch. 3 logs waiting for your phone.' Below: creatine and reading rows scrollable with the crown. No 'connect your phone' error anywhere, by design.

screens.title: The handshake
screens.purpose: The sync-conflict state the mechanics demand: watch and phone both logged, and the app resolves it without asking.
screens.hero: A quiet merge card that appears once, already resolved, in the app's inbox.
screens.data: 'Your watch synced 3 logs from this morning. One overlap found: creatine logged on the widget at 7:42 and on the watch at 7:43. We kept the earlier one.' Single button: 'Fine'. Footnote: 'Both timestamps preserved in history in case we chose wrong.'

screens.title: Say it and go
screens.purpose: The voice mechanic: the phrase works out of the box and answers with the count, not a menu.
screens.hero: A Siri transcript pane over a blurred kitchen, response rendered in the app's mono numerals.
screens.data: Her: 'Hey Siri, log reading.' Siri: 'Reading logged, 8:56 PM. That is 12 days in a row.' Nothing else: no disambiguation question, no 'open the app to finish'. Below in spec: the phrase also works from CarPlay and AirPods.

screens.title: You are at the gym

habit-tracking-3.territory: A parent sets up tomorrow morning at 10 pm, knowing that whether the schedule holds decides whether the whole family's morning holds. The interface answers with crisp, predictable calm: big pictogram cards, one step at a time, checkmarks that land with quiet satisfaction and never with confetti. For the child it feels safe because it looks exactly the same every single day, on every device.

palette.note: Teal means done and only done; each role wears a soft fixed tone (parent slate, child sun-yellow card borders, observer gray) so who-can-do-what is visible at a glance.

habit-tracking-3.typography: Nunito on the child's screens, round and steady like the pictograms, with Inter for the parent's editing tools.
habit-tracking-3.motif: The flip: each pictogram card physically flips face-down when its step is done, like a paper first-then board, leaving a growing row of quiet teal card backs.

ia.coreObject: the routine (an ordered strip of pictogram steps belonging to one child, live on every connected device)
ia.primaryLoop: The parent tunes tonight what tomorrow looks like, the child flips through the morning card by card, and everyone who cares watches the strip fill from wherever they are.

habit-tracking-4.territory: It is 9:40 pm and you have not run yet, and the only thing that gets you off the couch is knowing Dana will see the empty dot. The interface answers with the crisp satisfaction of a scoreboard kept between friends: rhythmic, honest, a little competitive, never preachy. Every screen is built around the moment two marks land side by side.

palette.note: You are always deep green and your partner is always warm ochre (#D98E22), so any grid of dots reads as two people at a glance; red never appears, a miss is simply an unfilled ring.

habit-tracking-4.typography: Manrope for everything with tabular numerals for streaks and counts; tight, geometric, and rhythmic like a well-kept ledger, with weight jumps (800 for today's number, 500 for labels) doing the emphasis instead of color.
habit-tracking-4.motif: The twin dot: every habit-day is a pair of circles side by side, yours left and theirs right, and the daily payoff is watching both fill within hours of each other.

habit-tracking-7.territory: It is 03:40 in a break room lit by a vending machine, and every habit app on her phone insists her day ended four hours ago. The interface answers with the steady warmth of a night-shift ward lamp: dark because her eyes are adapted, calm because her streak is safe, and built on the radical premise that her clock is the real one. Small wins still click satisfyingly shut, they just click on her schedule.

palette.note: A deep night-blue field with a single sodium-lamp amber that marks completed habits and the live position on the dial, kept dim enough to read at 3 a.m. without lighting up the ward.

habit-tracking-7.typography: Suisse Int'l with Suisse Int'l Mono for all times and counters: crisp Swiss neutrality for labels, monospaced digits that read like good shift-board signage.
habit-tracking-7.motif: The rotated dial: a 24-hour-plus ring whose zero point sits wherever the user's day starts, with the sleep arc shaded, so the entire product visibly orbits their clock instead of midnight.

habit-tracking-8.territory: She is about to log a meal she half-dreads writing down, braced for a verdict the way old apps trained her to be. The interface answers with the warmth of a table set for one: sensory, quick, and completely free of judgment, so the log feels like noticing rather than confessing.

habit-tracking-8.motif: The before-and-after pair: every plate photo wears two small dots joined by a soft arc, hunger going in and fullness coming out, the only measurement in the entire product.

habit-tracking-9.territory: Someone starting 75 Hard has already decided to be hard on themselves; they are not looking for encouragement, they are looking for a referee who cannot be argued with. The interface answers with the stark clarity of a signed contract: black ink on white paper, rules printed in full, a stamp for every honest day. Its warmth is respect, never softness, and its strictness is always by the book they chose.

palette.note: Stark black-on-white like a printed rulebook, with one safety-orange ink reserved for the stamp of a completed day and the verdict of a failed one, so the same color certifies both truths.

habit-tracking-9.typography: Druk Condensed for day numbers and verdicts with Neue Haas Grotesk for rules and body: poster-weight condensed capitals for the numbers you earn, cool grotesque for the fine print you agreed to.
habit-tracking-9.motif: The ink stamp: every completed day is certified with a heavy circular 'DAY 23 · COMPLETE' stamp pressed onto its ledger card, slightly imperfect like real ink, and a failed round's cards stay stamped in the archive.

ia.coreObject: The day card (one dated ledger card holding the protocol's full checklist and its verdict)
ia.primaryLoop: Each day the participant works through the printed checklist, shoots the progress photo, and earns the stamp before their own day boundary; the growing stack of stamped cards is the pull.

hiking-trails-1.territory: The user opens the app on the couch the evening after a hike, boots off, legs pleasantly sore, annoyed that a 30 km drive home is glued to their beautiful loop. The interface answers with the calm of a well-organized map table: warm cartographic paper, precise tools, the quiet satisfaction of cropping a photograph. Not an adventure app, a darkroom for tracks.

palette.note: The paper-cream background stays constant like a topo sheet; the single blaze-orange is reserved for the track polyline and trim handles, so color always means 'your route'.

hiking-trails-1.typography: IBM Plex Sans for UI and IBM Plex Mono for every number that matters (distance, elevation, coordinates), giving stats the honest feel of surveyor's field notes rather than fitness-app bragging.
hiking-trails-1.motif: Trail-blaze trim handles: the drag handles on the track slider are painted rectangles like the orange blazes on trees, and every trimmed-away segment fades to a dashed pencil line instead of vanishing.

ia.coreObject: The track (a recorded polyline with edit history)
ia.primaryLoop: Record the hike, come home, trim the junk in under a minute, name it, and export or save a clean keepsake worth revisiting.

hiking-trails-8.territory: The user is standing on a fire line or a logging road, gloved, squinting into full sun, radio on the shoulder, and the map has to answer a question in five seconds or it has failed. The interface answers with the blunt confidence of issued equipment: nothing decorative, everything oversized, high-contrast, and exactly where muscle memory expects it. It should feel like a tool that ships in a Pelican case.

palette.note: Near-white for sunlight legibility with hi-vis chartreuse strictly on interactive targets and your own position, so the accent literally means 'safe to touch'; a red-shifted night scheme replaces the whole palette after dark.

hiking-trails-8.typography: FF DIN and FF DIN Condensed at generous sizes with wide tracking on labels, the same engineering voice as the signage and equipment stencils these crews already trust; coordinates always set in DIN tabular figures.
hiking-trails-8.motif: The graticule crosshair: a thin surveyor's cross with tick marks sits at screen center over every map, and all readouts (coordinates, datum, bearing) hang off its arms like a plotted point on an incident map.

ia.coreObject: The georeferenced map file (geoPDF/GeoTIFF) with its marker layer
ia.primaryLoop: Load the day's agency map before leaving coverage, navigate and drop photo markers all shift with gloves on, hand the marker layer to the crew boss at debrief.

interior-design-1.territory: The user is standing in their actual living room, phone raised, already burned once by an AI that bricked over their window and handed back a stranger's house. The interface answers with architectural sobriety: it treats their room like a surveyed site, drawing what is locked before it dreams about what could change. Trust is built by showing the geometry being held, not by promising it.

palette.note: Blueprint blue is reserved exclusively for locked structure, so anywhere blue appears the user knows the AI is forbidden to touch it.

interior-design-1.typography: Founders Grotesk for UI and GT Sectra for style names and result captions; the grotesque does the surveying, the serif does the desiring.
interior-design-1.motif: The blueprint lock: walls, windows, and doors traced in fine blueprint-blue linework with tiny padlock tick marks at corners, visible before, during, and after every generation.

ia.coreObject: The room (one photo with a locked structural map and a stack of makeovers on top)
ia.primaryLoop: Photograph a room, confirm the locks, and generate style passes until one is worth acting on, returning with each new room or each new decision (sofa, paint, rug)

screens.title: Onboarding: the promise, drawn
screens.purpose: State the one differentiator visually before asking for anything.

interior-design-6.territory: A realtor or owner is racing a listing deadline with photos of a cold, echoing apartment, and they have been burned by AI toys that melted the windows or returned the photo untouched. The interface answers like a trusted staging vendor: warm, unhurried, editorial, and obsessively honest about what was changed and what was not. It should feel like an interiors magazine spread run by a licensed surveyor.

palette.note: Walnut brown appears only where furniture was added, on seam handles, staging tags and confirm buttons, so the accent itself marks what is virtual and the photography stays untinted.

interior-design-6.typography: GT Sectra gives headlines and property names the voice of an interiors editorial, while Söhne handles labels, dimensions and integrity reports with vendor-grade neutrality.
interior-design-6.motif: The staging seam: every furnished photo carries a draggable hairline seam between the empty original and the staged result, with a small brass 'Virtually staged' tag riveted to the lower corner that survives export.

ia.coreObject: The property, a set of rooms each holding an original photo and its staged twin
ia.primaryLoop: Upload the rooms of today's listing, review each staged result against the original along the seam, approve, export to the listing platform, and come back with the next mandate.

intermittent-fasting-1.territory: He wakes up realizing he never tapped start last night, already braced for the app to have punished him again. The interface answers with unbothered calm: time is soft here, the record bends to the truth in one drag, and nothing you fix is ever treated as cheating.

palette.note: Mist and dusk violet keep the clock feeling like evening-to-morning rather than a stopwatch; edited entries render in the same violet as live ones, because corrected time is not second-class.

intermittent-fasting-1.typography: Suisse Int'l in light weights with tabular numerals, so an 18:24 fast reads as quiet fact rather than scoreboard.
intermittent-fasting-1.motif: The elastic band: every fast is a soft rounded band on the day column that you stretch or slide by its ends, giving a little rubbery resistance as it snaps to real times.

ia.coreObject: Fast
ia.primaryLoop: Glance at the timer while fasting, and each morning nudge yesterday's band to what actually happened.

screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: match the app to a practice that already exists.

intermittent-fasting-2.territory: It is 6:40 pm and the person glances at the clock wondering if dinner still fits inside the window. Months past the point where fasting itself was hard, what needs tending now is the edge of the eating window, not willpower. The interface answers with the calm of a well-made wall clock: two quiet hands, no cheering, no shame, just the honest time on both sides of the line.

palette.note: Sage belongs to the eating window and the fasting arc stays graphite, so color alone tells you which clock is live right now.

intermittent-fasting-2.typography: Söhne for interface text and Söhne Mono for the timer digits, a quiet Swiss neutrality that makes the two clocks feel like instruments rather than alarms.
intermittent-fasting-2.motif: One circle, two hands: a single dial where the graphite fast arc and the sage window arc chase each other around the same ring, always meeting at the exact minute the window opens.

ia.coreObject: The eating window, a daily entry with a real open time and a real close time
ia.primaryLoop: Twice a day, at the edges of the window, the person opens the app to open or close on time, and the one-hour closing alert is what brings them back every single evening.

intermittent-fasting-3.territory: Hour 17 of an OMAD fast, and the practitioner does not want cheerleading, they want to know what their liver is doing and whether the next two hours are worth it. The interface answers with the composure of a laboratory field notebook: precise, unhurried, honest about ranges instead of stopwatch promises. It treats the user as a colleague studying their own physiology, which is exactly what keeps them holding the fast.

palette.note: Ecru paper like a lab notebook page, with a deep viridian that marks the single stratum your body currently occupies, so the scale reads at a glance without a flame graphic in sight.

intermittent-fasting-3.typography: Tiempos Text for the physiology explanations and National 2 for interface and timers: a scientific-journal serif that earns trust in long passages, paired with a grotesque that keeps numbers matter-of-fact.
intermittent-fasting-3.motif: The strata scale: fasting phases drawn as a vertical geological core sample, each stratum labeled and calibrated to the user's protocol, with the current hour marked as a depth line descending through it.

intermittent-fasting-4.territory: The user is 50 hours into a 72-hour fast, slightly cold, wide awake at 2 a.m., and needs to know that what their body is doing is normal and that someone built this room for people like them. The interface answers with the calm of a night vigil: dark, quiet, unhurried, counting hours in a single unbroken line that treats midnight as just another hour. Nothing celebrates, nothing nags, everything explains.

palette.note: Deep night-indigo ground that never flashes; the warm ember accent marks only the present hour and reached milestones, glowing brighter as the fast goes deeper instead of shouting.

intermittent-fasting-4.typography: Suisse Int'l in light weights with large tabular numerals for hour counters, so 52:14:08 reads like a quiet instrument panel rather than a stopwatch under pressure.
intermittent-fasting-4.motif: The unbroken line: one continuous horizontal hour-line that runs through faint moon ticks at each midnight it crosses, never resetting, never splitting a fast at a calendar boundary.

intermittent-fasting-5.territory: She finished the book with a highlighter in hand and opened the App Store expecting the calendar it describes, and found generic timers wearing pink labels. The interface answers with the quiet authority of a well-made almanac: warm, literate, unhurried, organized around her cycle the way the protocol actually is. It treats the luteal slowdown as wisdom, not weakness, and never once pressures her with a scale or a deadline.

palette.note: Warm linen with deep aubergine ink and a single mulberry accent that always marks 'where you are in your cycle today', so the color system itself is keyed to the body, not the weekday.

intermittent-fasting-5.typography: Ogg for headings and Basis Grotesque for the working interface: a bookish, editorial serif that honors the fact this audience came from a book, grounded by a plainspoken grotesque for plans and timers.
intermittent-fasting-5.motif: The spiral month: the cycle drawn as a single inward spiral starting at day one of menstruation, with fasting windows wrapping it as bands that widen and narrow with the phases, a calendar no weekday grid could produce.

ia.coreObject: The cycle-keyed fasting plan (one spiral where cycle days and fasting windows are the same object)
ia.primaryLoop: Each morning she sees today's position on the spiral and the fast length her phase calls for, logs the fast, and trusts the plan to soften on its own as her period approaches.

intermittent-fasting-7.territory: Six weeks into 16:8, twelve pounds down, he keeps toggling between the fasting app and the weight chart trying to hold both shapes in his head at once. The interface answers like a well-kept lab notebook: two instruments on one page, drawn on the same time axis, so the sentence 'the weeks I held my windows are the weeks the line went down' becomes something he can see instead of believe. Calm, gridded, evidentiary.

palette.note: Pale graph-paper blue-grey with a faint printed grid; the weight curve alone owns the warm persimmon, fast bars stay slate, and nothing on the chart is ever red because a bump is a data point, not a verdict.

intermittent-fasting-7.typography: Suisse Int'l with tabular figures for every axis, weight, and hour count so the two registers align to the pixel, and Suisse Works italic reserved for the user's own annotations, which read like margin notes in a lab book.
intermittent-fasting-7.motif: The dual register: one shared time axis with the persimmon weight curve riding above and slate fast bars stacked below, joined by faint vertical gridlines, a chart format that belongs to this app the way the candlestick belongs to trading.

ia.coreObject: The timeline: one continuous record where every fast bar and every weigh-in share the same dated grid

invoice-maker-1.territory: A contractor is sitting in the truck after a site visit, quoting the job while the details are fresh and the homeowner is still warm. They are selling, not bookkeeping, and every minute of friction costs commitment. The interface answers with showroom confidence: clean daylight paper where three options stand side by side and the middle one quietly looks like the right call.

palette.note: Green appears only where money commits, tier totals, the client's accept button, the paid stamp, so the whole app reads as paper until a number is about to be agreed to.

invoice-maker-1.typography: Söhne in medium weights for labels and trade names, with Söhne Mono tabular for every dollar figure so the three tier columns line up to the cent.
invoice-maker-1.motif: The triptych: every estimate lives as three physical side-by-side columns, Good, Better, Best, with the middle column raised a few points like the recommended door in a showroom, echoed down to the app icon's three bars.

ia.coreObject: The estimate, a three-tier quote that becomes an invoice the moment the client signs one column
ia.primaryLoop: After each site visit, build the three tiers from trade templates in the truck, send the link before leaving the driveway, and get the push when the client picks and signs.

invoice-maker-3.territory: The user is a freelancer who did the work weeks ago and now carries the awkward weight of chasing money, rehearsing a follow-up text they never send. The interface answers with the composure of a well-run back office: crisp paper, plain daylight, statuses stamped in ink, and a quiet machine that does the chasing so the owner never has to sound desperate. Certainty replaces guessing: you know the moment they looked.

palette.note: Ledger paper and ink; the single green accent is earned only by money states (paid, opened-and-moving), while overdue renders as heavy ink weight and stamps, never as panic red.

invoice-maker-3.typography: Founders Grotesk for interface and headers with its mono companion in tabular figures for every amount and timestamp, so $1,850.00 and 'opened Wed 8:15 am' line up like entries in a well-kept book.
invoice-maker-3.motif: The live stamp: every invoice wears an ink-stamp status block (SENT, OPENED x3, PAID) that visibly re-inks itself the moment the client acts, like a ledger that updates while you watch.

ia.coreObject: The invoice as a living document: amount, recipient, and a timeline of every time it was seen
ia.primaryLoop: Send an invoice as a link, get pinged the moment it is opened, and let scheduled reminders escalate politely until the stamp flips to PAID; check the feed each morning to see what moved overnight.

invoice-maker-4.territory: The person is mid-workday, switching from one client's project to another's with a call starting in three minutes, and every unlogged stretch is money quietly evaporating. The interface answers with the clarity of a paper timesheet in good daylight: white, exact, and one motion, press the row, the meter runs. It feels less like software and more like a well-kept ledger that bills for you at the end of the week.

palette.note: Highlighter yellow behaves like a marker on paper, sweeping across the one client row that is currently on the clock and across billable lines in the invoice, never used decoratively.

invoice-maker-4.typography: Suisse Int'l throughout with strict tabular numerals for every timer and money figure, so columns of hours and dollars align like a printed timesheet.
invoice-maker-4.motif: The highlighter stripe: running time is drawn as a yellow marker stroke growing across the active client's row, and the same stroke reappears on the invoice under the lines those hours became.

ia.coreObject: The client, a row holding a rate, a running or resting timer, and the week's accumulated hours
ia.primaryLoop: All week the user taps client rows to start and switch timers as work shifts, and on Friday one button turns each highlighted row into a sent invoice.

invoice-maker-5.territory: A tech in a crawlspace finishes a condenser swap and needs the invoice sent before the truck door closes, while the owner back at the desk wants to see the day's numbers without calling anyone. palette.note: Ledger blue marks sync state and primary actions only, money figures are always ink so a total never looks like a button.

invoice-maker-5.typography: Tiempos Text on the invoice sheets so documents read like documents, Untitled Sans for the interface around them, both set with roomy tabular figures for totals.
invoice-maker-5.motif: The carbon copy: every invoice sheet carries a faint offset duplicate behind it that snaps flush the instant the cloud confirms the save, so sync is something you see, not a spinner you trust.

ia.coreObject: The invoice, a server-truth document identical on every screen that shows it
ia.primaryLoop: The tech writes invoices on-site through the day and the owner watches them land in the office list the same minute, which is the daily heartbeat of the business.

invoice-maker-6.territory: The person is kneeling by a wheel they just mounted, hands not quite clean, and the only thing between them and being paid is whether the client sees the invoice before they drive off. The interface answers with professional daylight: paper-document calm on top, messenger immediacy underneath. It feels like handing over a printed bill that happens to arrive as a text.

palette.note: Ink navy carries all document chrome and the green appears only when money moves: sent is navy, opened is navy, paid is the single green moment the whole screen is built to reach.

invoice-maker-6.typography: Spectral for invoice numbers, totals and the client-facing bill, Inter for app chrome: the serif makes every invoice feel like a printed document, the sans keeps the sending fast and workmanlike.
invoice-maker-6.motif: The fold: every invoice is a white paper sheet that visibly folds down into a message bubble when sent, and the bubble keeps a tiny folded corner so you can always tell a bill from a chat.

ia.coreObject: The invoice, carrying its own delivery trail: which channel, opened when, paid how
ia.primaryLoop: Finish the job, build the invoice in under a minute, fire it into the channel the client actually reads, and watch it flip to green before the van door closes.

invoice-maker-8.territory: A contractor with dusty hands at the end of a job, wanting to get paid without a single argument about what was done. The interface answers with the calm of a well-kept job folder in daylight: paper clarity, everything already in order, the photos doing the talking so the person never has to defend their work out loud.

palette.note: Documentary neutrals let the job-site photos carry all the color; the safety-orange accent appears only on the seam between before and after and on the one button that sends money.

invoice-maker-8.typography: IBM Plex Sans for labels and line items with IBM Plex Mono for amounts and invoice numbers, the engineering-document pairing that makes a $840 total read like a fact, not a pitch.
invoice-maker-8.motif: The seam: a thin vertical hairline that splits every before/after photo pair, reused as the divider element across the entire app so every screen quietly says proof.

journaling-mood-1.territory: The person is carrying a week of half-finished thoughts toward a fifty-minute appointment that costs real money, afraid the important thing from Wednesday will vanish in the waiting room. The interface answers with the privacy and warmth of a good notebook, cream paper and ink, where flagging a thought feels like folding a page corner for later. It is quiet, unhurried, and always oriented toward one date: the next session.

palette.note: Ink on cream everywhere, with the wax-seal red spent only on the fold of a flagged entry and the session date, so red always means 'this goes to Thursday'.

journaling-mood-1.typography: Tiempos Text for entries and the compiled sheet, Graphik for interface labels, so the user's own words always look like a book and the chrome stays invisible.
journaling-mood-1.motif: The folded corner: flagging a note visibly dog-ears its top-right corner in seal red, and the night-before summary opens by unfolding those corners into a single page.

ia.coreObject: The entry, a short note or mood check-in that either rests in the week or gets folded toward the next session
ia.primaryLoop: During the week the user drops in notes and moods and folds the ones that matter, and the night before the appointment the app hands them one page that makes the session start at minute one.

journaling-mood-3.territory: Hands are full, the day is full, and the thought arrives in the car or over a sleeping baby's shoulder. The interface answers with warm, low-light patience: one press, two minutes of talking, and the promise that both the words and the voice itself will still be here in ten years.

palette.note: Warm neutrals hold everything still; mulberry breathes only in the record ring and playback thread, so the loudest thing on screen is always your own voice.

journaling-mood-3.typography: Tiempos Text sets every transcription like a printed diary page while National 2 keeps buttons and timestamps quiet; the entry reads as literature, the chrome as furniture.
journaling-mood-3.motif: The twin thread: a soft waveform strand that ties into a straight text baseline, the recording and its sentence joined as one continuous line.

ia.coreObject: The entry pair: one recording and its transcription, permanently together
ia.primaryLoop: One press, two minutes of talking wherever the day allows, then coming back later to read the week in clean text and hear the days that mattered.

journaling-mood-5.territory: It is one in the morning in the second month after the loss, and the words have nowhere to go. The interface answers like a lamplit desk: dark, warm, unhurried, holding the page open without ever suggesting she should be further along than she is.

palette.note: Light behaves like a lamp on a desk, the gold touches only the salutation and the pen, and the screen never brightens itself, least of all on the hard dates.

journaling-mood-5.typography: Lyon Text carries every word, the letters open in italic salutations, and the interface whispers in small caps of the same face so nothing on screen sounds like software.
journaling-mood-5.motif: The salutation: every letter begins with the person's name already set in italic, Dear Anna, so the page is never blank and the conversation never has to restart.

ia.coreObject: the letter, an entry addressed to the person who is gone
ia.primaryLoop: She writes when a wave comes, not on a schedule, and the letters and the memory room are where she returns on the hard days.

journaling-mood-6.territory: The person opens this at 4:30 PM with a spiraling thought still hot, and they already know the method that works because a therapist taught it to them. The interface answers like the paper workbook they trust: cream, ruled, structurally strict, asking the seven questions in order and never chatting back, because the protocol itself is the therapy.

palette.note: Fountain-ink blue belongs to the user's own written words and the intensity numbers; the app's structural text stays in warm ink-black, so the page always reads as theirs, not ours.

journaling-mood-6.typography: Charter carries every written thought like typeset prose in a well-bound workbook; National 2 in small sizes does the column labels and distortion tags with clinical quietness.
journaling-mood-6.motif: The intensity pair: every completed record ends in two inked numbers joined by a thin rule, 85→40, and that falling pair appears everywhere from entry rows to monthly charts as the product's signature of work done.

ia.coreObject: The thought record: one seven-column entry (situation, automatic thought, emotion, intensity, distortion, balanced response, re-rating) accumulating into monthly pattern statistics
ia.primaryLoop: Catch a hot thought, walk the seven columns in order, watch the intensity number drop, and return monthly to see which distortions repeat and what actually brings them down.

screens.title: Onboarding — the seven columns
screens.purpose: One-screen orientation showing the full worksheet structure so a CBT-literate user recognizes the real protocol immediately.
screens.hero: A miniature filled worksheet with all seven columns labeled, drawn like a page from Greenberger and Padesky.
screens.data: Columns: 'Situation · Automatic thought · Emotion · Intensity (0–100) · Distortion · Balanced response · Re-rate'. Caption: 'The full thought record. All seven columns, in order, every time.' Button: 'Set up my journal'.

language-learning-3.territory: An adult with an exam date on the calendar and four apps open in frustration, wanting one disciplined path instead of a juggling act. The interface answers with the bright, ordered calm of a beautifully made Japanese textbook: encouraging in color, rigorous in structure, never cute.

palette.note: Vermilion behaves like a teacher's hanko: it stamps corrections, today's seal and passed milestones, and is never used as a large decorative wash.

language-learning-3.typography: ABC Diatype carries the Latin interface while Hiragino Mincho ProN sets all Japanese study text; the kanji under study is always the largest element on screen, presented like a type specimen.
language-learning-3.motif: The practice square: a genkō yōshi grid cell with a faint centerline cross that frames every character you write, review or master.

language-learning-4.territory: An adult who quit Duolingo out of respect for their own time sits down for twenty real minutes with German cases. The interface answers like a brilliant tutor's whiteboard: bright, friendly, and absolutely rigorous, celebrating a correctly built sentence instead of a streak. Every color on screen means something grammatical.

palette.note: Cobalt carries structure; each grammatical role owns a fixed secondary hue (nominative teal, accusative orange, dative plum) used only inside sentence scaffolding, never as decoration.

language-learning-4.typography: Source Serif 4 for explanations, reading like a well-set textbook page, with General Sans for exercises and UI keeping the reps brisk.
language-learning-4.motif: Sentence scaffolding: color-coded brackets drawn under every example sentence that expose its structure like an engineer's drawing, and collapse away as your mastery grows.

ia.coreObject: the rule (one grammatical mechanism with its explanation, contexts, and review schedule)
ia.primaryLoop: Sit down for one rule or a review set, build every answer word by word, and watch the grammar map light up where the logic finally holds.

screens.title: Your language, your wall
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: pick the language and name the thing that never clicked.
screens.hero: A short list of honest walls instead of a marketing quiz
screens.data: Language: German. 'What never clicked?' — der/die/das and cases · word order · adjective endings · verb position. Selected: cases. 'Good. That's a system, and systems can be learned.'

screens.title: Build one sentence
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: a diagnostic where you construct, not guess, so placement is earned.
screens.hero: Word tiles being assembled over faint scaffolding brackets
screens.data: Tiles: Ich / gebe / dem Mann / den Schlüssel. Result: 'You placed the dative correctly but flipped the objects. Starting you at Case System, unit 2 of 9 — not from zero.'

screens.title: The unlit map
screens.purpose: First state: the whole grammar of German visible at once, honestly unmastered.
screens.hero: A constellation-style map of the language's structures, all nodes dim
screens.data: Cases: 0 of 12 rules · Word order: 0 of 8 · Verb system: 0 of 14 · Adjective endings: 0 of 6. One node pulsing: 'Start here: why German marks the receiver.'

screens.title: The mechanism
screens.purpose: Rule step 1: explain why the language does this, in plain prose, before any exercise.
screens.hero: A textbook-set explanation with one moving diagram: the tag traveling with its noun
screens.data: 'Dative marks the receiver. English shows it with position: give the man the key. German tags the noun instead — dem Mann — and because the tag carries the meaning, the words are free to move.'

screens.title: In the wild
screens.purpose: Rule step 2: the same mechanism found in a real text, brackets and all.
screens.hero: A genuine Berlin apartment listing with scaffolding drawn under one sentence
screens.data: 'Dem Mieter stehen Keller und Stellplatz zur Verfügung.' Plum bracket under 'Dem Mieter' — tap it: 'dative: the tenant is the receiver of the availability.'

screens.title: Now you build it
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: rule step 3, constructing the sentence word by word.
screens.hero: Word tiles snapping onto scaffolding, the dative slot glowing plum when filled right
screens.data: Task: 'Say: I'm giving my sister the car for the weekend.' Tiles placed so far: Ich gebe / meiner Schwester… Remaining: das Auto / für das Wochenende. Timer absent; a rep counter reads 4 of 9.

screens.title: Which logic broke
screens.purpose: The mistake breakdown: name the broken reasoning, not just the right answer.
screens.hero: The wrong tile lifted out, its bracket recolored to show the mistaken role
screens.data: You built: 'Ich gebe meine Schwester das Auto.' → 'Not wrong words — a wrong tag. You marked your sister as the thing being given (accusative). The receiver takes dative: meiner Schwester. Hook: the receiver wears the -er/-em tag.'

screens.title: It comes back
screens.purpose: The forgetting-curve return: the same rule, six days later, in a sentence you have never seen.
screens.hero: A single review card stamped with the rule's map node and days elapsed
screens.data: 'Back after 6 days: dative with feminine nouns. New sentence: Er dankt ___ Ärztin (der/die/den).' Correct returns in a row: 3. 'Next return in about 2 weeks if this holds.'

screens.data: Cases: 7 of 12 solid · 2 wobbly (adjective endings after ein-words, flagged from Tuesday's review) · 3 not started. Word order: unlocked. Line: '38 rules to a complete German scaffold.'

language-learning-8.territory: An evening study session with an exam date circled on the calendar: the person is disciplined but weary of swiping flashcards that evaporate by morning. The interface answers with the energy of a beautiful modern dictionary, bright and rigorous at once, where every word is a small story with an origin and a job to do. Encouragement here means clarity of progress, never cartoon confetti.

palette.note: Each of a word's four layers owns a color, slate for pronunciation, marigold for etymology, cobalt for contexts, green for your own sentence, so a fully learned word literally shows all four inks.

language-learning-8.typography: Literata gives headwords and etymologies the authority of a printed dictionary, while Work Sans keeps the drill mechanics brisk and modern.
language-learning-8.motif: The four-rung ladder: every word is a stacked card of four rungs, say it, trace its origin, see it used, use it yourself, and the word only counts as yours when the top rung is inked with your own sentence.

ia.coreObject: The word entry: a four-layer card of pronunciation, etymology, real contexts, and your own production
ia.primaryLoop: A daily session where due words come back demanding to be written and spoken, not just recognized, ticking down toward the exam date.

meal-prep-grocery-2.territory: One of them is in aisle 7 with a cart, the other is at home remembering the parmesan, and the entire relationship with this app hangs on one question: am I looking at the current list. The interface answers with greenhouse calm and receipt-level honesty about sync, always showing when the other phone last confirmed, so standing in the store never feels like guessing.

palette.note: Market green belongs to you and a soft plum belongs to your partner, so every mark on the list quietly says whose phone it came from.

meal-prep-grocery-2.typography: GT Walsheim in generous checkable rows gives the list a friendly grocery voice, with tabular figures for quantities and the sync timestamp.
meal-prep-grocery-2.motif: The two-dot sync mark: every item carries a pair of dots, green for your phone and plum for your partner's, that snap together into one mark the moment an edit lands on both.

ia.coreObject: The shared list: one living document two phones edit at once
ia.primaryLoop: Add items through the week from the couch and the kitchen, then shop against the list knowing every checkoff lands on the other phone within seconds.

meal-prep-grocery-3.territory: The person is standing in a store aisle or unpacking bags onto shelves, half-sure there is already ketchup at home and mildly annoyed at the thought of buying a third bottle. The interface answers with grocer's-ledger calm: everything on the shelf is simply known, by everyone in the house, without ceremony. It should feel like a well-kept kitchen notebook the whole family can read at once.

meal-prep-grocery-3.motif: The ripening dot: every pantry item carries a small circle that shifts from green through amber to brown as its expiry approaches, readable at a glance across a whole shelf row.

meal-prep-grocery-5.territory: Pushing a cart under fluorescent light with a hard hundred-dollar ceiling and a school-night dinner plan, doing register math in the head. The interface answers with fresh, list-driven calm: one big number that counts down instead of up, so the register can never spring a surprise.

meal-prep-grocery-5.motif: The ceiling line: a fixed rule at the top of the screen that the cart's total-bar rises toward, so the budget is architecture, not a stat.

meal-prep-grocery-6.territory: The user is a numbers person on a Sunday evening, planning a week they intend to execute exactly, and slightly braced for the app to argue with their macro targets. The interface answers with the calm of a well-run kitchen: fresh, gridded, list-driven, and completely non-judgmental about where the numbers point. It respects the target the way a scale respects weight.

palette.note: Green means on-target and nothing else; the macro tri-bar carries its own fixed trio (protein slate, fat butter, carb wheat) so numbers read before words.

meal-prep-grocery-6.typography: Rubik for UI with tabular lining figures everywhere numbers appear, and Rubik Medium for gram counts; the type is practical and roundly confident, like good packaging.
meal-prep-grocery-6.motif: The macro tri-bar: a three-segment stacked bar (protein/fat/carbs) that appears under every meal, every day, and the whole week, always drawn to the same scale so a keto day and a cutting day look visibly different.

meal-prep-grocery-7.territory: It is 6 pm, the fridge door is open, and the person is staring at spinach that has two days left and a shelf of half-ideas, tired of deciding. The interface answers with list-driven kitchen calm: it has already done the matching, tells the truth about what is missing, and turns tonight's decision into a pick between three honest cards.

palette.note: Herb green means 'you have it' and is earned segment by segment, while the single missing ingredient always shows as a warm amber gap, never red, never blame.

meal-prep-grocery-7.typography: Recoleta for recipe names, warm and cookbook-like, with Karla for lists and labels, so dinner reads like food and the pantry reads like a well-kept list.
meal-prep-grocery-7.motif: The missing slice: every recipe wears a segmented ring, one segment per ingredient, filled green for what you have, with the one amber gap you can tap to send the missing item to the shopping list.

meal-prep-grocery-8.territory: The user is half-watching a TikTok on the couch or holding grandma's grease-stained index card, afraid the find will vanish into a camera roll. The interface answers with the warmth of a well-organized family kitchen shelf: everything gets a card, every card shows where it came from, and everyone in the house can reach it. It should feel like a shared recipe box passed across generations, not a food database.

palette.note: Warm off-white kitchen light with basil green doing the work of confirmation and family presence, plus a small tomato red #D64533 used only for failed imports so honesty is visible.

meal-prep-grocery-8.typography: Fraunces for recipe titles with its warm cookbook character, Inter for ingredients and steps, and Caveat sparingly for the handwritten-source stamp, so grandma's card still feels handwritten inside the app.
meal-prep-grocery-8.motif: The source-stamped index card: every recipe is a lined index card with a taped top edge and a provenance stamp in the corner (TikTok, Instagram, handwritten, cookbook page, plus who in the family added it), so the shelf reads as a family history.
