period-cycle-1.territory: It is 7:04 AM and she is holding an LH strip over the bathroom sink, on cycle day 34 of a cycle that might run 60, tired of apps that congratulate her on a day-14 ovulation she never had. The interface answers with lab-bench composure: it reads her strip like an instrument, states its confidence out loud, and treats a cycle with no ovulation as a recorded fact rather than a failure. Nothing pink, nothing predicted that the data cannot back.

palette.note: Warm ivory like lab paper with a deep sea-teal reserved for measured values; forecast areas render in translucent teal whose opacity literally encodes confidence, and nothing on screen is ever red.

period-cycle-1.typography: GT Sectra for section heads and report prose to carry unhurried clinical authority, Untitled Sans with tabular figures for every LH ratio and temperature reading, so numbers always align like a lab table.
period-cycle-1.motif: The confidence band: every forecast is drawn as a translucent teal band across the timeline that is honestly wide when data is sparse and visibly narrows as strips and temperatures accumulate, so trust is something the user watches tighten.

ia.coreObject: The cycle chart: one continuous record of LH ratios, basal temperatures, and bleeding days with a confidence band ahead of today
ia.primaryLoop: Photograph the morning strip, let the ring's temperature flow in on its own, glance at whether the line is climbing, and come back tomorrow because the band around ovulation just got narrower.

screens.title: Your cycles, as they actually run
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: accept long, erratic, and absent cycles as the starting truth instead of forcing a 28-day default.
screens.hero: A single question, 'How long do your cycles usually run?', with ranges that go far past what other apps allow.
screens.data: Options: 21-35 days, 35-50 days, 50-90 days, 'honestly, they vary too much to say', 'sometimes months without a period'. Optional toggle: 'I have a PCOS diagnosis'. Footer: 'We will never assume day 14. Every forecast here is built from your tests and temperature, not a textbook average.'

screens.title: Your instruments
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: register the LH strip brand and temperature source so readings are calibrated from the first photo.
screens.hero: Two instrument cards, 'Test strips' and 'Temperature', each with concrete supported hardware.
screens.data: Strips: Wondfo, Easy@Home, Pregmate, 'other brand, calibrate from my first photo'. Temperature: Oura ring, Garmin watch, Apple Watch, manual thermometer. Selected: Easy@Home plus Oura. Button: 'Start cycle day 1 from my last period, February 8'.

screens.title: Cycle day 34
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: today's position on the chart with the confidence band ahead and both quick actions in thumb reach.
screens.hero: The full cycle chart: teal LH dots rising along the bottom, the temperature line above, and a wide translucent band covering days 36-47 labeled with its own confidence.
screens.data: Cycle day 34 of an open cycle. LH ratio this morning: 0.62, up from 0.43 two days ago. Basal temp: 97.41 F from Oura, arrived automatically at 6:50 AM. Band: 'Likely ovulation window: days 36-47, confidence moderate, built from 4 recorded cycles.' Buttons: 'Photograph strip', 'Add a note'.

screens.title: Reading your strip
screens.purpose: The core capture mechanic: the photo becomes a number in seconds, with the raw image kept as evidence.
screens.hero: The camera frame with an alignment guide over the strip, then the computed ratio appearing beside the test line.
screens.data: Photo taken 7:04 AM. Test line to control line ratio: 0.81. Plotted immediately as today's dot. Caption: 'Darker than yesterday's 0.62. Original photo saved to this cycle.' Suggestion, stated as one: 'Lines this dark often precede a peak. Testing again tonight would tighten the window.'

screens.title: The line is climbing
screens.purpose: The rising-LH moment that Premom users call the breakthrough: three strips in a row telling a direction.
screens.hero: A zoomed three-day strip gallery, actual photos side by side, with their ratios stepping upward beneath them.
screens.data: Day 32: 0.43. Day 33: 0.62. Day 34, this morning: 0.81. Note: 'Three rising readings. This is a real climb, not noise.' The confidence band on the mini chart visibly narrows from 11 days wide to 6. Button: 'Remind me to test at 9 PM tonight'.

screens.title: Peak caught
screens.purpose: Confirm the surge honestly: the LH peak is one signal, and the app says plainly that it is waiting on the second.
screens.hero: The day-35 dot at the top of the LH curve, ringed, with a watch note where other apps would print a verdict.
screens.data: Day 35, 9:12 PM: ratio 1.24, your highest this cycle. Status: 'LH peak detected. Watching your next 3 mornings of temperature for the shift that confirms ovulation.' Two mornings later: 97.38 to 97.82 F. Confirmation: 'Ovulation confirmed on day 36, backed by both signals.'

screens.title: An honest forecast
screens.purpose: Show what the confidence band is made of, so 'not sure yet' reads as rigor rather than weakness.
screens.hero: The band anatomy: layers labeled with which data source contributes what width.
screens.data: 'Window: days 36-47. Why this wide: your 4 recorded cycles ran 39, 47, 52, and 61 days. What narrows it: each strip photo this week, roughly minus 1 day per reading; a confirmed thermal shift, minus 4. What we will never do: name a single date we cannot defend.'

screens.title: Closing a cycle without ovulation
screens.purpose: The anovulatory mechanic: end a cycle that never peaked and file it as a normal, first-class record.
screens.hero: A calm closing sheet titled 'Close this cycle as anovulatory' with the flat LH curve shown as the reason.
screens.data: Cycle of 61 days, 14 strips logged, no ratio above 0.55, no thermal shift. Confirmation text: 'Anovulatory cycles are common with PCOS. This one stays in your history and improves future forecasts.' History strip below: 47 days, 61 days marked with a small open circle, 39, 52. Button: 'Close cycle, start day 1'.

screens.title: While you slept
screens.purpose: The wearable mechanic earning its keep: temperature arrives on its own, no 6 AM thermometer alarm.
screens.hero: A nightly ledger of Oura readings flowing into the chart, each stamped with its arrival time.
screens.data: Last 5 nights from Oura: 97.38, 97.41, 97.44, 97.82, 97.85 F, all imported before she woke. Note: 'Nights with under 3 hours of wear are excluded rather than guessed. March 12 was skipped for this reason and the chart simply bridges it.'

screens.title: The doctor report
screens.purpose: Compile six months of strips, temperatures, and cycle records into the PDF that makes the appointment count.
screens.hero: Page 1 preview: LH and temperature charts per cycle stacked above a plain summary table.
screens.data: Range: October 2 to March 28, 178 days. Contents: 3 full cycles of 39, 52, 61 days, one closed as anovulatory; 41 strip readings with 2 confirmed peaks; basal temperature curve with both thermal shifts marked. Footnote: 'Every value timestamped at capture. Raw strip photos available on request.' Button: 'Generate PDF'.

screens.title: The math you are already doing

screens.data: Yearly $49.99, noted as $4.16 a month. Monthly $8.99. Both include: strip photo reading, confidence forecasts, wearable import, unlimited doctor reports. Free forever: manual logging and cycle history. Equal-weight links: 'Restore purchase', 'Stay on the free journal', 'Privacy policy'.

screens.title: Day 1 of knowing
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state: an honest chart with nothing on it yet, and the exact first action to change that.
screens.hero: The empty cycle chart with the confidence band absent and a caption explaining why.
screens.data: 'No band yet, and that is the point: we have not measured anything. Your first strip photo starts the curve. Most users see their first real window within one cycle.' Buttons: 'Photograph a strip', 'Connect Oura', 'Enter last period date'.

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Privacy first, instruments second, alerts calibrated to her longest cycle rather than a calendar's.
screens.hero: A grouped list opening with a plainly worded privacy block.
screens.data: Privacy: all data on device, Face ID lock on, 'cycle data never leaves your phone except in PDFs you export'. Instruments: strips Easy@Home, temperature Oura, recalibrate brand. Alerts: 'late-period notice only after 61 days, your longest recorded cycle', evening test reminder 9 PM. Export: full CSV. Delete: 'Erase everything', two-step.

period-cycle-10.territory: The person opening this app has been burned: by a tracker that pivoted to pregnancy, by an ovulation banner that landed like a slap after years of infertility, or by the fear of someone glancing at their phone. The interface answers with the flat, trustworthy neutrality of a paper pocket calendar: nothing to explain, nothing to hide, nothing that will ever ambush them. Its personality is the discipline of staying plain.

palette.note: A near-monochrome ink-on-paper scheme where the only accent is a reserved slate blue for logged days, so from any distance the app reads as a plain calendar and nothing more.

period-cycle-10.typography: IBM Plex Sans throughout with tabular numerals for all dates: engineered, gender-neutral utility type that carries the promise 'this is a calendar, not a lifestyle brand.'
period-cycle-10.motif: The removable acetate: fertility content lives on a literal overlay sheet that slides off the calendar when toggled off, and the slide-away animation is the product's signature moment of relief.

ia.coreObject: The month grid (periods and symptoms as plain marks on plain days)
ia.primaryLoop: Log the period when it starts, add a symptom mark when something is worth remembering, glance at the next predicted window; the app asks for nothing else.

screens.title: What is this for you

Buttons: 'Buy once' · 'Restore purchase'. Free tier stays: calendar and period logging, forever.

Notifications: 'Discreet wording — On (says: Reminder)' · 'Expected window heads-up, 2 days before — On'. Fertility layer: Off. Data: 'Export all' · 'Delete everything'.

period-cycle-4.territory: Two people in a month that quietly matters, carrying hope they don't always say out loud, and one of them holds all the data while the other doesn't know how to help. The interface answers with adult calm and clear roles: her screen feels like a private medical journal she fully controls, his feels like a considerate briefing that tells him exactly what today asks of him. Nothing pink, nothing cutesy, nothing that leaks.

palette.note: Warm ivory paper with a muted terracotta accent for her thread; the partner's thread renders in a quieter honey #C79A5F, and the two hues only appear together on data she has explicitly shared.

period-cycle-4.typography: Tiempos Text for headings and cycle-day numerals, Graphik for UI labels; serif warmth keeps it human and adult, never clinical-cold and never nursery-soft.
period-cycle-4.motif: Two threads, one terracotta and one honey, drawn as thin arcs across every screen that run parallel and braid together only inside the fertile window and only where she has granted visibility.

ia.coreObject: The shared window: the current cycle with a per-field visibility boundary between her account and the partner's
ia.primaryLoop: She logs a test or symptom in under ten seconds each morning, the partner's briefing updates the same minute, and both come back because the day's status tells each of them a concrete next move.

screens.title: Onboarding: who is here
screens.purpose: Set up both roles without assuming gender or method of conception.
screens.hero: Two role cards side by side, terracotta and honey, no illustrations of couples
screens.data: Card 1: 'I'm tracking my cycle'. Card 2: 'I'm the partner'. Below, method picker with equal visual weight: 'Intercourse', 'Home insemination', 'Donor', 'Prefer not to say'. Footnote: 'You can change this anytime. It only tunes the prompts.'

period-cycle-6.territory: She is in the worst week of her cycle, exhausted from not being believed, and she opens the app to do one minute of work that has to count. The interface answers with clinical dignity: quiet, precise, adult, treating every entry as evidence that will stand up in a doctor's office rather than a mood to be decorated.

palette.note: Muted iris marks luteal-phase data and nothing decorative, follicular data renders in warm sand, so the two phases read apart at a glance without a single flowery metaphor.

period-cycle-6.typography: Tiempos Text gives the diary the seriousness of a physician's letter, Söhne keeps scales, dates, and criteria exact, nothing rounded or cute anywhere.
period-cycle-6.motif: The paired phase bands: every symptom renders as two horizontal bands sharing one baseline, luteal in iris above follicular in sand, so the diagnostic gap is visible before anyone says a word.

ia.coreObject: the daily symptom record, rated on the DSM-5 scale
ia.primaryLoop: One rated entry a day in under a minute, and the growing two-cycle record that finally gets a doctor to nod is what brings her back tonight.

period-cycle-9.territory: She stopped the pill six weeks ago and her body is a stranger sending unsigned letters: no period yet, odd spotting, forums full of contradictory horror stories. The interface answers with the calm of a good clinician who says 'this is normal, here is what we are watching for' and refuses to invent a prediction it cannot back. Warm, adult, unhurried, honest about not knowing yet.

palette.note: Warm ivory stays quiet everywhere; the single clay accent is spent only on confirmed signals from your body, never on projections, so color itself tells you what is real.

period-cycle-9.typography: Canela for headings and Graphik for body: a literate serif that reads like a well-edited health letter, never a pink pamphlet, with Graphik keeping the data plain and adult.
period-cycle-9.motif: The emergence line: every timeline is drawn as a dotted line that turns solid segment by segment as real ovulation signs accumulate, so the interface literally renders 'still figuring it out' becoming knowledge.

ia.coreObject: The recovery timeline (days since stopping, annotated with confirmed body signals)
ia.primaryLoop: Each morning she logs waking temperature (or Oura pulls it), adds strip and mucus notes, and checks whether the dotted line grew another solid segment.

screens.title: What did you stop, and when
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: anchor the whole product to her specific method and stop date.
screens.hero: A single question card with method list and a date wheel
screens.data: Combined pill (Yaz) · Hormonal IUD (Mirena) · Implant (Nexplanon) · Injection (Depo-Provera) · Ring (NuvaRing). Selected: Combined pill, stopped March 14, 2026. Footnote: 'Typical return of ovulation after combined pills: 1 to 4 months. We will not pretend to know your date.'

screens.title: What we can watch
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: connect signal sources and set the honesty contract.
screens.hero: Three source rows with connect toggles and a plain-language promise beneath
screens.data: Oura ring — Connected, syncing nightly temperature. Apple Watch — Not connected. Manual: LH strips, cervical mucus, spotting. Promise text: 'No ovulation predictions until your body gives us two stable cycles. All data stays on this phone.'

screens.title: Day 2, and that is fine
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state that makes the absence of data feel correct rather than broken.
screens.hero: The emergence line, entirely dotted, with a single solid dot at day 0 labeled 'Stopped Yaz'
screens.data: Header: 'Day 2 since stopping.' Body: 'Nothing to read yet, and that is exactly right. Log your first waking temperature tomorrow. Most people on combined pills see the first ovulation signs between day 30 and day 120.'

screens.title: Today, day 54
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: the morning check-in with fresh Oura data and quick logging.
screens.hero: Large waking temperature figure pulled from Oura with a 7-day sparkline beneath
screens.data: Waking temp 36.42°C (Oura, synced 07:12). 7-day trend: 36.31, 36.29, 36.33, 36.30, 36.35, 36.39, 36.42. Quick log chips: 'LH strip — negative', 'Mucus — creamy', 'Spotting — none'. Status line: 'Day 54 of recovery · no ovulation confirmed yet · this is within the normal window for your method.'

screens.title: First sign
screens.purpose: The earning-its-keep moment: a real temperature shift plus LH peak is named as a sign, not a verdict.
screens.hero: A clay-colored solid segment appearing on the emergence line with the annotation card above it
screens.data: Card: 'Possible first ovulation. Your temperature rose 0.28°C over 3 days (36.38 → 36.66) after an LH peak on Tuesday. One sign is not a pattern. If a period follows in 10 to 16 days, this was likely your first ovulation since stopping.'

screens.title: Where you are
screens.purpose: The recovery timeline situating day 54 against typical windows for her exact method.
screens.hero: Horizontal band chart: her marker at day 54 over the distribution for combined-pill recovery
screens.data: Bands: 'First ovulation returns — days 25 to 120 for combined pills, median day 74.' Her marker: 'You, day 54.' Annotations pinned to the line: day 31 'light spotting', day 51 'LH peak', day 54 'temp shift'. Caption: 'IUD and injection users see different windows. This chart is for Yaz.'

screens.title: Week 8: what is normal
screens.purpose: The week-by-week explainer at the exact week she is living through.
screens.hero: A single editorial card, serif headline, no illustrations of babies or flowers
screens.data: Headline: 'Week 8 after combined pills.' Body: 'Spotting between bleeds is common as your own estrogen finds its level. Skin changes and heavier discharge are typical. Your cycle length may swing widely for the first two or three cycles.' Link: 'When to call your doctor instead →'

screens.title: When to call
screens.purpose: Clear red-flag checklist separating normal chaos from things that warrant an appointment.
screens.hero: A short, sober checklist with the clay accent used only on the flag items
screens.data: Call your gynecologist if: bleeding soaks a pad hourly for 3+ hours · no period at all by day 120 · severe one-sided pelvic pain · you had unprotected sex and a period is 2+ weeks late. Footer: 'Everything else you have logged so far is within normal recovery.'

screens.title: Two stable cycles
screens.purpose: The self-obsoleting moment: the app itself suggests leaving recovery mode.
screens.hero: The emergence line now solid across two full arcs, with a hand-off card
screens.data: Card: 'Cycle 1: 29 days, ovulation day 15. Cycle 2: 31 days, ovulation day 17. This looks like a settled pattern. Ready to switch to regular tracking? Recovery mode will archive itself either way.' Buttons: 'Switch to regular mode' / 'Give it one more cycle'.

screens.title: Paying for a window, not forever
screens.purpose: Paywall matched to the finite nature of recovery: a subscription designed to end.
screens.hero: A timeline graphic showing the subscription with a marked exit point
screens.data: 'Recovery mode — $8.99/month. Most people need 3 to 8 months. When your cycles stabilize, we will tell you to stop paying.' Included: Oura and Apple Watch sync, method-specific timeline, week-by-week guidance, doctor-visit flags. Free forever: manual temperature log. Buttons: 'Start with 14 days free' · 'Restore purchase'. No annual push, no countdown timer.

screens.title: Settings

screens.hero: Grouped list with the privacy section given equal visual weight to sources
screens.data: Sources: Oura (connected), Apple Health temperature (off), manual entries. Privacy: 'All data on-device · Export everything as PDF for your doctor · Delete all data'. Method: 'Combined pill (Yaz), stopped March 14, 2026 — edit'. Notifications: 'Morning log reminder 07:30'.

personal-finance-3.territory: Two people who love each other but split the money work unevenly: one carries the whole budget in their head, the other just wants to know what's safe to spend without a dinner-table interrogation. The interface answers with quiet domestic competence, morning-kitchen daylight, numbers stated once and clearly, and a tone that treats a $310 tire purchase as a note between partners, not an audit finding.

palette.note: Warm greige daylight with a deep teal accent for the household, and each partner gets a soft personal tint (teal and ochre) that blend into one bar wherever money is truly shared.

personal-finance-3.typography: National 2 with tabular figures for every amount and Founders Grotesk for labels; numbers align like a well-kept household book while the words stay conversational.
personal-finance-3.motif: The two-strand bar: every shared number is drawn as two interleaved strands, one per partner, that visibly braid into a single bar, so who-contributed-what is legible without anyone asking.

ia.coreObject: The household ledger: one shared money picture assembled from two separate accounts, viewed through two different roles
ia.primaryLoop: The manager checks category health each morning while the partner glances at one safe-to-spend number, both log purchases in two taps, and Sunday brings a five-minute summary for the money conversation.

personal-finance-5.territory: This is the quiet adult pleasure of knowing March's insurance bill is already handled in November: no market anxiety, no expense-tracking guilt, just known future costs being met in weekly steps. The interface answers with daylight-neutral ledger calm, precise numbers that line up, and progress that accumulates visibly like coins in a jar. It should feel like competence you can glance at.

palette.note: Progress fills in brass like coins accumulating; red never appears anywhere, a behind-schedule fund simply turns slate and gets a plan, because a vacation fund is not an emergency.

personal-finance-5.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk with tabular figures makes every amount sit in perfect ledger columns, while Tiempos Text carries the calm explanatory sentences underneath the math.
personal-finance-5.motif: The year skyline: twelve months rendered as columns whose heights are your due amounts, filling with brass week by week, so a crowded March is visible from across the room a year in advance.

personal-finance-6.territory: A freelancer on the 11th of the month who doesn't know yet what the month will bring, only what it will take: rent on the 1st, insurance on the 5th, taxes on the 25th. The anxiety isn't 'where did money go', it's 'will there be enough by the date'. The interface answers with the quiet competence of a good bookkeeper: daylight neutrals, precise tabular figures, and one unambiguous answer per screen — this much is covered, this much is left to earn.

palette.note: Cool paper gray with near-black ink; pine green appears exclusively as the fill of covered obligations, so a glance at how much green is on screen answers the month's only question.

personal-finance-6.typography: Untitled Sans for all UI with IBM Plex Mono for every monetary figure; tabular mono numbers line up like a ledger and make precision feel like the product's character, not decoration.
personal-finance-6.motif: The fill line: every obligation is a slim horizontal bar that fills left to right with pine ink as real payments land, and the month itself is the stack of those bars.

ia.coreObject: The obligation: a fixed amount with a due date that incoming payments cover in order
ia.primaryLoop: Log each payment the day it lands, watch it split into tax reserve and obligation fill, and come back because the dashboard answers 'how much more do I need to earn before the 25th' in one number.

personal-finance-7.territory: He is standing at a checkout with a cart and a flicker of doubt, and he has no patience left for an app that asks anything of him. The interface answers with instant daylight clarity: one number in one color, already on the lock screen before the thought is gone, and never a word of blame after.

palette.note: Color exists only as the state of the single number, green then amber then red, never as a banner, a chart, or a scold.

personal-finance-7.typography: Helvetica Now with big tabular lining figures, the number is the typography and everything else on screen is a caption to it.
personal-finance-7.motif: The one number: a screen-filling tabular figure that is always current and simply changes hue, with nothing else competing for the glance.

personal-finance-9.territory: The person opens this at the kitchen table after another statement, carrying the low hum of when does this end. pet-care-1.territory: The user is one of two adults keeping a diabetic cat alive, and the recurring fear is quiet and specific: did anyone give the 7 o'clock shot, or worse, did we both. The interface answers with the warmth of a kitchen-corkboard system that finally works: soft, domestic, unfussy, and absolutely certain about one thing, the actual moment the dose went in and who gave it. Relief, shared between two phones.

palette.note: Warm cream like a kitchen wall with white cards; the terracotta accent is spent only on the act of giving (the give button, the stamped time, the second checkmark), so the warmest color always means 'done and seen'.

pet-care-1.typography: Recoleta gives headers a soft household roundness without turning childish, while Nunito Sans keeps dose times and schedules plainly readable at 7 a.m. before coffee.
pet-care-1.motif: The double check: every dose carries two small paw-shaped checks, the first inked at the actual give-time, the second filling in when the rest of the household has seen it, like message delivery for medicine.

ia.coreObject: The given dose: medication, pet, the real timestamp, and who in the household gave it

pet-care-2.territory: Two working people orbiting one dog: 7 am rush, one already on the train texting 'did you feed him?'. The moment of use is a half-second between coat and door. pet-care-3.territory: An owner whose dog has a chronic condition is standing at a new clinic's front desk, being asked for a history that lives scattered across three old clinics and a dead app. The feeling is protective and a little burned. The interface answers like a well-kept family filing cabinet: warm kraft-paper order, everything findable by tab, and an unmistakable sense that this drawer belongs to you.

palette.note: Kraft-manila surfaces make every record read as a physical folder while teal marks only what is current and actionable, the valid vaccine, the due reminder, the live QR.

pet-care-3.typography: GT America for labels and pet names, warm and legible like good form design, with GT America Mono for dates, lab values and record IDs so the archive feels checkable.
pet-care-3.motif: The file tab: every record is a folder with a colored tab on its top edge, teal for vaccines, clay for labs, sand for visits, and the pet's whole life reads as a spine of tabs down the timeline.

pet-care-8.territory: The owner of a cat with kidney disease lives in low-grade vigilance: is she drinking more, is she lighter, is the diet working. They open the app in quiet worry and it must answer like a good vet tech, calm, precise, never alarmist. Clinical clarity delivered with the gentleness of someone who also loves the cat.

palette.note: Cool exam-room white with a sage-teal accent used strictly for trend lines and confirmed actions; alerts speak in the same teal with plain words, red is reserved and almost never seen.

pet-care-8.typography: Inter with tabular numerals keeps every reading vet-chart precise, while Source Serif 4 in chart annotations and alerts makes the app's voice read like a considered clinical note rather than a push notification.
pet-care-8.motif: The whisker tick: data points and event flags on every chart are drawn as fine curved whisker strokes, so a six-month trend line reads like a cat's profile in cross-section.

ia.coreObject: The reading: one dated measurement of weight, litter visits, water, or food, editable forever
ia.primaryLoop: A minute a day logging or auto-syncing weight, litter, and water, then a weekly glance at the long trend to see whether the diet or the meds are working.

photo-editing-1.territory: The traveler is on the hotel bed the same evening, culling the day's shots, annoyed that one wire ruins the best frame. The interface answers with darkroom discipline: neutral graphite chrome that never tints the photo, one tool, and the quiet confidence of a machine that does its single job on the first stroke. No feed, no filters, no personality except precision.

palette.note: Color-neutral graphite measured to not shift photo perception; the only chromatic element is the rubylith-red brush overlay, so red always means exactly one thing — this is what will disappear.

photo-editing-1.typography: Suisse Int'l with tabular figures — cool, Swiss, instrument-neutral — set small and out of the way, because the photograph is the typography of this app.
photo-editing-1.motif: Rubylith: brush strokes render as the translucent red masking film of a real darkroom, a working material rather than a UI highlight, peeling away when the removal completes.

ia.coreObject: The removal (one photo, one masked region, three candidate fills, and a verified-at-100% result)
ia.primaryLoop: Same-day culling: open the day's best frames, stroke out the wire or the stranger, verify at 100%, export — a two-minute ritual after every shooting day.

photo-editing-10.territory: The person is bent over one frame the way a printmaker leans over an enlarger: patient, exacting, allergic to distraction. The interface answers with total achromatic calm, a room with the lights off where the photograph is the only bright thing and every control feels machined, not decorated.

palette.note: The UI is strictly achromatic so the photo owns all tonal attention; safelight amber appears only on the one active control, the way a darkroom permits a single working light.

photo-editing-10.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk in small technical sizes with tabular numerals for every zone value and exposure figure, engraved-on-a-lens-barrel restraint rather than expressive display type.
photo-editing-10.motif: The ten-step zone strip (0 to X) that runs beneath every frame and doubles as histogram, thumbnail badge, batch progress bar and export seal.

ia.coreObject: The frame: one monochrome negative with its zone map and processing recipe
ia.primaryLoop: Import a shot, read its zone map, pull individual zones and grain until the print is right, then export or push the recipe across the series; the unfinished series is what brings them back.

photo-editing-3.territory: It is 7 a.m. and 42 earring photos have to become Etsy cards before the post office opens. The seller's fear is not bad taste, it is surprise. The interface answers like a calibrated machine shop: neutral gray chrome, nothing decorative, every limit and version number printed where you can see it before you commit.

palette.note: Chrome stays in flat neutral grays so the product photos are the only color on screen, and signal orange appears solely on commitments: the process button and the pinned-version stamp.

photo-editing-3.typography: Suisse Int'l with tabular figures wherever counts and limits appear, so a line like 458 remaining reads like an instrument panel, not marketing copy.
photo-editing-3.motif: The pin stamp, a small engraved chip reading Engine v4.2 · pinned Mar 3, traveling with every batch, export, and history row as the visual contract that nothing changed without sign-off.

photo-editing-4.territory: The creator opens a selfie they almost like, wary from years of apps that reshape their jaw before asking, and what they want is control with proof. The interface answers like a precision darkroom: neutral graphite chrome that never competes with the photo, a warm safelight amber on the tools, and instruments that can verify their own restraint.

palette.note: The chrome is strictly neutral gray so skin tones read true, and the safelight amber marks only the active tool and the honest-zero detent, never washing over the photograph itself.

photo-editing-4.typography: Untitled Sans for all interface text with tabular figures for slider values: deliberately styleless type, because in a darkroom the photograph is the personality and the tools should disappear.
photo-editing-4.motif: The registration grid: a fine surveyor's mesh that overlays the face on demand and sits identically on before and after, the standing proof that geometry never moved.

ia.coreObject: The edit: one portrait with brush-applied skin work and a verifiable untouched geometry
ia.primaryLoop: Several times a week the creator imports a selfie, lets their saved level auto-apply, spends ninety seconds with the spot brush, checks the grid, and exports knowing they still look like themselves.

photo-editing-5.territory: He shoots RAW on his phone, knows exactly what Portra 400 does to skin in late sun, and is mildly insulted by filters named 'Vibes 03'. The interface answers like a darkroom: neutral chrome that disappears around the photograph, measured claims, numbers where numbers belong. Calm competence, lit by a single safelight.

palette.note: The chrome is strictly neutral gray so it never tints the photograph; safelight amber appears only on the active control and the film-edge markings.

photo-editing-5.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk for the interface, OCR-B for emulsion edge codes and export figures: Swiss restraint carrying genuine darkroom markings.
photo-editing-5.motif: Film-edge markings: every profile wears its real emulsion name and frame number printed along a sprocket-holed strip, like the edge of a developed negative — KODAK PORTRA 400 › 24A.

ia.coreObject: the emulsion profile (a measured film stock applied to your photograph)
ia.primaryLoop: Import the day's RAW frames, find the stock by name, tune grain and warmth to taste, export at full size.

screens.title: What do you shoot?

screens.title: Your negatives stay yours

photo-editing-6.territory: The job seeker needs to look hireable by Monday and is caught between a $400 studio session and an AI generator that returns a stranger's face. The interface answers like a working photographer's studio in daylight: seamless-paper calm, honest appraisal of what you brought, and craftsmanship applied to your real face. The promise it must radiate from every pixel: this will still be you.

palette.note: Seamless-backdrop warm gray so every portrait sits as if on studio paper; the deep teal accent marks approvals and selections, while appraisal marks on the contact sheet are drawn in china-marker black, like a photographer's grease pencil.

photo-editing-6.typography: Canela for headings — the warmth of a portrait studio's letterhead — over Graphik for instructions and labels, keeping guidance crisp where the imagery is soft.
photo-editing-6.motif: The contact sheet: your uploads are appraised as a numbered contact sheet with grease-pencil circles on the keepers and honest cross-outs on the rejects, exactly how editors have chosen portraits for seventy years.

ia.coreObject: The headshot job (your uploaded shots, the ranked pick, its finished versions in each format)
ia.primaryLoop: Not daily — episodic and high-stakes: upload the shots you have, get one finished headshot in every needed format, return each time the job hunt, agency, or new role demands a fresh card.

screens.title: What's it for

screens.data: Slider: 'Finish' at 40% — under-eye shadows eased, shirt wrinkle smoothed, razor nick gone. Locked and labeled: 'jawline, nose, eyes, skin texture untouched. The 100% zoom keeps your pores.' Toggle: 'Compare with original'.

photo-editing-8.territory: It is the evening before her mother's birthday, an hour of layout work is already on the canvas, and the old fear of a crash eating it sits in her shoulders. The interface answers like an archivist's table: warm, unhurried, everything dated, stamped, and filed, so the work feels physically incapable of being lost.

palette.note: Color behaves like ink on paper, the library-stamp blue marks saves, versions, and anything the app promises to keep, while family photos stay untinted on warm paper.

photo-editing-8.typography: Canela for occasion titles so they feel like a good card shop, National 2 for the workbench chrome, both set warm against paper tones.
photo-editing-8.motif: The library-card stamp: every project carries a visible column of dated save stamps, and a new stamp presses on with every auto-save, like a due-date card that only ever fills.

plant-care-2.territory: The owner opens the app already flinching, because the last app's confident commands killed a succulent in January. The interface answers with a field guide's patience: it asks before it tells, in botanical calm, and visibly changes its mind when the soil disagrees with the textbook. The feeling to earn is not delight but relief — finally, an app that admits your apartment is not a laboratory.

palette.note: Herbarium off-white with chlorophyll green reserved for living things — plant names, healthy intervals — while the soil chips carry their own literal browns and never borrow the accent.

plant-care-2.typography: GT Alpina for plant names and field notes, its botanical-plate italics doing the Latin binomials justice, with Untitled Sans for the quiet machinery of buttons and schedules.
plant-care-2.motif: The soil chip: every watering question is answered by tapping one of two circular soil-texture swatches — pale dry crumb or dark damp — and the chips are the app's handshake, appearing wherever a decision was made.

ia.coreObject: The plant (species, pot, its learned interval, and the trail of soil answers that shaped it)
ia.primaryLoop: On check days the owner feels the soil, taps dry or still damp, and watches each plant's schedule quietly bend toward the truth of their home.

screens.title: Who lives with you
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: add plants from the database by name — no camera, no guessing.
screens.hero: A search field over botanical-plate illustrations of common species
screens.data: Search: 'monstera' → Monstera deliciosa. Added: nickname 'Delia', 8-inch terracotta pot, bright indirect, living room. Starting interval: 'Textbook says every 7 days. We'll learn your home's real number.'

screens.title: When should we ask
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: the reminder time that fits the owner's life, not a global 10am.
screens.hero: A single time picker on a paper card with a small watering can etching
screens.data: 'When do you actually have two minutes for your plants?' Selected: Evenings, 7:00pm. Note: 'We ask, you feel the soil, you answer. Two taps. Never a command.'

screens.title: An empty shelf
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state for anyone who skipped adding plants.
screens.hero: A blank herbarium page with pressed-leaf outlines where plants will go
screens.data: 'No plants yet. Add your first and we'll start from the textbook — then let your answers overrule it.' Button: 'Add a plant'. Small line: '10 to 50 pots is our comfort zone.'

screens.title: Today, three questions
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: check day for three plants, each a question rather than an order.
screens.hero: Three plant cards, each ending in the pair of soil chips
screens.data: 'Delia (Monstera deliciosa) — day 9 of a learned 9-day rhythm. Feel the soil an inch down.' Chips: Dry / Still damp. Below: 'Zeze (ZZ plant) — day 18 of 21, early check after your last damp answer.' 'Callie (Calathea) — day 5, she's the thirsty one.'

screens.title: Still damp
screens.purpose: The core mechanic at its moment: a damp answer visibly shifts the schedule instead of arguing.
screens.hero: The tapped damp chip settling into Delia's card as the next date slides forward
screens.data: 'Still damp — got it. Next check moves from today to Friday (+3 days). That's the third damp answer this month: Delia's interval is drifting from 7 toward 10 days. Cooler room, less light — makes sense.'

screens.title: What we've learned
screens.purpose: The learning view: proof the app adapts, shown as a month of answers reshaping the interval.
screens.hero: A gentle line drifting from the textbook interval to the learned one, dotted with soil chips
screens.data: 'Delia: textbook 7 days → your home 9.5 days, learned from 6 answers since June 3. Callie: textbook 4 → holding at 4, your bathroom humidity suits her. Zeze: 14 → 21 and still drifting. Overwatering risk: low across the shelf.'

screens.title: Winter arrived on its own
screens.purpose: The seasonal mechanic: dormancy mode activating automatically, with succulents on separate logic.
screens.hero: The Today list under a pale winter-light header, intervals visibly stretched
screens.data: 'October 26 — winter mode on. Delia 9.5 → 14 days. Sylvia (Echeveria) 14 → 28 days, succulent logic: bone dry between waterings. Fertilizer paused for everyone until March. You can override any of this per plant.'

screens.title: Your call stands
screens.purpose: The manual override earning its keep: one tap, and the algorithm respectfully stands down.
screens.hero: A single interval stepper on Hoya's card with a small padlock note beneath
screens.data: 'Hank (Hoya carnosa): set by you to every 21 days on Jul 2. We'll remind on your number and keep learning silently in the background — tap to see our suggestion (currently 18 days), apply it only if you want.'

screens.title: Before you go
screens.purpose: Away mode: what to water before a trip and how schedules shift on return.
screens.hero: A packing-list card: four plants queued above a calendar span
screens.data: 'Trip: Jul 18–27. Water before leaving: Callie (Thu), Delia (Fri), the two ferns (Fri). Skip: Sylvia and Hank — they'd rather you left. On return, everyone gets a check day Jul 28 instead of guessed catch-up waterings.'

screens.hero: The new plant's card waiting politely behind a paper gate
screens.data: 'Five plants free, forever. Room for the whole shelf: $19.99/year or $29.99 once, yours for good.' Line: 'What you're buying is a schedule that learns your home — and plants that survive January.' Link: 'Restore purchase'. No trial countdown, the five free never expire.

screens.purpose: Reminder time, seasons, and data — everything adjustable, nothing bossy.
screens.hero: A grouped list with the reminder card first
screens.data: Check-in time: 7:00pm. Winter mode: automatic (Oct–Mar, northern hemisphere) or set your own dates. Notifications: one evening summary, never per-plant pings. Export notebook (CSV). 'No account needed — your shelf lives on this phone, iCloud backup optional.'

plant-care-3.territory: The collector opens the app the way a registrar opens a ledger: 240 living things depend on this record being right, and the fear is quiet chaos, the mealybug spreading while you scroll. The interface answers with field-guide calm: paper, ink, stamped accession numbers, the confidence of a herbarium archive that has survived a century and will survive your next phone.

palette.note: Chlorophyll green is reserved for living status and actions, overdue states shift to a dried-leaf ochre #B07C2E rather than alarm red, and the paper ground never changes.

plant-care-3.typography: Tiempos Text for plant names and headings, National 2 for data rows and controls: the serif carries the field-guide authority, the grotesk keeps 400-row tables legible at a glance.
plant-care-3.motif: The accession tag: every plant carries a stamped specimen label (No. 217 of 243, acquired 03.2024, Rack B) rendered like a herbarium slip, and the tag is the unit the whole interface is built from.

ia.coreObject: The plant record: an accession tag with species, location, care log, and photo timeline
ia.primaryLoop: Each morning the collector opens Attention, works down the overdue-sorted list watering and logging by room, and returns because the ledger only stays true if fed daily.

plant-care-5.territory: The gardener opens the app with dirt still on their hands and a low hum of doubt: is it too early, will a late frost take the seedlings. The interface answers like a trusted regional almanac, calm and paper-quiet, certain about two dates and honest about everything built on them. Patience is the mood; nothing blinks, nothing rushes the season.

palette.note: Chlorophyll green is reserved for living, growing things on the timeline; frost is always a pale ice-blue #C9DEE7 band that green never crosses.

plant-care-5.typography: GT Alpina for crop names and season headings with Untitled Sans for labels and dates: the serif reads like a printed field guide, the sans keeps the schedule legible at a glance.
plant-care-5.motif: The frost line: a pale ice-blue horizontal band bounding every timeline, so each crop's green bar visibly grows only in the safe space between last and first frost.

ia.coreObject: the crop plan (one crop's dated run from seed packet to harvest)
ia.primaryLoop: Check today's column on the season timeline, do the one task that is due (sow, harden off, transplant), and tick it into the plan's history.

plant-care-6.territory: The orchid grower works in weeks and months: misting on Sunday, then watching a spike lengthen a millimeter a day. The mood at the moment of use is patient devotion tinged with worry about getting a phase wrong, and the interface answers with the unhurried authority of a hand-annotated field guide, where nothing flashes, nothing gamifies, and every plant is treated as a specimen worth documenting properly.

palette.note: Aged-paper cream carries everything; deep fir green appears only as the ink of annotations and the current-phase marker, while bloom photos are the sole moments of saturated color on the page.

plant-care-6.typography: GT Sectra for species names and plate headings with Untitled Sans for care data and labels, so every orchid reads like a herbarium entry annotated by a careful hand.
plant-care-6.motif: The specimen plate: each orchid is a numbered plate (No. 04 — Vanda coerulea) with a four-stop lifecycle arc stamped beneath it, the current phase inked solid like a botanist's field mark.

ia.coreObject: The specimen: one orchid with its species record, current phase, care schedule, and bloom history
ia.primaryLoop: A weekly bench check: open the app, see which plants need water or feeding this week given their phase, log what was done, and note any phase change the plant is showing.

screens.title: Onboarding — Name your first specimen
screens.purpose: Add the first orchid by honest selection from a list, deliberately without photo identification, and set its growing medium.
screens.hero: A browsable genus list with clean botanical thumbnails, no camera button anywhere
screens.data: Genus: Phalaenopsis (most common gift orchid) → Species/hybrid: Phalaenopsis 'Kaoda Twinkle' · Medium: bark / sphagnum moss / hydroponics → bark · Pot: clear plastic, 4 in · 'Can't find yours? Add it by hand with your own name.'

screens.title: Onboarding — What is it doing right now
screens.purpose: Set the current phase honestly so the very first schedule is phase-correct, teaching the core concept in one question.
screens.hero: The lifecycle arc as a large tappable diagram: growth → dormancy → spike → bloom
screens.data: 'Look at your plant. Any new leaf or root tip?' → Growth · 'A stem with buds forming?' → Spike · Selected: Spike, appeared ~2 weeks ago · Result: 'Watering every 6 days, fertilizing paused until first flower opens'

screens.title: First launch — The empty bench
screens.purpose: An empty state that frames the collection as a bench waiting for specimens, not a hollow dashboard.
screens.hero: A ruled, empty shelf illustration with one plate outline labeled No. 01
screens.data: 'Your bench is empty. Most collectors start by adding the whole windowsill — it takes about a minute per plant.' · Button: Add specimen No. 01 · Footnote: 3 specimens free, unlimited with one purchase

screens.title: Bench — mid-use, eight specimens
screens.purpose: The main screen: every orchid as a plate with its phase mark, and this week's tasks summarized on top.
screens.hero: A grid of numbered specimen plates, each with its lifecycle arc inked at the current phase
screens.data: This week: water 3, feed 1, check spike on No. 04 · No. 01 Phal. 'Kaoda Twinkle' — Spike, day 18 · No. 02 Phal. schilleriana — Dormancy · No. 03 Dendrobium nobile — Dormancy (cool rest) · No. 04 Vanda coerulea — Growth, bare root · No. 05 Oncidium 'Sharry Baby' — Bloom, day 9

screens.title: Specimen plate — Vanda coerulea
screens.purpose: One plant's full record: care by medium, phase history, and next actions, laid out like a guide page about your plant.
screens.hero: The plate header with species name in GT Sectra and the lifecycle arc beneath
screens.data: No. 04 · Vanda coerulea · bare root, basket-hung · Phase: Growth since May 12 · Water: daily soak 20 min (bare root), skip if roots still green · Feed: ¼ strength weekly · Light: bright, some direct morning sun · Last watered: yesterday · Phase history: Bloom Feb 1–Mar 9, Growth since

screens.title: Phase change — entering dormancy
screens.purpose: The moment the app earns its existence: the routine visibly rewrites itself when a phase changes.
screens.hero: The arc mark sliding from Growth to Dormancy with the schedule diff shown as before/after
screens.data: No. 03 Dendrobium nobile → Dormancy confirmed · Watering: every 7 days → light misting every 14 days · Fertilizer: paused until spring · Temperature: 'A cool rest at 50–57 °F now sets up spring flowering' · Reminders thinned: 6 fewer notifications this month

screens.title: Bloom trigger — the pre-spike push
screens.purpose: Cue the temperature drop and watering reduction at the right calendar moment, the advice general apps never give.
screens.hero: A dated instruction card pinned to the specimen's arc between Growth and Spike
screens.data: No. 01 Phalaenopsis 'Kaoda Twinkle' · 'Mature growth complete. To trigger a spike: night temperature 55–60 °F for 3–4 weeks, reduce watering by a third. Start this week — a spike would show by late August.' · Buttons: Start trigger routine / Not this year

screens.title: Bloom journal — logging a peak
screens.purpose: Record the payoff: dates, flower count, cycle length, and the one photo at peak that the whole year was for.
screens.hero: The peak photo, the only large saturated image in the app, above a spare data line

screens.hero: A guide page with a medium switcher that visibly rewrites the care columns
screens.data: Phalaenopsis · in bark: water every 7–10 days when roots silver · in moss: every 12–14 days, moss dry to the knuckle · hydroponics: top up to 1 in, full change monthly · Light: bright shade, no midday sun · Bloom trigger: 10 °F night drop · 214 species and hybrids in the guide

screens.title: Add a hybrid by hand
screens.purpose: The honest escape hatch: any unnamed windowsill hybrid gets a record with a custom name instead of a wrong identification.

screens.data: Name: 'Grandma's white one' · Closest genus: Phalaenopsis (sets baseline care) · Medium: moss · Source: gift, Feb 2025 · 'We'd rather you name it than we misname it — care follows the genus, your notes make it yours.'

screens.title: Paywall — the fourth orchid

screens.hero: The bench with plate No. 04 outlined and waiting, purchase card beneath

pregnancy-tracker-1.territory: It is week seven of her first pregnancy, it is 2 a.m., and one cramp has her halfway into a search spiral she already regrets. The interface answers like a hand on the shoulder: warm linen light, one small thing at a time, and the day's fear already named and quietly talked through before she can google it. It feels like being told 'this is normal, and here is exactly when it wouldn't be' by someone unhurried.

palette.note: Soft sage does all the reassuring: the settled state of a closed fear, the 'normal' band of the traffic light, the breathing circle; alarm red exists only inside the 'call today' band of the traffic light and appears nowhere else in the app.

pregnancy-tracker-1.typography: Source Serif 4 for the daily cards, set generously like a good bedside book, and GT Walsheim for navigation and labels: the serif slows the reading down on purpose, the rounded sans keeps controls warm without being infantile.
pregnancy-tracker-1.motif: The settled pebble: each day's fear, once read, becomes a small smooth pebble added to the week's cairn on the home screen, a quiet stack of everything already worried about and set down, growing across all forty weeks.

ia.coreObject: The daily fear card: one common worry of this exact week, talked through in plain words with its honest 'when to call' line
ia.primaryLoop: Open the day's card, read the fear before it finds her, set it down as a pebble, and come back tomorrow because the week always has one more worry and the cairn keeps growing.

screens.title: Onboarding, step 1: where you are
screens.purpose: Get the due date without a single clinical or alarming word.
screens.hero: A soft linen calendar wheel settling on a date, the week count fading in below
screens.data: Prompt: 'When is the little one due? A guess is fine, you can adjust anytime.' Set: 'September 18'. Result line: 'Week 7, day 3. We'll walk it a week at a time.' No weight fields, no risk questionnaire.

screens.title: Onboarding, step 2: heavy topics, your call
screens.purpose: Set the boundary on difficult content before any content is shown.
screens.hero: A single fabric-textured switch card, off by default
screens.data: Copy: 'Some readers want the hard topics covered, some never want them appearing uninvited. Risks and loss stay behind this switch, off unless you turn it on. You can change this whenever you like.' Switch label: 'Show heavy topics: OFF'. Button: 'Begin week 7'.

screens.title: Today, mid-use
screens.purpose: The main screen on an ordinary Tuesday of week 7: the day's fear card open, half-read.
screens.hero: One serif card filling most of the screen, the week's cairn of six pebbles resting beneath it
screens.data: Card title: 'Cramping that feels like a period is coming'. Body excerpt: 'At week 7 your uterus is doing quiet construction work, and mild, period-like cramping is one of the most common feelings there is. Here is the plain version of when it's routine and when it's worth a call...' Footer: 'When to call: cramping with heavy bleeding, or one-sided pain that makes you catch your breath — call your provider today.' Button: 'Set this one down'.

screens.title: The pebble settles
screens.purpose: The tiny closing ritual that makes a read fear feel finished, not just dismissed.
screens.hero: The card folding gently into a small sage pebble that drops onto the cairn with a soft haptic
screens.data: Cairn caption: 'Week 7: five worries read and set down.' Whole-journey line: '31 pebbles since week 4.' Tomorrow's teaser kept unscary: 'Tomorrow: why food you loved suddenly disgusts you.'

screens.title: Symptom traffic light
screens.purpose: The is-this-normal instrument: three bands, plain words, no diagnosis theater.
screens.hero: Three stacked fabric bands — sage, amber, soft red — with the searched symptom sorted into one
screens.data: Search: 'light brown spotting'. Result lands in amber: 'Can wait for your next appointment: light brown spotting without cramping is common after week 6; mention it at your Feb 24 visit.' Sage band example: 'sore breasts, food aversions, exhaustion'. Red band, used sparingly: 'Heavy red bleeding, fever over 100.4°F, one-sided sharp pain — call your provider today.' Footer: 'We're not diagnosing. We're sorting what can wait from what shouldn't.'

screens.title: I'm spiraling
screens.purpose: The button for the moment panic outruns reading: breath first, words second.
screens.hero: A full-screen sage breathing circle, expanding four counts in, six counts out
screens.data: On-screen line rotating slowly, one at a time: 'This feeling at week 7 is common enough that we wrote this screen.' After 5 breaths: 'What set it off?' chips: 'a symptom', 'something I read', 'no reason, it just came'. Choosing 'a symptom' opens the traffic light, choosing 'no reason' offers: 'That happens. Hormones are loud right now. Stay another minute?'

screens.title: Ask at 2am
screens.purpose: The night screen for the middle-of-the-night question, so the answer comes from here and not from a search spiral.
screens.hero: The interface dimmed to warm candlelight tones, one large question field, short answers stacked
screens.data: Screen auto-dims after 10pm. Top of list, this week's most-asked: 'Cramping woke me — normal?', 'My symptoms suddenly feel weaker', 'I had wine before I knew'. Answer excerpt for the second: 'Symptoms ebbing for a day or two in week 7 is common and usually means nothing. It does not reliably signal anything on its own...' with its own quiet 'when to call' line. Footer: 'Every answer written and reviewed by humans, sources listed, jargon left out.'

screens.title: My week
screens.purpose: The week-by-week home: what week 7 is doing, sized in kindness rather than clinical charts.
screens.hero: A soft illustrated card of the week, blueberry-scale comparison, the week's seven fear cards fanned beneath
screens.data: Header: 'Week 7 of 40'. Body: 'About the size of a blueberry. The heart is beating fast — around 150 a minute — and that's exactly right.' Week's cards fan: 5 settled pebble-marked, 2 upcoming. Next appointment chip: 'First ultrasound: Feb 24, 11 days'.

screens.title: Heavy topics, opened deliberately
screens.purpose: Show the switch honored: the hard content exists, arrives only when chosen, and is written with the most care of all.
screens.hero: A plain serif page behind a gentle threshold screen: 'You chose to read this. Take your time.'
screens.data: Topic: 'Miscarriage risk in the first trimester, honestly'. Excerpt: 'Here are the real numbers, and what they actually mean by week 7 with a heartbeat seen...' Exit note at the end: 'This page will not resurface on its own. The switch in Settings is still yours.'

screens.title: Quiet mode, week 36
screens.purpose: The late-weeks state: the app itself gets softer as delivery nears, by design not neglect.
screens.hero: The Today card in a visibly calmer layout, cairn nearly complete at 200+ pebbles
screens.data: Card: 'Week 36: the waiting is the work now.' Copy note: 'Quiet mode is on: no statistics, no what-could-go-wrong framing from here to delivery. Just what each day tends to feel like, and your hospital-bag list when you want it.' Toggle visible: 'Quiet mode: ON (came on automatically at week 35, you can turn it off)'.

screens.title: Paywall
screens.purpose: Offered at the end of the free first week, sold as calm for the whole term, no fear leverage.
screens.hero: The week-7 cairn beside a faint outline of the full 40-week cairn it could become
screens.data: Header: 'Week 7 is set down. Thirty-three weeks of worries to go.' Copy: 'Every one of them has a card already written: plain, honest, checked by humans.' Offer: '$4.99/month for the length of the pregnancy, or $29.99 once for all 40 weeks.' Context: 'Weekly-content apps here run $30–60/year.' Buttons: 'One price, whole pregnancy — $29.99', 'Monthly, $4.99', link 'Restore purchase'. Footnote: 'The spiraling button and the traffic light stay free for everyone, always.'

screens.title: First launch, before the due date is set
screens.purpose: The empty state for the very first open, likely minutes after a positive test.
screens.hero: A single pebble resting on warm linen, nothing else
screens.data: Line: 'However you're feeling right now — thrilled, terrified, both — that's the normal we start from.' Button: 'Tell us your due date'. Sub-note: 'No account needed. Everything stays on your phone.'

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Few controls, all in the service of calm, the heavy-topics switch living here permanently.
screens.hero: A short linen list with the heavy-topics switch given its own card at top
screens.data: Rows: 'Heavy topics: OFF', 'Quiet mode: automatic at week 35', 'Night dimming: after 10pm', 'Due date: Sep 18 (edit)', 'Notifications: one gentle card a day at 8am, nothing else, OFF available', 'Data: stored on device, export or erase anytime', 'If this pregnancy ends: one tap pauses everything, no questions, no emails', 'Restore purchase'.

qr-scanner-2.territory: Mid-shift at the receiving desk: gloves on, a pallet half-unwrapped, a forklift beeping somewhere behind you. The person needs unbroken rhythm and total certainty that every scan landed without ever stopping to look down. The interface answers with industrial calm: one giant tally that never lies, zero dialogs, and a beep you can trust with your back turned.

palette.note: Gunmetal green-black keeps the camera feed dominant under warehouse fluorescents; the confirm-green fires only as the per-scan flash and the tally digits, so a glance from two meters away reads pure signal.

qr-scanner-2.typography: IBM Plex Mono carries every number (tally, quantities, timestamps) at heavy weights so counts read like a hardware display, with IBM Plex Sans doing the quiet labels around it.
qr-scanner-2.motif: The odometer tally: a mechanical split-flap counter whose digits physically roll on every scan, echoed in miniature wherever a count appears (session rows, export previews, quantity steppers).

ia.coreObject: The session: a named, timestamped stream of scans with quantities
ia.primaryLoop: Open a session at the start of a pass, scan continuously while the tally rolls, adjust the odd quantity, close and export; the shift itself brings them back every receiving day.

screens.title: Camera, once
screens.purpose: Single permission ask framed in the language of the job, not the OS.
screens.hero: Full-bleed viewfinder mock with a barcode centered and the odometer at 0000
screens.data: Headline 'The camera is the whole app.' Sub: 'One permission, then you scan until the pallet is empty.' Button 'Allow camera'. Secondary link 'What we never do: open links from scanned codes.'

screens.title: What kind of pass?

screens.title: No sessions yet

recipes-meal-planning-3.territory: It's 5:40pm, the fridge is half-full of things bought with good intentions, and the person staring into it feels the small guilt of last week's tossed spinach. The interface answers like afternoon light on a well-stocked kitchen shelf: warm, appetizing, and immediately practical — it already knows what's in the house and leads with what can be cooked right now, not with aspirational food photography.

palette.note: Warm cream like flour-dusted counter light; basil green marks only what you already have, and the small amber tag (#D98E2B) is reserved for ingredients about to expire, so the palette itself reads the fridge.

recipes-meal-planning-3.typography: GT Super for dish names and Untitled Sans for ingredients and amounts; the serif gives dinner some appetite while the workhorse sans keeps quantities and shelf rows strictly practical.
recipes-meal-planning-3.motif: The stocked shelf: the pantry is drawn as literal horizontal shelf rows (fridge, freezer, spice rack) where ingredient chips sit like labeled jars, and every recipe card echoes the motif with its ingredient chips pre-lit green for what's already on your shelf.

ia.coreObject: The living pantry: a stock list that recipes rank themselves against and that updates itself every time you cook
ia.primaryLoop: Glance at what's cookable right now, cook it, mark it done so the pantry deducts itself, and watch tomorrow's suggestions reshuffle — with a weekly top-up of the shelf.

recipes-meal-planning-4.territory: It's Sunday at 1:45pm and a batch cooker stands before six recipes, one oven, and four burners, feeling the familiar dread of the 3pm moment when everything needs stirring at once. The interface answers like a calm kitchen dispatcher: cool porcelain surfaces, a big legible clock, and one voice telling you exactly what your hands, your oven, and your stove should each be doing right now. The reward it sells is quiet weeknights, and it looks like it knows that.

palette.note: Cool porcelain and graphite like clean kitchen steel, with timer orange spent only on the step demanding your hands right now — everything else waits its turn in gray.

recipes-meal-planning-4.typography: Suisse Int'l for instructions and labels with Suisse Int'l Mono for every countdown and clock time; the mono timers tick like kitchen equipment while the text stays as terse as a line cook's calls.
recipes-meal-planning-4.motif: The three-lane board: every session is drawn as a horizontal dispatch board with three parallel lanes — Oven, Stove, Hands — where recipe steps sit as colored blocks sliding left toward now, like trains approaching a platform.

ia.coreObject: The session: 4 to 6 recipes compiled into one timed three-lane plan from grocery list to labeled containers
ia.primaryLoop: Pick the week's dishes midweek, shop from one merged list Saturday, run the guided three-hour session Sunday, and eat from containers all week — then come back and do it again.

recipes-meal-planning-5.territory: It is 5:40 p.m., three people will be at the table within the hour, and one of them refuses mushrooms on sight. The interface answers with kitchen daylight: warm, appetizing, and above all practical, promising a dinner nobody has to negotiate. Every screen keeps the whole family visible at once.

palette.note: Warm cream and white keep food photography appetizing, the roasted-tomato accent marks approvals and fixes, and each family member owns one of four fixed dot colors that never change.

recipes-meal-planning-5.typography: Recoleta for dish names, warm and a little homemade, with Inter for lists, quantities, and everything read while stirring a pot.
recipes-meal-planning-5.motif: The four-dot verdict: every dish carries one dot per family member, filled when it clears their list, hollow with a tiny wrench when a one-step fix makes it work.

recipes-meal-planning-7.territory: The person is years into keto, standing in kitchen daylight with a tested repertoire they genuinely fear losing to someone else's app update. The interface answers like a well-thumbed personal cookbook that happens to count: warm, appetizing, unhurried, with the arithmetic of net carbs handled quietly and the collection treated as an heirloom.

palette.note: Butter-cream warmth keeps food photos appetizing while the avocado green lives almost exclusively inside the net-carb stamp, making the one number that matters instantly findable.

recipes-meal-planning-7.typography: Recoleta for recipe titles and shelf names with Karla for ingredients and figures; the soft serif gives the cookbook warmth while Karla keeps the nutrition math crisp and trustworthy.
recipes-meal-planning-7.motif: The net-carb stamp: a circular green seal (like a preserve-jar lid stamp) showing net grams per serving, pressed onto every recipe card, plan slot, and list entry, with the total-minus-fiber math engraved around its rim.

ia.coreObject: The recipe: user-owned, locally stored, with per-serving net carbs, calories, protein, and fat that recalculate on the fly
ia.primaryLoop: Each week the person drags tested recipes into the plan, watches the daily net-carb counter stay under their limit across strict and flex days, and cooks off the combined grocery list, returning nightly to log and tweak.

recipes-meal-planning-8.territory: She's finally opened the shoebox after her mother's house sold — half grief, half duty, and a real fear of getting it wrong. The interface answers like an archivist's table: warm light, unhurried, and the original handwriting always face-up, treated as the treasure rather than the input.

palette.note: Cream and ink-brown keep every screen at paper temperature; jam red appears only on uncertain words waiting for your eye and on the finished book's spine.

recipes-meal-planning-8.typography: Lyon Text sets the transcribed recipes like a printed family cookbook, Untitled Sans stays out of the way in the chrome, and the real star, the handwriting, is always a photograph, never a font.
recipes-meal-planning-8.motif: The taped card: every recipe carries its original photographed card fastened with a visible linen-tape corner, so the source is part of the page, never an attachment.

resume-builder-1.territory: He is seventeen, applying to a grocery store, staring at a field labeled 'Work experience' with nothing to put in it, certain the blankness means he has nothing to offer. The interface answers as a kind interviewer with a typesetter's hands: it only ever asks one easy question, and while he talks, a real document assembles itself in the corner, proving line by line that his life already contains a resume. Career confidence, manufactured honestly.

palette.note: Gallery white around a living document, with an editor's-pen red used only for the interviewer's questions and the marks where his spoken answers become typeset lines; the resume itself stays strictly black on white, because it has to look real.

resume-builder-1.typography: Graphik for the conversational questions, warm and plain, while the growing resume is set in Charter, a serious document face, so the user watches his own words cross the line from chat into print.
resume-builder-1.motif: The living page: a miniature resume pinned to the corner of every screen that visibly typesets a new line the moment a question is answered, growing from blank to finished, so progress is measured in document instead of percent.

ia.coreObject: The answer: one plain-language fact about school, a team, a side gig, or volunteering, which the app typesets into a resume line
ia.primaryLoop: Answer the next simple question in his own words, watch the living page absorb it, and leave with a one-page PDF he is not embarrassed to hand over.

resume-builder-2.territory: About to send the application that matters, haunted by the invisible failure that might be sitting inside the PDF. resume-builder-5.territory: The wording took years to earn and one careless AI tap could smear it. The interface answers like a trusted editor's markup: every suggestion sits beside the original in a second column, written in another color, and nothing crosses over without the author's initials.

palette.note: Your text is always ink-black and the AI writes only in blue pencil, so authorship is legible at a glance on every screen.

resume-builder-5.typography: Ivar Text sets the resume itself while Graphik handles controls; suggestions render in the same face but in blue, so comparison is about the words, never the styling.
resume-builder-5.motif: The stitched gutter: the seam between your column and the AI's, where each accepted phrase crosses over with a small tick stitch that stays visible in history.

ia.coreObject: The suggestion: a phrase-level diff with its stated reason
ia.primaryLoop: Open a section, read the blue column against your own, accept or refuse phrase by phrase; every new job listing worth tailoring for brings them back to the gutter.

resume-builder-7.territory: The person is thirty applications deep, pasting a job listing at 11 pm and wondering whether their resume even speaks the posting's language. The interface answers like a sharp editor across the desk: it reads both documents, shows the gap without flattery, and never lets a rewrite touch the master.

palette.note: Documents live on pure white sheets over a quiet gray studio floor; cobalt marks only what the posting asks for and you haven't said yet.

resume-builder-7.typography: Tiempos Text sets the resume preview like a well-printed document; Söhne runs the analysis chrome, keeping 'your document' and 'our reading of it' visibly separate voices.
resume-builder-7.motif: The match ledger: a two-column typographic diff where requirements you already cover are set in solid ink and the gaps are set in outline type — the page literally shows what's missing as hollow words.

ia.coreObject: the application (a posting, its tailored resume version, and the outcome)
ia.primaryLoop: Paste each new posting, close the gaps in a one-tap tailored version, send it, and log what came back — returning as the tracker shows tailored versions out-earning the identical blast.

ride-hailing-2.territory: It is 4:55 in the morning, the flight leaves at 8:10, and the booked taxi has gone silent. The person is running on adrenaline, checking three apps at once, doing airport math in their head. The interface answers like a night-shift dispatcher: dark, unhurried, one authoritative timeline that already has the plan B loaded.

palette.note: Amber is reserved for time itself, countdowns, deadlines and the flip board, so the one number that matters glows against a cool quiet cabin.

ride-hailing-2.typography: IBM Plex Mono carries every timestamp and countdown, Söhne handles labels and prose, the mono gives times the authority of an airport departure board.
ride-hailing-2.motif: The split-flap row: every critical moment (confirm driver, last safe minute, leave now) renders as a departure-board line that physically flips when its status changes.

ia.coreObject: the departure plan, one flight paired with one booked ride
ia.primaryLoop: Before each trip the traveler pairs flight and taxi booking, then on flight day follows the flip-board timeline and checks the driver at exactly the right minute.

ride-hailing-4.territory: The driver works nights knowing one anonymous complaint can erase six years of income before breakfast, a low hum of professional dread. The interface answers like well-made protective gear: matter-of-fact, always recording, everything sealed and timestamped, ready the moment it is needed. Dark because the cab at night is dark, utilitarian because panic needs big buttons, never theatrical.

palette.note: Asphalt charcoal tuned for a dash-mounted phone at night, with hazard-vest yellow carrying the two things that matter, the recording indicator and the incident button, and a steady green dot proving the recorder is alive.

ride-hailing-4.typography: Archivo for interface text at glanceable dash-mount sizes, with IBM Plex Mono for timestamps, GPS coordinates, and evidence IDs, because the product's whole promise is precise records.
ride-hailing-4.motif: The custody chain: every recording, GPS point, and note is a link in a visible chain strip running under each trip, unbroken links meaning sealed evidence, so a shift reads as a chain no one can quietly edit.

ia.coreObject: The sealed trip record (audio or video, GPS track, timestamps, notes)
ia.primaryLoop: The driver taps Start shift once at the beginning of the night, the app records and chains every trip automatically, and they come back because it is the only archive that answers for them when a complaint lands.

run-tracking-2.territory: A beginner is on the sidewalk at 6:40 AM, out of breath in week four, stealing a half-second glance at their wrist mid-interval. No phone, no free hands, low patience. The interface answers with ruthless glanceability: three enormous numbers on OLED black, a voice in the earbuds, and nothing that asks for a decision while legs are moving.

palette.note: Pure black is a battery decision on OLED as much as a visual one, and amber does exactly one job: it is the color of the current interval, run segments burn amber, walk segments rest in gray.

run-tracking-2.typography: SF Compact Rounded in heavy weights for the three run numbers with tabular figures so pace never jitters, SF Pro on the iPhone companion where reading happens at rest.
run-tracking-2.motif: The segment strip: the day's run/walk plan rendered as one horizontal band of thick amber and thin gray blocks, always showing where you are inside the workout, worn like a progress spine across watch, phone and complication.

ia.coreObject: The workout, one day of the plan as a segment strip that records itself on the wrist
ia.primaryLoop: Three mornings a week: raise the wrist, tap start, obey the voice through the intervals, and let the finished run sync itself to the phone by the time the kettle boils.

run-tracking-3.territory: It is January, 6:15 am, treadmill number four, and the runner is staring at a gym wall worried that winter will punch a hole in the running history they spent all autumn building. The interface answers with planted, unmissable numbers and the steady scroll of the belt: quiet proof that this mile counts exactly like an outdoor one.

palette.note: Safety orange, the color of the treadmill emergency clip, appears only on live numbers and the active interval, everything at rest stays gym-concrete gray.

run-tracking-3.typography: Archivo Expanded for the numerals and Inter for interface text, wide planted figures built to be read mid-stride from an arm's length away.
run-tracking-3.motif: The belt: a ribbed horizontal band that scrolls across every running screen at the speed you entered, its slats doubling as distance ticks that accumulate into your mile count.

ia.coreObject: The run, indoor or outdoor, one record type with no second-class citizens
ia.primaryLoop: Show up for the next Couch-to-5K session three times a week, type one belt number, run, and watch the winter chart stay unbroken, which is exactly why they come back.

run-tracking-4.territory: Mid-run, music carrying the pace, and the familiar dread of a coach voice about to kill the track. The interface answers with daylight clarity and audible good manners: the promise, demonstrated up front, that sound in this app is handled with respect.

palette.note: Chartreuse works like a hi-vis vest: worn as a marker band behind dark text and on the live duck indicator, never as thin type on white.

run-tracking-4.typography: Suisse Int'l with tabular numerals throughout; pace and distance are set enormous and unambiguous, readable at arm's length in full sun at stride.
run-tracking-4.motif: The duck curve: the music waveform dipping a gentle 12 dB notch while the voice band passes over it, drawn live during runs and preserved in every summary.

ia.coreObject: The run: a GPS track with its audio timeline of every cue and every duck
ia.primaryLoop: Start music, start the run, hear cues arrive without the track ever stopping; the post-run audio timeline proving zero interruptions is what keeps trust compounding.
