run-tracking-5.territory: The person is mid-interval, heart pounding, one second of attention to spare and a rising panic that they went out too hot again. The interface answers with open-air calm: one full-bleed color that says on pace, ease up, or back off, readable through sweat at arm's length in direct sunlight. Everything else in the app exists to earn the runner's trust in that single glance.

palette.note: The UI stays daylight-neutral so the three zone colors (green #0B8A3E, amber #E8A200, red #D8402C) own all emotional meaning; color is never decorative, it is always a pace verdict.

run-tracking-5.typography: Barlow Semi Condensed for giant tabular pace numerals and Inter for everything else; numbers are set enormous and condensed like stadium clocks so a split second of peripheral vision is enough.
run-tracking-5.motif: The zone band: a full-bleed field of green, amber or red that floods the entire watch face and echoes as an edge-to-edge horizontal band across every phone screen, so the product's one promise, color equals pace, is literally its surface.

ia.coreObject: The interval, a timed running segment with its own target pace range
ia.primaryLoop: Start the day's workout, run each interval by color instead of numbers, then check the per-interval breakdown afterward to watch the ranges tighten week over week.

screens.title: Onboarding, one honest question
screens.purpose: Set expectations without asking for a goal time that scares a beginner off.
screens.hero: A single card asking how running feels right now, three options, no numbers.
screens.data: "How does running feel these days?" options: "I'm brand new", "I can run 10 minutes without stopping", "I've done a 5K before". Footnote: "No target times. Your first workout sets your pace, not a form."

screens.title: Onboarding, calibration run
screens.purpose: Explain that workout one measures instead of judges.
screens.hero: An empty zone band in soft gray with the caption that it earns its colors today.
screens.data: "Workout 1 is a listening run. Run 3 easy intervals of 2:00 and we'll set your green zone from what your body actually does. Today the band stays gray." Button: "Start listening run".

screens.title: Watch face, on pace
screens.purpose: The core moment: mid-interval verdict with zero reading required.
screens.hero: The entire watch face flooded green, one condensed numeral pair floating on it.
screens.data: Full green field. Center: "7:41" (current pace /km). Small top line: "Run 3 of 6 · 1:12 left". Nothing else on screen.

screens.title: Watch face, too fast
screens.purpose: Show the ease-up state and the 30-second voice rule doing its job.
screens.hero: Full red field with a downward chevron, pace numeral unchanged in position.
screens.data: Full red field. "6:58" with chevron down. Haptic tap. Caption in spec: voice fires only after 30 s outside the zone: "Ease off. Your green zone is 7:30 to 7:50."

screens.title: Phone screen mid-run
screens.purpose: For the runner who pockets the watch UI but glances at a strapped phone.
screens.hero: Edge-to-edge zone band across the top third, interval rail beneath.
screens.data: Amber band, "7:24 /km · a touch fast". Interval rail: W1 done 7:44 · W2 done 7:38 · W3 running 1:12 left · W4–W6 upcoming. Target range pill: "7:30–7:50 /km".

screens.title: Post-run breakdown
screens.purpose: Replace the lying overall average with per-interval truth.
screens.hero: Six horizontal interval bars, each colored by how much of it was spent in zone.
screens.data: Tue 14 Apr · Week 4, Day 2. Intervals: R1 7:36 (92% in zone), R2 7:41 (100%), R3 7:29 (71%, started hot), R4 7:44 (100%), R5 7:48 (97%), R6 7:52 (88%). Footer: "Old-app average would have said 7:42 and told you nothing."

screens.title: Zone width setting
screens.purpose: Let a shaky beginner widen the corridor without shame.
screens.hero: A slider that visibly fattens or narrows the green band on a live preview.
screens.data: Options: "Tight ±5 s/km, for steady runners" and "Wide ±15 s/km, recommended for your first 6 weeks". Preview: green zone 7:25–7:55 at wide. Note: "Wide is not easier. It's honest for where you are."

screens.title: Progress, week over week
screens.purpose: Prove improvement with numbers the runner can feel.
screens.hero: Four stacked week rows, each showing its green-zone pace range sliding left.
screens.data: Week 1: 8:10–8:40. Week 2: 8:02–8:32. Week 3: 7:48–8:18. Week 4: 7:30–7:50. Callout: "Your green zone moved 40 s/km in four weeks. Time in zone: 61% → 89%."

screens.title: Paywall
screens.purpose: Sell color zones and breakdowns to someone already paying Runna for cues.
screens.hero: A split image: gray numbers-only watch face labeled Free, green flooded face labeled Zones.
screens.data: "Live pace stays free, always. Zones on your wrist, per-interval breakdowns and weekly comparison are $6.99/month. Cancel anytime in Settings." Buttons: "Start Zones · $6.99/mo", "Keep running free", link "Restore purchase".

screens.title: First-launch empty state
screens.purpose: A home screen with no runs yet that still feels like open air.
screens.hero: The gray uncalibrated zone band with a single inviting start button.
screens.data: "No runs yet. Your first workout teaches the app your pace, it doesn't grade it. 3 × 2:00 easy intervals, about 14 minutes with warmup." Button: "Start Workout 1".

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Few controls, all of them about the run.
screens.hero: A short plain list, zone width first.
screens.data: Zone width: Wide ±15 s. Voice alerts: On, after 30 s out of zone. Units: km. Watch haptics: On. Recalibrate my zones. Manage subscription · Restore purchase. Export runs (GPX).

run-tracking-6.territory: She is a nurse on rotating shifts training for her first 10K, and Tuesday's run just died under a double shift and a sick kid. The old app would greet her with a red 'MISSED'. This interface answers with daylight and a shrug: the plan slides to Thursday like a meeting politely moved, her progress untouched. The feeling is open air and a training partner who has a life too.

palette.note: Cool morning-air white with a trail green that marks every completed and every rescheduled run identically, because in this app a moved run is a kept run; red does not exist in the palette.

run-tracking-6.typography: GT America for everything, compressed weights for in-run numbers readable at a bouncing arm's length, standard widths for the calm planning voice; splits and paces always in tabular figures.
run-tracking-6.motif: The sliding week: workouts are smooth green stones resting on a continuous path, and rescheduling is the visible, frictionless glide of a stone along the line to a new day, never a deletion, never a gap with a mark of shame.

ia.coreObject: The training week: three stones on a seven-day path, each movable, together always adding up to the plan
ia.primaryLoop: Glance at where this week's stones sit, run when one comes due or slide it when life hits, and watch the projected race date stay honest either way.

screens.title: The goal, and the shape of your week
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 1: set the race and pick three preferred days that are explicitly promises to try, not contracts.
screens.hero: A race card above a seven-day path where she drops three stones onto her usual days.
screens.data: Goal: 'First 10K, Riverside Run, September 20'. Stones placed: Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday. Line beneath, load-bearing: 'These are preferences, not locks. Any stone can slide inside its week and the plan holds.' Current base: 'I can jog about 20 minutes', from three options. Button: 'Build my 12 weeks'.

screens.title: How this plan treats a miss
screens.purpose: Onboarding step 2: show the fork once, up front, so the first real miss feels familiar instead of frightening.
screens.hero: A tiny animated demo: a stone sliding from Tuesday to Thursday, the path unbroken.
screens.data: Copy: 'When you miss a run, you get two buttons: slide the plan, or skip that one and carry on. No questionnaire about why. Sick? One tap pauses everything and your progress waits.' Footer: 'You will probably reschedule 10-15 times in 12 weeks. That is what real schedules do.' Button: 'Start week 1'.

screens.title: This week
screens.purpose: Main screen mid-use: week 5 of 12 with one run done, one due today, one already slid, all reading as normal.
screens.hero: The seven-day path with three stones: Monday filled, today pulsing gently, Saturday's stone shown mid-glide to Sunday.
screens.data: Week 5 of 12. Monday: easy 25 min, done, 3.1 km. Today, Thursday: intervals, 6 x 400 m, due. Saturday to Sunday: long run 5 km, slid yesterday because of a shift, marked in the same green as the completed run. Header: 'On track for September 20.' Button: 'Start today's run'.

screens.title: You missed Tuesday
screens.purpose: The fork at its moment: the morning after a miss, two honest options and no third button asking why.
screens.hero: The Tuesday stone lifted off the path with exactly two landing spots lit: the whole path shifted, or the next stone.
screens.data: 'Tuesday's intervals did not happen. Two ways forward: Slide the plan: everything moves 2 days, race projection moves to September 22. Skip it: keep the calendar, this session is dropped, projection unchanged, week stays 2 of 3.' Both buttons the same size and the same green. Nothing else on the screen.

screens.title: Sick mode
screens.purpose: The one-tap pause: illness suspends the plan, the streak, and the notifications in a single motion.
screens.hero: One large button, 'I am sick', over a path visibly settling into a resting state, stones dimmed but intact.
screens.data: Tapped: 'Plan paused. Nothing counts against you. Notifications are silent until you come back.' Below: 'Your 4-week consistency streak is frozen, not lost.' Return flow shown: 'Back on my feet' offers 'ease in with one short run' or 'resume where I left off'. No date pressure, no daily are-you-better ping.

screens.title: Reschedule from the notification
screens.purpose: The mechanic nobody else has: moving tonight's run from the lock screen without opening the app.
screens.hero: A lock-screen notification expanded, with time chips inside the notification itself.
screens.data: Notification, 4:45 PM: 'Intervals at 6:00 PM tonight.' Long-press actions: 'Push to 8 PM', 'Move to tomorrow 6 AM', 'Slide to Saturday'. She taps 8 PM; confirmation in the notification: 'Done. See you at 8.' Spec note: no app launch, three taps total, works from the watch too.

screens.title: Moved three times, still on plan
screens.purpose: The reschedule history mechanic: normalize the slides by showing them as the plan working, not failing.
screens.hero: Week rows with slide arcs drawn between days, every arc in the same calm green as a completed run.
screens.data: Week 3: long run slid Sat to Sun, done. Week 4: intervals slid Tue to Thu, done; one skip. Week 5: long run slid Sat to Sun, done. Caption: '4 slides, 1 skip, 13 of 14 sessions completed. Plans that bend get finished. Rigid ones get deleted in week 3.'

screens.title: Your real finish line
screens.purpose: The projection mechanic: a race-readiness date computed from her actual rhythm, updating without judgment.
screens.hero: A horizon line with two small flags: the race date fixed, the readiness date floating just ahead of it.
screens.data: 'At your real pace, 2.7 runs a week, you are race-ready September 14, six days before the start.' History of the projection: 'Sept 9 after week 2, Sept 16 after your sick week, Sept 14 now.' Line: 'This date is computed from what you actually ran, never from the plan as written.'

screens.title: Mid-run
screens.purpose: The run screen at speed: split-second legibility in open air, nothing that needs reading twice.
screens.hero: Three enormous compressed-type numbers on white, high contrast, thumb-size lap button at the bottom.
screens.data: Interval 4 of 6. Current: 400 m rep, 2:04, pace 5:11 /km. Rest next: 90 s. Heart rate 162 from watch. Auto-pause on. Voice in earbuds at rep end: 'Four done. Ninety seconds easy.' Everything visible at arm swing in sunlight; no map on this screen by default, map lives one swipe left.

screens.title: Run done, plan updated
screens.purpose: The completion moment folds straight back into the week: the stone fills, the projection breathes.
screens.hero: The interval session's stone filling green on the path, with the week's remaining stone and the projection line beneath.
screens.data: 'Intervals done: 6 x 400 m, average 5:08 /km, 34 minutes.' Week: 2 of 3, long run Sunday. Projection: 'September 14, unchanged.' One quiet stat that respects her reality: 'That is 5 weeks running at least twice, through 3 reschedules and a sick week.'

screens.title: Pay for the bend, not the miles
screens.purpose: Paywall in the product's forgiving voice: tracking stays free, the flexibility engine is the paid thing.
screens.hero: Two price cards under one sentence: 'The base plan is free. The plan that bends around your life is $4.99 a month, or $19.99 once, forever.'
screens.data: Free forever: the 12-week plan, run tracking, one manual reschedule a week. Flex, $4.99 a month or $19.99 lifetime: unlimited slides, sick mode, reschedule-from-notification, the real-rhythm projection. Copy: 'Runna charges $17.99 a month and locks the calendar. We charge less to unlock it.' Links, equal size: 'Restore purchase', 'Stay on the free plan'.

screens.title: Week zero
screens.purpose: First-launch empty state: no runs yet, the path empty, the first session sized to be unmissable.
screens.hero: An empty seven-day path with a single ghosted stone on the day she picked, labeled with a 20-minute session.
screens.data: 'Nothing logged yet, and week 1 is deliberately light: 20 minutes, any pace, walk breaks welcome. The plan starts adapting from your very first run.' Buttons: 'Start run 1 now', 'It is scheduled for Tuesday, leave it there'.

screens.title: Settings
screens.purpose: Quiet hours, notification behavior, watch and health connections, all consistent with the no-guilt contract.
screens.hero: A grouped list opening with 'How we speak to you', because tone is a setting here.
screens.data: Notifications: reminders on, 'never send guilt copy' shown as a fixed statement, quiet during sick mode automatic. Reminder times editable per weekday: Tue 6 PM, Thu 6 PM, Sun 8 AM. Connections: Apple Watch, Apple Health, Garmin. Units: km. Data: runs exportable as GPX and CSV. Delete account and data: two-step.

run-tracking-8.territory: Jet-lagged at 5:50 am in a city they cannot pronounce yet, the runner wants to just go without becoming a tourist squinting at a phone on a dark corner. The interface answers like a calm co-pilot in the pre-dawn: one giant next instruction, silence on the straights, and the quiet certainty that a wrong turn costs nothing.

palette.note: Hi-vis chartreuse, the color of a runner's vest, is reserved for the next instruction and the route stroke only, everything else stays dim so the one thing that matters reads in half a glance.

run-tracking-8.typography: Frutiger for instructions and numerals, the airport wayfinding face, because a turn call in a strange city should read like signage in a terminal, with everything set oversized and tabular.
run-tracking-8.motif: The closed loop: every route is drawn as one continuous chartreuse stroke that starts and ends at the same knot, your hotel, never as a map with a pin.

ia.coreObject: The loop, a generated closed route of an exact length from wherever you are standing
ia.primaryLoop: Land somewhere new, tap a distance, run by voice with the phone in your pocket, and come home with the loop closed, which is why the app opens in every new city.

scanner-pdf-1.territory: It is the last day of the month and a freelancer faces a fist of crumpled receipts with pure dread of the data entry ahead. The interface answers with conveyor-belt speed: paper goes in one end, a finished table comes out the other, and every screen exists to keep the belt moving. No decoration, no dashboard poetry, just the satisfying mechanics of a machine that types for you.

palette.note: Flat white with hairline rules like ledger paper; the ledger green appears only on extracted money amounts and confirmed rows, so green literally means captured value.

scanner-pdf-1.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk for interface labels with JetBrains Mono for every extracted amount, date, and merchant string; the mono treatment makes OCR output look like verifiable machine fact rather than a guess.
scanner-pdf-1.motif: Paper-to-row: the signature transition where a photographed receipt visibly compresses into a single spreadsheet row (merchant, date, amount) that clicks into the table, repeated on every capture like a mechanical stamp.

ia.coreObject: The receipt row: one photographed receipt reduced to date, merchant, amount, and category, living inside a monthly table
ia.primaryLoop: A few times a week the person shoots whatever receipts accumulated, spends thirty seconds confirming low-confidence fields, and at month's end exports the finished table for their report, which is the entire reason the app stays on the home screen.

scanner-pdf-2.territory: The user is sitting with a shoebox of their grandmother's letters or a colleague's field notebook, braced for an afternoon of squinting. The tone hint says utility speed, and capture is exactly that, but the heart of this product is the proofreading hour, so the interface answers with the calm of an archivist's desk: original and transcription side by side, doubt marked honestly in amber, and the quiet satisfaction of watching a page clear as you confirm it.

palette.note: Amber exists for exactly one reason, marking words the model doubts; as you confirm words the amber drains out of the page, so color literally measures remaining work.

scanner-pdf-2.typography: Charter for the transcribed text, chosen because it reads like a typeset book and makes the family archive feel finished, with IBM Plex Sans for chrome and confidence figures.
scanner-pdf-2.motif: The doubt wash: a soft highlighter stroke of amber behind every uncertain word that fades to clean paper the moment you confirm or fix it, so a finished page looks visibly at rest.

ia.coreObject: The page pair: one photographed page and its editable transcription, joined for life
ia.primaryLoop: Photograph a few pages, then sit with the split view fixing amber words until the document reads clean, and come back tomorrow for the next batch of letters.

screens.title: Onboarding: the promise
screens.purpose: Show the split view on a real letter in ten seconds so the buyer understands this is a correction desk, not a blind converter.
screens.hero: An animated split: cursive letter on the left, typed text appearing on the right with three amber words
screens.data: Sample: a 1962 letter, right pane reads 'We drove to Asheville on the [Tuesd?y] after Easter' with 'Tuesd?y' washed amber, caption: 'We show you exactly where we're not sure.'

screens.title: Onboarding: what you're transcribing

screens.title: First launch, empty
screens.purpose: Turn the empty library into an invitation to fetch the box of letters.
screens.hero: An empty document shelf with one oversized Capture button
screens.data: 'No pages yet. Most people start with the letter they can't read.' · Capture a page · Import from Photos or Files

screens.data: Letter from Ruth, March 1962 · page 3 of 4 · 214 words recognized · 11 words below 80% confidence will be marked · about 20 seconds

screens.title: The correction desk (main, mid-use)
screens.purpose: The core screen: scan left, text right, amber words waiting, this is where the product earns its price.
screens.hero: The split view with synchronized scroll, amber washes on the right, matching outlines on the left scan
screens.data: Ruth · March 1962 · page 3: '...the peach trees took the frost badly and your father says we may lose the [orchard/orchards]' · 7 of 11 doubts remaining · pinch to zoom the scan independently

screens.purpose: Multi-page progress tracking so a 40-page journal feels like a countable project instead of a wall.
screens.hero: A page grid where each thumbnail carries its remaining-doubt count
screens.data: Field notebook, R. Okafor · 38 pages · 22 clean · 9 in progress (3–14 doubts each) · 7 not yet recognized · resume at page 23 · total time in this document: 2 h 40 m

screens.purpose: Show the multilingual mechanic earning its keep on the exact page type that breaks other apps.
screens.hero: A letter switching mid-line from English to German, both transcribed in place

scanner-pdf-3.territory: The person is faxing the IRS or a court once this year, it absolutely must arrive, and every fax app they have tried felt like paying $12 to shout into a pipe. The interface answers like a post-office counter run by someone competent: stark, instant, one-thumb, where the product's whole personality is the stamped receipt proving the other machine answered.

palette.note: Certified-stamp red is spent only on the moment of proof, the delivery receipt stamp and true failure notices, while the entire sending flow stays black-on-white so the one red stamp reads like ink hitting paper.

scanner-pdf-3.typography: Public Sans at heavy weights runs the interface with government-form plainness; OCR-B renders station IDs, response codes, and timestamps so every receipt looks machine-verified because it is.
scanner-pdf-3.motif: The receipt strip: every completed transmission produces a dot-matrix-styled slip with station ID, result code, and page count, torn-edge top and bottom, and these slips are the app's entire visual memory.

ia.coreObject: The transmission: an outbound fax with its machine-issued receipt slip, or an inbound fax on your permanent number
ia.primaryLoop: Scan, send, and pocket the receipt slip in under three minutes on the rare day it matters, and keep the app because your permanent inbound number catches the agency's reply.

scanner-pdf-4.territory: A lawyer at 17:50 needs one clause from one scan among nine hundred files named scan_0231, and every second of hunting is billable time bleeding out. The interface answers with the flat competence of a well-run records room: dense, instant, zero decoration, where the only flourish permitted is the yellow marker stroke on the exact words you searched for. Relief here is measured in seconds-to-found.

palette.note: Cool archival gray and white keep every pixel administrative, and the single highlighter yellow is spent exclusively on search matches, so the eye learns that yellow always means 'found'.

scanner-pdf-4.typography: Helvetica Now Text for the interface and JetBrains Mono for filenames, dates and extracted OCR text: filing-system neutrality with monospace for anything the index actually read off the paper.
scanner-pdf-4.motif: The marker stroke: search hits are painted as translucent highlighter directly on the photograph of the document itself, page after page, as if someone went through your archive with a yellow marker overnight.

ia.coreObject: The indexed document (a scan plus its background-built, searchable OCR text layer)
ia.primaryLoop: Capture or import papers in seconds, then return whenever something must be found and get the highlighted page in under a second.

scanner-pdf-5.territory: A front-desk clerk has a guest waiting and a passport in hand: fifteen seconds, one thumb, no second take. scanner-pdf-7.territory: The person is in a hallway, a parked car, or a client's kitchen with a contract on their phone and someone waiting for it back. The interface answers with magnetic precision: fields reveal themselves, the signature lands exactly where it belongs on the first try, and the document leaves the phone in one motion. The feeling is a fountain pen that never misses, not a PDF editor.

palette.note: Cool document-gray desk beneath true-white pages; the ink blue belongs to everything the user adds — fields light up in it, signatures render in it — so your marks are always distinguishable from the printed form.

scanner-pdf-7.typography: Instrument Sans for the interface with Caveat rendering the sample signature strokes; the contrast between the precise grotesk chrome and the human ink line is the whole personality.
scanner-pdf-7.motif: The magnetic snap: user-placed objects (signature, initials, dates) glide with a visible pull-line into detected fields and settle with a soft tick, making correct placement feel like a physical property of the document.

ia.coreObject: The document: a PDF with its fields detected, filled, signed, and sent, leaving a history entry
ia.primaryLoop: Several times a week a contract arrives by mail or messenger, the person opens it here, fills and signs in under two minutes, and fires it back without touching a computer, which is why the share-sheet shortcut becomes muscle memory.

scanner-pdf-8.territory: You just finished a watercolor and you are bracing for the app to bleach it, because every scanner before this one did. palette.note: The chrome is a true neutral gray so it never skews color judgment; the violet appears only on controls and never near the scanned image itself.

scanner-pdf-8.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk in one quiet weight for everything, sized small and set wide, because in this app the type is signage and the artwork is the show.
scanner-pdf-8.motif: The swatch handle: every before-and-after divider is dragged by a small color-checker chip, the universal mark of calibrated color, and it recurs as the app icon of every saved scan.

ia.coreObject: The scan: a color-managed capture of an artwork or document with its correction decisions recorded
ia.primaryLoop: Point, capture, drag the swatch handle to compare, approve or reject the correction, export losslessly; artists return every time a piece leaves the desk.

shopping-ecommerce-2.territory: The box just arrived, the sneakers are in hand, and a $340 doubt is climbing: real or not, and the return window is already counting down. The interface answers with the composed authority of an appraisal desk: white space, unhurried serif, procedure over reassurance. The feeling is of handing the object across a counter to someone whose word will hold up in a dispute.

palette.note: Gallery white lets the user's own product photos carry all the color; the deep archival green appears exclusively on verdicts and the seal, so its rare arrival lands like a stamp on a document.

shopping-ecommerce-2.typography: GT Sectra for verdicts and report headings, giving findings the gravity of an appraisal letter, with Untitled Sans for instructions and interface labels.
shopping-ecommerce-2.motif: The dated seal: a circular embossed stamp bearing the verdict and the exact date-time (VERIFIED GENUINE · 11 JUL 2026 · 14:32) that closes every report and appears half-inked while a check is pending.

ia.coreObject: The check: one item, its guided photo set, the expert's dated verdict report
ia.primaryLoop: After each secondary-market purchase, shoot the guided photo set the day the box arrives and get the verdict inside 24 hours; buyers return before purchases too, to look sellers up in the flagged-counterfeit registry.

shopping-ecommerce-3.territory: The user is a burned buyer with a $180 package problem, bracing for a procedural fight they've lost before against a platform that wins on paperwork. The interface answers as a paralegal's desk: cream paper, indexed folders, and timestamps stamped on everything, so calm and procedural that panic converts into filing. It never cheerleads; it documents.

palette.note: Ink navy does the reading, and the red is rationed to deadlines and countdowns only, so red on this desk always means a date, never decoration.

shopping-ecommerce-3.typography: Spectral for case text with the gravity of a legal brief, Söhne Mono for every timestamp, case number, and deadline; the mono stamps make the evidence feel notarized.
shopping-ecommerce-3.motif: The evidence stamp: a mono, boxed timestamp (SAVED 14:32 · MAR 3) pressed onto every captured listing, message, photo, and video, proving when each artifact entered the file.

ia.coreObject: The case file (one order: captured listing, messages, media, deadlines, and claims)
ia.primaryLoop: Forward each order email as it happens so evidence accrues silently; when something goes wrong, open the case and follow the countdown-driven next step

shopping-ecommerce-6.territory: A reseller photographing a thrifted Coach bag on the kitchen table, part shopkeeper, part curator, drowning in four apps that all want the same twelve fields. The interface answers like a well-lit stockroom crossed with a lookbook: gallery white, product photography first, and the quiet operational certainty that one card truly controls every storefront.

palette.note: Gallery white lets product photos carry all the color; the oxblood red is spent on exactly two things, the sold stamp and primary actions, so a sale reads across the room like a red dot on a gallery wall.

shopping-ecommerce-6.typography: Canela sets item titles with editorial desire, the way a catalog makes a used jacket feel collectible, while Untitled Sans runs the operational layer of fields, statuses, and platform names without stealing a glance.
shopping-ecommerce-6.motif: The card fan: one master item card that fans into four platform copies like a hand of cards, spreading on publish and snapping back into one when the item sells.

ia.coreObject: The item card: one canonical listing that projects itself onto every connected platform
ia.primaryLoop: Photograph and card up new inventory, publish the fan in one action, and return for the red sold stamps, each one confirming the other three storefronts already cleaned themselves up.

sleep-tracking-1.territory: A nurse getting home at 8:40 AM, blinds down against full daylight, opening the app with gritty eyes and braced for the usual red scolding about sleeping at the wrong time. The interface answers like a quiet night corridor: dim, soft, unhurried, and structurally on their side, because here the day begins at their shift, not at midnight, and daytime sleep is simply sleep.

palette.note: Moonlit ink blues with a silver accent, no neon anywhere; sleep renders as soft luminous fills and the only warm tone is a low amber #D9A05B reserved for wake-up and shift-start moments.

sleep-tracking-1.typography: Atkinson Hyperlegible for everything because it stays readable to someone at hour nineteen of being awake, with generous sizes and loose leading that never make tired eyes work.
sleep-tracking-1.motif: The shift ribbon: a horizontal timeline that anchors to work blocks instead of midnights, with sleep drawn as soft glowing pools before and after each shift that visibly pour into one shared total.

ia.coreObject: The work block: one shift with its surrounding sleep pools and its own quota
ia.primaryLoop: Log or auto-detect sleep around each shift, see the block quota fill regardless of the clock, and check which rotation patterns are quietly building debt.

sleep-tracking-2.territory: A couple at the breakfast table replaying a decade-old argument: who was sawing logs at 3 am. Under the joke sits real worry about apnea. The interface answers like moonlight on the bed: dark, hushed, and scrupulously fair, showing each person only what their own side of the mattress said, with the receipts to end the argument kindly.

palette.note: Midnight blue with moonlight periwinkle for shared elements; each partner owns a constant personal hue, warm amber for one and cool sky for the other, so attribution reads at a squint from bed.

sleep-tracking-2.typography: General Sans in light weights keeps the night pages airy and dim-room legible, while decibel readings and timestamps set in Spline Sans Mono glow like instrument readouts on a bedside dial.
sleep-tracking-2.motif: The center seam: every visualization is split down a soft vertical seam like the gap between two pillows, left side and right side of the bed, and nothing ever crosses it without evidence.

sleep-tracking-4.territory: The user is a mother at 19:40 with a heavy, almost-asleep baby on one arm and exactly one thumb free, operating in a dark nursery where any bright pixel is sabotage. The interface answers like moonlight: dark, soft, one enormous button, and data that glows gently instead of shouting. Everything it knows, it learned from her baby, and it says so quietly.

sleep-tracking-4.motif: The breathing ripple: slow concentric rings that pulse outward from the put-down button at the tempo of the playing sound, standing in for both 'sound is on' and 'sleep is being kept'.

sleep-tracking-5.territory: It is 1 a.m., the user is in bed with a ringing only they can hear, tired of sound libraries that were never built for them. The interface answers with the stillness of a dark bedroom: near-black, no celebration, one soft band of light that says we found it. Everything is dimmed except the single thing that matters, their frequency.

sleep-tracking-5.motif: A thin luminous vertical band on a horizontal frequency spectrum, your pitch as a single lit slice of the audible range, recurring on the test dial, the mask preview, and the monthly recheck.

sleep-tracking-6.territory: The person is chronically underslept and quietly angry at apps that prescribe a 7:30 wake-up their 5:30 alarm will never allow. Starting from the night-depth tone but bending it warmer: this is the hour of the bedside lamp, not the void, someone doing honest arithmetic about rest before turning it off. The interface answers like a patient financial planner for sleep: dim, warm, matter-of-fact, treating the debt as payable and the person's calendar as law.

palette.note: Lamplight amber is the color of the plan itself, the thread and tonight's step, while your immovable constraints render in bone-white and the debt figure in plain text, so what you must do glows and what cannot move stays solid.

sleep-tracking-6.typography: Söhne Mono sets every duration and debt figure with ledger precision, while Söhne carries the plan's instructions in the low, even voice of someone who has stopped moralizing about bedtimes.
sleep-tracking-6.motif: The immovable posts: fixed alarms, work evenings and flights stand on the week timeline as solid bone-white pillars, and the amber payoff plan threads between them like a river finding the only path it can actually take.

ia.coreObject: The payoff plan, a day-by-day schedule that retires your sleep debt inside your real constraints
ia.primaryLoop: Each evening the app names tonight's one step (a bedtime, an added 40 minutes, a nap slot), Apple Health confirms what actually happened overnight, and the thread re-routes every morning, which is exactly why the person checks it.

sleep-tracking-7.territory: The person is exhausted, a little frightened by what their partner says they sound like at night, and tired of not being taken seriously. The interface answers with the calm of a night ward: dark because it lives on a nightstand at 1 am, precise because everything it records may be read by a physician. No games, no sleep scores, just evidence accumulating with quiet gravity.

palette.note: Data glows softly like moonlight on a chart; red exists in exactly one place, oxygen readings below 90 percent, so when it appears it means something.

sleep-tracking-7.typography: IBM Plex Sans carries the clinical copy and IBM Plex Mono sets every timestamp and SpO2 value, because numbers headed for a doctor's desk should look like instrument output.
sleep-tracking-7.motif: The night strip: every recorded night is one horizontal midnight-to-morning band with event ticks and vitals beneath it, identical on screen and in the physician PDF, so the app and the document are visibly the same evidence.

sobriety-1.territory: The person opening this app may have just slipped after 89 days, ashamed and braced for the app to shame them too. The interface answers like dawn after a hard night: warm, unhurried, and certain that everything they built is still there. Nothing here judges, nothing flashes, nothing resets to a void.

palette.note: Dawn apricot appears only on the accumulating lifetime number and the current chapter; past chapters render in deepening warm neutrals like sediment, and red is banned from the entire product.

sobriety-1.typography: Tiempos Text for day counts and chapter headings gives numbers the dignity of a memoir; Söhne in a quiet weight handles labels, so the serif moments feel earned rather than decorative.
sobriety-1.motif: Strata: every sober period is a horizontal sediment band that stacks upward and never erodes, so the whole history reads as accumulated ground you stand on rather than a streak that can snap.

ia.coreObject: The chapter (one sober period with its start, end, length, and optional note), stacking into a lifetime strata
ia.primaryLoop: Open once a day to watch the current chapter and the lifetime total both tick up, and return after any slip because restarting adds a layer instead of erasing six months of proof.

sobriety-4.territory: The person here has years, not days: they open the app once a month the way you open a drawer with medals in it, wanting quiet confirmation that the long road still counts and still leads somewhere. The interface answers like an archive built for decades: patinated, unhurried, and visibly designed to outlast every milestone it has already given.

palette.note: Bronze is reserved for earned things only: rings, badges, and anniversary dates; everything unearned stays in parchment and ink, so the accent itself reads as a decoration you were given, not a UI color.

sobriety-4.typography: Canela for years and milestone names lends the lapidary feel of an engraved plaque; GT America in small caps carries dates and labels like museum wall text.
sobriety-4.motif: Growth rings: the sobriety record is a cross-section that adds one bronze-edged ring per year, so a ten-year profile is physically wider and visibly rarer than a one-year one, with no outermost ring ever drawn as final.

ia.coreObject: The ring record: one continuous sobriety span rendered as accumulating year-rings, carrying earned badges and personal milestones on its rim
ia.primaryLoop: Open monthly to see the rings and the countdown to the next rare mark, and come back on every anniversary for the generated journey page worth showing family.

sobriety-5.territory: Someone mid-taper checking how much runway is left in the day, half hopeful and half braced for judgment. The interface answers with dawn-lit dignity: warm neutrals, no alarms, no red, a plan that visibly bends instead of breaking, because the person has already had enough of feeling like a failure.

palette.note: Warm dawn neutrals stay quiet all day; the amber horizon of the daily limit pales toward gold as the taper descends and never once turns red, even when the count goes over.

sobriety-5.typography: Canela serif reserved for milestone moments that deserve dignity, Graphik for counts and controls, so the numbers stay matter-of-fact and the words stay kind.
sobriety-5.motif: The sinking horizon: the daily limit drawn as a thin dawn-lit horizon line that sits a little lower each day, with the puff count rising toward it like a slow tide that must stay below the light.

ia.coreObject: The day: its horizon (limit), its logged puffs, and where it sits on the descending curve
ia.primaryLoop: Tap the widget with each puff, glance at what's left before the horizon, and come back nightly to watch the weekly line step down.

screens.purpose: The no-shame state: going over shifts the plan instead of breaking it.

screens.data: '121 of 118 — over by 3.' Copy: 'Tomorrow's line moves to 116 instead of 112. The plan bends. It doesn't break.' Single button: 'Okay'

sobriety-6.territory: It is Sunday evening and someone who would never call themselves a problem drinker is quietly deciding what this week should look like. They want fewer drinks, zero witnesses and zero sermons. The interface answers like a private ledger kept in dawn light: neutral words, small numbers, a curve that drifts down over months without ever once congratulating or scolding.

palette.note: Sage is the color of the plan and the average, never of praise or warning, and nothing in the palette shifts red when a week runs over, the ledger simply records.

sobriety-6.typography: Lora for the weekly plan numbers and monthly average, lending the calm of a printed almanac, with Söhne Leicht for logging and settings so daily entry feels weightless.
sobriety-6.motif: The descending line: one thin hand-drawn-feeling curve of the rolling weekly average, always present like a horizon at the top of the ledger, redrawn a hair lower each good month.

ia.coreObject: The week, a self-set plan of two numbers with seven evening facts logged against it
ia.primaryLoop: Reply to one neutral evening message with a number, and on Sundays spend ninety seconds setting next week's plan while the average curve inches down.

screens.title: Your first plan, step 1 of 2

sobriety-7.territory: It is early in the day and early in recovery, and the person wants structure that doesn't preach — they've already walked out of rooms that opened with a prayer. The interface answers with dawn light and a steady editorial voice: one page today, one written exercise, and the visible fact of ground already covered.

palette.note: A parchment field that warms slightly toward the top of every screen like first light; terracotta is reserved for the single action each day asks of you.

sobriety-7.typography: Newsreader carries the daily readings with the dignity of a printed essay; Figtree keeps the exercise forms plain and unclinical, so writing in them feels like a notebook, not a chart.
sobriety-7.motif: The ascending horizon: every completed day lays one thin dawn-colored band above a fixed horizon line, so twelve weeks accumulate as a slowly rising sunrise the person built themselves.

ia.coreObject: the day (one three-minute reading plus one written exercise)
ia.primaryLoop: Open the app once a day, read for three minutes, write one structured exercise, and mark the evening check — the rising horizon records the run without gamifying it.

sobriety-8.territory: The person opens this app in a fragile minute, sometimes proud, sometimes one urge away from breaking a 47-day streak, and what they cannot afford is a number that lies to them. The interface answers with dawn light and ledger honesty: warm, unhurried, and utterly stable, every figure traceable and no surface that ever moves on its own.

palette.note: Everything holds a dawn temperature of warm paper and ink, and the terracotta accent appears only when a milestone is reached, never as an alarm.

sobriety-8.typography: Untitled Serif sets the day number and every milestone line like a quiet congratulation, Inter handles the working interface underneath it.
sobriety-8.motif: The dawn line: a thin horizon gradient near the top of every screen that climbs one degree brighter with each recovered-body milestone, so the app literally gets lighter the longer you stay quit.

ia.coreObject: Your quit: one protected start date with a recovery timeline and a money ledger growing from it
ia.primaryLoop: Open once a day to watch the day count and the money total rise, check which body system recovers next, and put the saved amount against a real goal.

stock-investing-3.territory: The subscriber has just watched a signal land in Telegram and feels the old split-second doubt: is this channel real, or will this loss quietly vanish from its history next week. The interface answers as a notary, cool, procedural, incorruptible: every signal stamped with price and time the instant it arrives, and a ledger that physically cannot be rewritten, not even by the user.

palette.note: Cool document gray-blue keeps the terminal precision without the black-screen theater; the oxblood accent is reserved for the seal, the stamp of immutability on every entry, never for gains or losses, which stay in quiet ink green #1E6B4F and ink red #9E3B32.

stock-investing-3.typography: Söhne for interface text and IBM Plex Mono for every price, timestamp and percentage in tabular figures, so the ledger reads like a settlement document rather than a trading terminal.
stock-investing-3.motif: The seal: a small oxblood circular stamp with the capture timestamp that appears on each entry the moment it locks, tilted a degree like a real hand stamp, the visible proof that this row can never be edited or deleted.

ia.coreObject: The sealed signal entry: source, instrument, direction, capture price and timestamp, followed to its outcome
ia.primaryLoop: When a signal arrives, log it in seconds and let the app stamp the market price; return over the weeks to watch each source's honest scoreboard diverge from its advertising.

stock-investing-7.territory: It's Sunday night and the premium seller is squaring the book: what did the month actually pay, and what's still on the table into Friday's expiry. The interface answers like a beautiful ledger — terminal precision set in ink on paper, every spread finally folded into one line that adds up.

palette.note: Ivory paper and hairline rules do the structure; ledger green marks premium collected, and losses print in plain ink — never alarm red.

stock-investing-7.typography: Suisse Int'l for labels and headers; every figure set in Suisse Int'l Mono — tabular, right-aligned, kept like a book by hand.
stock-investing-7.motif: The strategy brace: a typeset curly brace that folds a position's legs — short call, long shares, every roll — into one line item, drawn down the ledger like a proof.

teleprompter-captions-3.territory: The person is on camera for work, three paragraphs deep, and carrying the old dread that one fumbled word erases the last twenty minutes. The interface answers like a calm floor director: only this paragraph exists right now, everything you already nailed is locked in the can. Recording stops feeling like a tightrope and starts feeling like laying bricks.

palette.note: Studio-dark stays out of the camera's way; the single tally-amber accent marks exactly one thing at a time, the live take, and completed takes cool down to neutral gray so finished work reads as settled.

teleprompter-captions-3.typography: Neue Haas Grotesk for prompter text and headings, sized huge and loose-tracked for reading at arm's length, with IBM Plex Mono for timecodes and take numbers so the app carries itself like broadcast equipment, not a social camera.
teleprompter-captions-3.motif: The take slate: every paragraph is a horizontal slate card with a stamped take counter (TAKE 2 OF 2) and a filled amber corner when it is in the can, and the row of slates is the spine of every screen from script to export.

ia.coreObject: The take, one recorded paragraph of a script
ia.primaryLoop: Paste a script, shoot it slate by slate, retake only what slipped, stitch and post, and come back every week because the ten-minute shoot replaced the hour-long one.

translator-2.territory: A traveler who once stood in a Oaxacan mountain town with a $30 offline pack that wouldn't load is packing again, and what they want is not features but certainty. The interface answers like a cockpit instrument panel the night before departure: dark, calm, and lit by green verification lights that were earned on the ground, not promised in marketing. Every claim about offline is something the app has already proven on this exact phone.

palette.note: Deep cabin navy for calm at 30,000 feet, with instrument green appearing only when a capability has actually been verified on this device — untested things stay amber (#E8B94A), never falsely green.

translator-2.typography: Frutiger (or Public Sans) at generous signage sizes for translations and Söhne Mono for verification logs and pack sizes; the airport-wayfinding voice keeps translations legible at arm's length across a market counter.
translator-2.motif: The flight check: three round instrument lights — Voice, Text, Camera — stamped on every language pack like a pre-flight panel, each one lit green only after a real on-device test with the network off.

ia.coreObject: The verified pack: a downloaded language bundle whose voice, text, and camera capabilities carry proof-of-test stamps earned on this exact phone
ia.primaryLoop: Before the trip: download and flight-check the pack; on the trip: open straight into two-voice translation that works identically with zero bars, coming back every conversation, menu, and sign.

translator-4.territory: You are sitting in a pew or a lecture hall while someone speaks a language you are still learning, and the twin fears are falling behind and disturbing anyone. The interface answers with the calm of a well-set page: a feed that never stops listening, lets you scroll back without losing the live thread, and never asks to be touched at the wrong moment.

palette.note: A near-monochrome reading surface built for arm's-length legibility; teal appears only on the live edge, the marker that shows where the speaker is right now.

translator-4.typography: Atkinson Hyperlegible carries the translation feed, sized generously for reading a phone resting on a knee in a dim hall; Inter Tight handles timers and controls so they stay out of the text's way.
translator-4.motif: The live edge: a thin teal rule that rides the newest translated line, so when you scroll back through the feed the edge keeps moving without you and you always know exactly how far behind you are.

ia.coreObject: the session (one continuous hour of live speech, kept bilingually)
ia.primaryLoop: Every week, sit down where the language is spoken, press start once, read at your own pace, and leave with the full bilingual transcript.

translator-5.territory: The person is standing at a counter or an ER desk, phone out between two strangers, terrified of being cut off mid-sentence and misread. The interface answers with the calm of a walkie-talkie: nothing happens until your thumb says so, and both people can see whose turn it is. It feels like handing the conversation a steering wheel, not a microphone.

palette.note: Two voices, two inks: everything you say is set in teal, everything they say in warm amber #C97F1B, so ownership of every line is readable at arm's length across a counter.

translator-5.typography: Halyard Display for the oversized conversation text and Atkinson Hyperlegible for labels and history: type is sized for two people reading one phone from opposite sides, legibility doing the reassuring.
translator-5.motif: The hold ring: a thick teal ring around the push-to-talk button that fills clockwise for as long as the thumb stays down, freezing mid-arc on release, so every utterance leaves a visible fingerprint of how long someone held the floor.

ia.coreObject: The turn: one held utterance plus its translation, stamped with speaker color and hold duration
ia.primaryLoop: Open the saved pair for the person in front of you, hold to speak, release to let the translation play, repeat until the errand is done, and come back tomorrow because the same counters and the same mother-in-law are still there.

translator-7.territory: The person is mid-sentence with a client in Lisbon or their abuela in Mexico City, braced for the app to slide into the wrong country's Spanish and embarrass them. The interface answers with quiet certainty: your variant is visibly pinned on every screen, in every mode, so you never have to double-check it again. It feels like a tool that finally knows which language you actually speak, not just which box you ticked.

palette.note: The accent hue is owned by the active dialect (rosa for es-MX, cobalt for pt-PT, sky for es-AR) and paints only the variant ribbon and confirmations, so a color change would be instantly noticed as a variant change.

translator-7.typography: Fraunces for headings and translated output, chosen for its warm, confident diacritics that make tildes and accents feel like first-class citizens, with Inter for UI chrome and labels.
translator-7.motif: The dialect ribbon: a thin colored band pinned to the top edge of every single screen carrying the variant name ('Español · México'), so the promise 'it never slips' is literally always visible.

ia.coreObject: The dialect profile (variant + register + voice) that every mode reads from
ia.primaryLoop: Open, speak or type in your working pair, get variant-true text and audio back, and glance at the ribbon for the reassurance that keeps you from re-checking competitors.

translator-8.territory: The person is holding an official letter they cannot read, and behind the language barrier there may be a deadline, a fine, or a benefit. The interface answers like a calm clerk who handles paperwork all day: unhurried, structured, nothing lost, nothing cut off mid-paragraph. It should feel like the document was processed, not chatted about.

palette.note: Color behaves like ink on archival paper: the page stays neutral and quiet while stamp blue marks exactly one thing per screen — progress, the active paragraph, or the export action.

translator-8.typography: IBM Plex Serif for document text in both columns, echoing official correspondence, with IBM Plex Sans for controls and page numbers, so the app reads like a well-set dossier rather than a chat.
translator-8.motif: The gutter spine: a single vertical hairline running down the center of every document view, original on the left, translation on the right, paragraphs pinned to each other across it.

ia.coreObject: The document job: one file in, one aligned bilingual document out
ia.primaryLoop: A new piece of paperwork arrives by mail or email, the person imports it, reads the two-column result to understand what is being asked of them, and exports a clean PDF to keep or forward.

travel-planning-1.territory: The person is a gate agent's daughter sitting on a suitcase, or a first officer commuting home, refreshing loads at midnight before a standby run — hopeful, wired, and burned before by a fake zero. The interface answers with the operational calm of a crew room: departure-board clarity, numbers with a name and a track record attached, the quiet joy of watching your flight open up. It should feel like a colleague you trust leaning over and saying 'you'll get on.'

palette.note: Daylight-terminal white and crew navy carry everything; high-vis ramp orange is spent only on live load numbers and the free-refresh window, so fresh data glows like a vest on the tarmac.

travel-planning-1.typography: B612 — the typeface Airbus designed for cockpit displays — sets every flight number and seat count, with Circular for prose; the data literally wears aviation instrument type.
travel-planning-1.motif: The split-flap row: every load answer lives in a Solari-style split-flap line that physically flips when fresher data lands, so recency is something you see and hear rather than a timestamp you hunt for.

ia.coreObject: The query — one flight on one date, its open-seat count, and the verified colleague who answered it
ia.primaryLoop: List tomorrow's standby options in the evening, watch the flaps flip as verified colleagues answer overnight, and burn the free refreshes in the final 24 hours to pick which gate to actually show up at.

travel-planning-3.territory: Month four on the road: heat, a market stall, a queue forming behind you, and the constant low hum of 'are we still on budget or do we go home early'. The wanderlust-with-a-plan tone here is less airport departures board, more sun-bleached passbook in a money belt. The interface answers with five-second certainty at the register and one honest number for the day, so the trip's freedom rests on quiet bookkeeping instead of anxiety.

palette.note: Bougainvillea ink is the stamp color of money leaving, every logged expense and the day coin's spent arc carry it, while what remains today stays calm paper-and-ink so the eye reads 'left' as rest and 'spent' as record.

travel-planning-3.typography: National 2 Condensed sets amounts and the day coin's big figure like stencil markings on a shipping crate, while Untitled Sans keeps labels and country names as quiet as a customs form.
travel-planning-3.motif: The day coin: today's budget is one large struck coin that visibly wears down as you log, re-mints at local midnight, and gets re-struck with a new face and currency the moment you cross a border.

ia.coreObject: The travel day, one dated, country-stamped ledger page with a cap, a rollover and its expenses
ia.primaryLoop: At every register the traveler logs the amount in five seconds offline, glances at what's left on today's coin, and returns nightly to see the honest daily average hold or drift.

travel-planning-5.territory: The organizer of a nine-person bachelorette is drowning in three parallel group chats where the Airbnb vote died on message 214 and two people still haven't confirmed flights. The wanderlust tone here is pre-trip effervescence with an undertow of herding-cats fatigue. The interface answers as the calm HQ: bright, social, but structurally strict, every open question has a deadline and a place, so the fun stays fun and the logistics stop leaking.

palette.note: Pool-water teal marks everything decided and docked, while anything still open wears a sandy undecided beige, so one glance at the itinerary shows exactly how much of the trip is still liquid.

travel-planning-5.typography: Bricolage Grotesque gives trip names and day headers the energy of a well-made invitation, while Inter runs votes, tallies and money with the neutrality a shared wallet demands.
travel-planning-5.motif: The snap-in ballot: an open vote lives as a loose card hovering beside the itinerary, and the instant its deadline passes the winning option audibly docks into its day slot, turning teal, debate becomes plan.

ia.coreObject: The trip HQ, one shared object holding the day-by-day plan, its votes, threads, money and people
ia.primaryLoop: The organizer posts questions as deadline votes and expenses as receipts; everyone else votes, replies under the exact day, and checks what docked, coming back because the plan is the only source of truth.

travel-planning-6.territory: The user forwards a booking email and feels the old TripIt anxiety: did it land, did it parse, will it silently vanish. The interface answers with air-traffic-control calm: every message visibly accounted for, every status stamped, nothing in an unknown state. It should feel like a meticulous operations desk that happens to love travel, crisp and procedural rather than dreamy.

palette.note: Cool paper-white with deep aviation blue as the trust color, amber #C77800 strictly for needs-one-fix states and green #1F7A4D for parsed-and-added, so the inbox reads like a status board at a glance.

travel-planning-6.typography: Suisse Int'l for interface text with its neutral operational authority, and IBM Plex Mono for confirmation codes, flight numbers, and timestamps, echoing the boarding-pass ephemera the app digests.
travel-planning-6.motif: The status stamp: every forwarded email carries an inked, slightly rotated passport-style stamp (Added, Needs one fix, Waiting) so the parser's work is physically visible, never silent.

ia.coreObject: The forwarded booking email and its parse status
ia.primaryLoop: The traveler forwards every confirmation to their trip address the moment it arrives, checks the status board to see each one stamped and accounted for, and returns during the trip because the full itinerary and documents live offline on the phone.

travel-planning-8.territory: The user is a week from departure, tabs open on four eSIM sellers, each waving an identical suspiciously green coverage map. The interface answers with field-instrument skepticism: measured numbers from travelers who stood on that street, presented like lab results rather than ads. It should feel like a trusted testing bench, slightly nerdy, allergic to marketing.

palette.note: Neutral lab-white with measurement violet for tested data points and verdicts, while anything unverified or marketing-sourced is rendered in flat gray, making the difference between claim and measurement a color rule.

travel-planning-8.typography: Space Grotesk for headings with its instrument-panel character, and Inter with tabular numerals for the dense Mbps, ms, and $/GB tables that are the product's actual substance.
travel-planning-8.motif: The ping ribbon: every country and provider carries a horizontal strip of small dots, one per real traveler speed test, colored by measured speed, so density of evidence is visible before any ranking is trusted.

ia.coreObject: The speed test measurement (Mbps, latency, local carrier, city, eSIM provider)
ia.primaryLoop: Before each trip the traveler asks one question, what do I buy for this country, and during the trip a one-tap test both answers 'is my eSIM behaving' and feeds the map everyone relies on.

video-streaming-2.territory: Friday night, popcorn made, and the film you saved three weeks ago has vanished from the catalog again, that small theater-lights-up betrayal. The interface answers like a trusted usher in a dark house: posters glowing, and a discreet tap on the shoulder days in advance, this one leaves Sunday, watch it first.

video-streaming-2.typography: GT Super Display for titles and shelf headers, carrying old-cinema warmth, over Graphik for labels and metadata that stay out of the posters' way.
video-streaming-2.motif: The last reel: leaving titles wear a film-leader countdown ring over the poster corner, 6, 5, 4, that ticks down a number a day until departure.

video-streaming-4.territory: The user is settling in at night with ten shows in flight, carrying a quiet dread that years of watch history live on someone else's dying server. The interface answers with the reassurance of a private film archive: dark like a screening room, posters glowing, and the vault door visibly yours. Dark is earned here, this product is used in the dark next to a TV.

palette.note: Screening-room black that lets poster art carry the color, with projector-amber reserved for the act of punching an episode watched and for waiting-status glints, never for ads or upsells.

video-streaming-4.typography: Archivo Expanded for show titles with marquee presence, and Inter for episode metadata and stats, keeping the archive legible at couch distance in the dark.
video-streaming-4.motif: The perforation punch card: every season is a strip of film-perforation holes, one per episode, and marking an episode watched physically punches the hole, so a whole library reads like reels of punched film.

video-streaming-7.territory: The stream ended at 1 AM, the streamer is on the train the next morning knowing the four-hour VOD holds three great moments that will die there unless they get clipped today. The interface answers like a bright, fast control room: daylight-clean, chat data doing the finding, so clipping feels like skimming peaks, not scrubbing a timeline at midnight.

palette.note: A cool studio-gray shell keeps game footage and camera thumbnails as the color; the magenta accent traces only chat energy, spike peaks, selection handles and the publish action, so pink literally means 'the audience reacted here'.

video-streaming-7.typography: Space Grotesk for headers and counters with Inter for dense labels: technical, quick, production-tool crisp rather than gamer-aggressive.
video-streaming-7.motif: The hype seismograph: every VOD is worn like a mountain-range strip of chat messages-per-minute, and the whole app navigates by its peaks instead of by a timecode ruler.

voice-recorder-1.territory: The user is minutes from a conversation they dread, hands not quite steady, and the worst possible outcome is the phone making a sound. The interface answers with graphite stillness: dark, matte, nothing that glints, every signal readable in a glance with the phone held low at their side. Its job is to be certain so the person does not have to be.

palette.note: Nothing blinks and there is no pure red: recording is a steady amber dot at 40% brightness, and the only saturated color is the custody green tick meaning this minute is already safe somewhere else.

voice-recorder-1.typography: Inter with strong weight contrast for the interface, and IBM Plex Mono for evidentiary fields like DATE, SHA-256, and CONTINUITY, because the passport must read like a document, not a feature.
voice-recorder-1.motif: The custody line: an unbroken hairline running beneath the waveform that grows a green tick every sixty seconds as that minute lands off-device, and any gap in the line is shown, never smoothed over.

ia.coreObject: The sealed recording: audio plus its passport of time, checksum, and continuity
ia.primaryLoop: Before any difficult conversation, one silent press, a glance at the custody line filling with green ticks, then attention back on the human in front of them.

voice-recorder-2.territory: The person just left a meeting where half the words were drug names, case citations, or colleagues' surnames, and they dread the hour of cleanup waiting for them. The interface answers with recording-studio composure: a dark, quiet room where the waveform is the only thing lit, and every uncertain word is flagged instead of hidden. It feels like a sound engineer who admits what they did not catch.

palette.note: Warm VU-meter amber is reserved for live audio and confirmed dictionary hits; uncertainty is never colored, it is underlined, so the eye scans transcripts for dashes, not alarms.

voice-recorder-2.typography: IBM Plex Sans for the interface and IBM Plex Mono for transcripts and timestamps: the mono transcript reads like studio tape logs, and dictionary terms sit in it with the fixed-width certainty of typed evidence.
voice-recorder-2.motif: The confidence underline: every word the engine was unsure of carries a dashed amber underline that dissolves into a solid one the moment you confirm or correct it, so a transcript visibly settles from sketch to record.

ia.coreObject: The recording with its twice-passed transcript and the personal dictionary that corrected it
ia.primaryLoop: Record the meeting, skim the flagged words, fix or confirm each with one tap, and watch tomorrow's transcript arrive cleaner because the dictionary learned today's fixes.

voice-recorder-3.territory: You are sitting across from your grandmother with tea going cold, aware that this conversation is finite and terrified of a service losing it. The interface answers like an archive room with warm lamps: unhurried, permanent, everything labeled in a steady hand, the file always within your reach.

palette.note: Warm cream like album paper; the burnt-sienna amber is reserved for the waveform and the record button, so sound itself is the only vivid thing on the page.

voice-recorder-3.typography: Tiempos Text gives names and stories the weight of a printed family history, with small-caps archive labels in the same face, and dates set in old-style figures.
voice-recorder-3.motif: The index card: every recording is a cream card with its amber waveform pasted across it like a strip of magnetic tape, titled by hand with who, when, and what.

ia.coreObject: The recording card: an open-format audio file plus its who-when-what label and its three storage locations
ia.primaryLoop: Record a conversation or a prompted story, label the card while the voice is fresh, watch it land in all three places; families return for the next question on the list.

voice-recorder-6.territory: The reporter is mid-conversation, half listening and half hunting for the line that makes the story, terrified of losing it. The interface answers with recording-studio stillness: one glowing control, zero chrome, and the quiet certainty that every flagged second is already saved. Later, at the desk, it becomes a print shop where quotes are set in type only after they are proven word for word.

palette.note: Tape-machine red is reserved for the live record state and quote flags, everything else stays matte warm charcoal so the red always means one thing.

voice-recorder-6.typography: Söhne carries the interface in quiet medium weights, Tiempos Text sets every verbatim quote so a verified line reads like it already went to print.
voice-recorder-6.motif: The quote flag: a small red serif tick planted on the waveform at the exact moment a line was flagged, and the same tick reappears beside every verified quote in the export.

voice-recorder-7.territory: The author is mid-sentence in their head, walking or driving, terrified the thought will evaporate before it lands anywhere permanent. The interface answers like a patient manuscript page that is always open to the right spot: not a recorder with a big red button, but a growing book that quietly takes dictation and never spawns another orphaned file.

palette.note: Ivory paper and warm ink everywhere; the single sienna accent marks only living audio, the recording pulse and the playback strips in the margin, so sound is visibly woven into the page.

voice-recorder-7.typography: Lora for the manuscript body because the author must see their book as a book, with Space Mono for timestamps, word counts and session metadata like a typesetter's slug line.
voice-recorder-7.motif: The margin waveform: every dictated paragraph carries a slim sienna waveform strip in the left margin of the page, so the manuscript reads as text but remembers itself as voice.

ia.coreObject: The manuscript, one continuous document organized by chapter, where every paragraph keeps its source audio
ia.primaryLoop: Open the current chapter, dictate a section that lands at the end of the text, and come back tomorrow to a book that is visibly longer.

voice-recorder-8.territory: Ninety minutes into a two-hour lecture, the only anxiety that matters is whether the recording is still running. The interface answers like a studio engineer: dark, unblinking, one live waveform that visibly never stops, and it saves all the studying for after class.

palette.note: Matte warm charcoal keeps the screen invisible on a lecture desk; the record red stays lit the entire session as standing proof the take is alive.

voice-recorder-8.typography: IBM Plex Sans carries notes and questions with textbook plainness; IBM Plex Mono sets the elapsed timer and every timestamp, because the numbers a student stares at deserve fixed-width certainty.
voice-recorder-8.motif: The unbroken ribbon: one continuous waveform that scrolls the full length of the lecture without a single cut mark — the standing visual promise that nothing gets clipped.

ia.coreObject: the lecture (a full-length recording plus its study kit)

wardrobe-outfit-1.territory: It is a Sunday evening cataloging session: a pile of clothes on the bed, a phone in one hand, and the memory of the last app that silently mangled thirty cutouts. The mood is productive but wary. The interface answers like an atelier table under gallery light: white space, crisp garment photography, and a fitter's honesty that says 'this cut is off, let's redo it now' while the item is still in your hand.

palette.note: The page stays gallery-white so garments carry all the color, and crimson is spent only on the cut, the dashed pattern line, the reshoot flag, the fix brush, never on decoration.

wardrobe-outfit-1.typography: GT Sectra Display for closet headings and category titles, giving the catalog a fashion-editorial voice, with Suisse Int'l for counts, tags and verdicts.
wardrobe-outfit-1.motif: The pattern cut line: a fine crimson dashed outline traces every garment like a sewing-pattern piece, drawn solid and confident on clean cuts, visibly broken where the mask failed.

ia.coreObject: The item, one garment photo with its cut mask, verdict and tags, the brick every closet is built from
ia.primaryLoop: Dump a batch of photos in, clear the reshoot pile while the clothes are still out, and come back to a closet that finally matches the real one.

wardrobe-outfit-2.territory: It is Sunday evening and she wants Monday through Friday to already be decided, because 7:40 am is when decisions go to die. The interface answers with the unhurried air of a fashion editor laying out a week's spreads: warm paper, garments photographed flat, everything already hung in order. It feels like closing the closet door on the whole week at once.

palette.note: Clay accent marks only what the week's memory forbids or freezes: a worn-this-week badge, a laundry tag, a repeat warning; approved days stay in quiet ink on oat paper.

wardrobe-outfit-2.typography: GT Sectra Display for day names and the Sunday session headline, Untitled Sans for everything functional: the serif gives each day the presence of a magazine spread while the sans keeps swapping and freezing brisk.
wardrobe-outfit-2.motif: The seven-day rail: the whole week rendered as one horizontal garment rail with seven hangers, and every item that gets used slides a small clay wear-tag onto its hanger hook, so the no-repeat rule is something you can literally see hanging.

ia.coreObject: The week: seven outfits with a shared wear-memory that no single item may cross twice
ia.primaryLoop: One Sunday session builds the week, mornings are just getting dressed off the rail, and Saturday's empty rail pulls her back to plan again.

wardrobe-outfit-3.territory: She is standing in front of a full closet feeling like she owns nothing, and she has already been burned by stylist apps that answered her question with a shopping cart. The interface answers with the composure of a trusted atelier consultation: gallery-white calm, her own clothes treated as the entire universe, and every suggestion arriving with its reasoning written in the margin. It feels like advice from someone with nothing to sell.

palette.note: Deep forest green is the color of the stylist's own hand: it appears only in the margin notes, the honest-refusal card and the wardrobe-only seal, never as decorative chrome, so green literally means 'this is the advice'.

wardrobe-outfit-3.typography: Freight Text Pro for the stylist's explanations, set like editorial body copy, and Founders Grotesk for garments, chips and controls: the serif voice belongs to the stylist, the sans belongs to the closet.
wardrobe-outfit-3.motif: The margin note: every suggested outfit is laid out like a magazine plate with the stylist's reasoning handwritten-set in green in the outer margin, connected to specific garments by fine ruled lines, an annotation system no shopping app would ever ship.

ia.coreObject: The consultation: an occasion, three wardrobe-only outfits, and a written why for each
ia.primaryLoop: Ask what to wear for wherever today is going, read the three reasoned answers built strictly from her own closet, wear one, and return tomorrow because the question returns tomorrow.

wardrobe-outfit-4.territory: She is in a fitting room holding a jacket she half-loves, phone in the other hand, trying to remember whether the near-identical one is already hanging at home. The interface answers with the crisp neutrality of a garment label: white, numeric, verdict-fast, built for one decision made standing up in bad lighting. It feels like a second opinion from someone who has actually seen her closet.

palette.note: Cobalt is the verdict ink: the outfit count, the keep/leave stamp and the pairing lines are cobalt on white like an inspection tag, and nothing decorative competes with the number.

wardrobe-outfit-4.typography: GT America Mono carries every number, count and verdict like stamped tag data, with Graphik for garments and explanations: the mono digits make the three-outfit math feel measured, not vibes.
wardrobe-outfit-4.motif: The hang-tag: every scanned item gets its result rendered as a woven care-label tag punched with one big mono number, the count of outfits it unlocks, string and eyelet included, so the purchase decision literally hangs off the garment.

ia.coreObject: The check: one photographed item, its unlock count, its pairings, and its duplicates at home
ia.primaryLoop: Snap the item in hand, read the tag in ten seconds, keep or leave it on the number, and every avoided duplicate makes the next fitting-room check reflexive.

screens.title: Onboarding, step 1: this only works with your closet in
screens.purpose: Set the honest precondition: the math needs the catalog, so the catalog comes first.
screens.hero: An empty hang-tag with a question mark where the number should be

screens.purpose: Teach the single decision rule the whole product enforces.
screens.hero: Three small outfit plates stacked above a cobalt threshold line, a fourth fading below it

wardrobe-outfit-5.territory: Packing night, flight at 9 a.m., the bed already lost under maybes. water-hydration-3.territory: Mid-morning, second espresso in hand, the person wants a straight answer rather than a lecture: where am I actually at? The interface answers with glass-of-water clarity — cool light, honest arithmetic, and one line that shows the net after the coffee is subtracted.

palette.note: Everything sits in ice-white light; aqua fills only the net water line — negative drinks never turn red, they simply lower the water.

water-hydration-3.typography: DM Sans with tabular figures keeps every millilitre honest and columnar; the big net number is the only large type on any screen.
water-hydration-3.motif: The meniscus: the daily goal drawn as a tall glass cross-section whose water line rises by each drink's real contribution — an espresso barely lifts it, a whisky visibly pulls it down.

ia.coreObject: the drink entry (volume × its hydration coefficient)

water-hydration-8.territory: The user was told by a nephrologist to hit a number every day, and behind that number sits a kidney stone, a transplant, or a clot risk; this is compliance, not wellness. The interface answers with the quiet competence of a good clinic: white space, large legible figures, a ruled chart that looks trustworthy enough to hand across a desk to a doctor. No mascot ever appears, nothing ever celebrates, everything is retrievable years later.

palette.note: Clinical white with pale blue-grey chart panels; the single deep teal-blue marks logged volumes and the doctor's target line, and it is the only color on the screen because a record has no mood.

water-hydration-8.typography: Atkinson Hyperlegible throughout, chosen because it was designed for readers with low vision, with oversized tabular numerals so 2,140 ml is readable at arm's length by a seventy-year-old.
water-hydration-8.motif: The ruled fluid column: every day renders as a vertical hour-ruled chart column, like an inpatient fluid balance sheet, where each intake is a horizontal tick at its exact timestamp and gaps are visibly blank.

ia.coreObject: The day column: a timestamped, hour-ruled record of every milliliter against the doctor's number
ia.primaryLoop: Log each glass in two taps at the moment of drinking, glance at the column to see gaps against the doctor's target, and hand over a clean report at every appointment.
